`0.99997` identical across all four cells.

### Where it started

Campaign open, same game, same machine: **`fps_p50` 5.02** (cells TNFIXA1/A2,
5.22 and 4.81) and **`tick_rate` 23.7** (23.71 and 23.67).

**So: ~8x on frame rate and ~1.67x on tick rate.**

### THE WINDOW -- read this before comparing any two numbers here

**Whole-run `tick_rate` is judged at a 5000-tick window. The campaign-open
figures above were taken at 1000 ticks.** They are **different
measurements, not a worse and a better one.**

The operator lengthened the window deliberately, after arithmetic showed
**1000 ticks could not pass on any binary**: whole-run is
`N / (fixed + N/steady)`, so a fixed startup cost is diluted by window
length, and at 1000 ticks the fixed term dominates whatever the engine
does. The same 5000-tick window applies to **all three gates**, so they
are judged consistently.

**It was not re-tuned to reach the number.** The operator's standing
decision (2026-09-18) was to *attack the fixed startup cost rather than
lengthen the window to dilute it* -- "Gate 1 stays open until it closes on
merit". It closed on merit: the pre-loop fell from 3098 ms to ~716 ms.

### Caveats that travel WITH the claim, not as a footnote elsewhere

- **The light table is "never built", which is exact -- but not free.**
  `generate_light_table()` still costs **9 ms** per room load, installing
  the identity table and testing whether the room declares darkening.
  "Never built" must not be read as "costs nothing".
- **BENCH8 is our own authored content.** The darkening evidence behind
  patch 0117's safety property establishes **the code path and the
  fallback behaviour** -- it is **not** evidence about how shipped AGS
  games use darkening. The light-table work is also **8-bit only** by the
  `game.color_depth == 1` guard, and of six sourced shipped titles exactly
  one is 8-bit.

### The patch chain behind it, in order

| patch | what it did |
|---|---|
| **0096** | clock + pacer -- the fixed-timestep foundation |
| **0104** | palette-only present |
| **0106** | placeholder-room fade skip |
| **0108** | restart-point save left uncompressed |
| **0117** | light-table build skipped when nothing can darken |

**0113** (light-table reuse cache) is deliberately **not** in that chain:
it is the player-experience fix, and it was pre-registered to move the
gate by **zero** -- which it did. It is listed here so its absence is
understood as designed rather than as an omission.

### Why the number is trustworthy rather than lucky

The margin was **pre-registered before any cell ran**: predicted **39.53**,
measured **39.54**; predicted `preloop_ms` ~709, measured 716. The
pre-registration also stated that a crossing by far less than predicted
would mean the model was wrong *even though the gate passed*, and would be
reported rather than banked. It did not need to be.

## Gates 2 and 3: re-reading the plan's own definitions before designing anything

Two of the three things to confirm check out. **One does not, and it needs
an operator decision rather than my assumption.**

### CONFIRMED: same window, same both-figures rule

- **Both tick figures must pass** -- operator decision 2026-09-17,
  recorded in this file: `tick_rate_steady` at 40 +/- 2% **AND** whole-run
  `tick_rate` at 40 +/- 2%. Whole-run is "a second gate on
  startup/fade/room-transition stall cost, not only a diagnostic".
- **Same 5000-tick window for all three** -- "Whatever window is adopted
  applies equally to BENCH8's and AGS Quest's gate cells when their turn
  comes, so all three gates are judged consistently."

### NOT CONFIRMED: the plan does not define Gate 2 as 8-bit

**As written (2026-09-17): "Gate 2 -- moving on-screen content holding
40/40."** No colour depth is specified.

The operator decision recorded the same day goes the *other* way:

> "**Moving-content workload: AGS Quest's AutoPilot, now.** Known gap,
> stated up front: that makes Gates 2 and 3 **the same 16-bit fixture**;
> there is NO 8-bit moving-content fixture until the self-authored BENCH8
> game exists. 8-bit moving content is therefore **inferred, not
> measured**, until then."

And later, when BENCH8 landed: "Gate 2 for 8-bit **becomes measurable**
once it is merged."

**So the record says Gate 2 is moving content measured on AGS Quest, with
BENCH8 later making an 8-bit version *possible* -- not that Gate 2 *is*
the 8-bit fixture.** Treating Gate 2 as BENCH8 8-bit would resolve the
"known gap" of Gates 2 and 3 sharing one fixture, which is very likely the
intent, **but that resolution was never recorded as a decision.**

**Flagging rather than adopting.** The difference is not cosmetic: if
Gate 2 is BENCH8, it is judged on our own authored content at 320x200
8-bit; if it is AGS Quest's AutoPilot, it is 640x360 16-bit and largely
duplicates Gate 3. **Operator decision requested.** Baselines on BENCH8
`walk`/`anim` are being taken regardless, since they are needed either
way and no post-0117 hardware numbers exist for them.

### Gate 3: expect a different cost profile, and say so up front

**Last real numbers (AQ102 ABBA, 2026-09-17): `fps_p50` 11.00,
`tick_rate_steady` 40.13, whole-run `tick_rate` 14.53.**

**Most of this campaign's wins do not apply there, by construction:**

| patch | applies to AGS Quest (16-bit)? |
|---|---|
| 0096 clock + pacer | **yes** -- depth-independent |
| 0104 palette-only present | **no** -- an 8-bit DAC path |
| 0106 placeholder fade skip | yes -- startup, depth-independent |
| 0108 restart-point compression | yes -- startup, depth-independent |
| 0113 / 0117 light table | **no** -- guarded on `game.color_depth == 1` |

So the transferable set is **startup cost only**, which moves whole-run
and does nothing for `fps_p50`.

**And `fps_p50` is Gate 3's real problem, not startup.** It is 11.00
against a bar of 40 -- **a 3.6x shortfall in rendering throughput** on a
640x360x16 surface (460,800 bytes per frame against Trilby's 76,800).
Gate 1 was won by removing *fixed startup cost*; **nothing in that chain
addresses per-frame cost at four times the pixel volume and twice the
bytes per pixel.**

**Stated deliberately in advance: predicting Gate 3 from Gate 1's result
would be wrong.** Gate 1's margin came from deleting ~2.4 s of startup
work. Gate 3 needs roughly 3.6x more frames per second out of the same
CPU, which is a different kind of problem and may not be reachable at all
on this hardware without a change to what is rendered.

## Gate 2 BASELINE on the current binary (post-0117), HW-486-66, 2026-09-18

No post-0117 hardware numbers existed for BENCH8's moving-content scenes.
Taken now, `binary_sha12=ccdc4269a903`, `build_dirty=0`, `exit_code=0`,
zero criticals and warnings.

**At the gate's 5000-tick window:**

| scene | `fps_p50` | `tick_rate_steady` | whole-run | frames_skipped | |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `walk` | **40.00** | 40.02 | **39.24** | 30 | fps PASS, ticks pass (marginally) |
| `anim` (12 objects) | **14.99** | 40.04 | **39.23** | **3106** | **fps FAILS by 25** |

### What this says about Gate 2

**Gate 2 is purely an `fps_p50` problem, and specifically an `anim`
problem.** Both tick figures pass on both scenes. `walk` is already at the
frame-rate bar; `anim12` is at **37% of it**, dropping **3106 of 5000
frames**.

**The whole-run pass is MARGINAL and is not being claimed.** 39.24 and
39.23 clear 39.2 by 0.04 and 0.03 -- far inside known variance. The
restart-point write alone swings 188-604 ms (see the corrected 0108
figure), which is worth about 0.13 on whole-run by itself. **Two single
cells that clear a bar by 0.04 establish that the tick figures are
approximately at the line, not that they pass it.** A four-cell ABBA would
be needed to claim either.

### A methodology point Gate 2 cells must respect

**BENCH8 scenes run for `hold_ticks`, not for the gate window.** The
default `hold_ticks=1000` produces a 1040-tick run, and the same binary
reported whole-run **36.39/36.62** there against **39.24/39.23** at 5000
ticks.

**Same binary, same scene, a 2.8-point difference from window length
alone.** Any Gate 2 cell must set `hold_ticks=4960` for a 5000-tick run,
or its whole-run figure is not comparable to Gate 1's and not a gate
measurement at all.

### Where the fps problem is

`anim` animates 12 objects at delay 1 (a new frame every 2 ticks) over a
320x200x8 surface. Unlike Gate 1, **this is per-frame rendering
throughput, not fixed startup cost** -- none of the Gate 1 chain addresses
it, and `walk` (one moving character) shows the engine holds 40 fps when
the per-frame sprite work is small.

**Not yet investigated: whether 12 animating objects is a representative
workload or an artificial stress.** `objects=N` is a BENCH8 parameter with
a default of 4; 12 is its maximum. **What Gate 2 should be judged at is an
operator question**, and it materially changes the difficulty -- the
number of animating sprites is the whole variable here.

## Gate 2 definition, amended -- operator decisions 2026-09-18

### 1. Gate 2 is BENCH8 (8-bit, 320x200). This SUPERSEDES the AGS Quest stopgap.

**Not a reinterpretation of the 2026-09-17 decision -- a replacement of
it.** Both are kept so the change is legible.

*The original (2026-09-17):* "Moving-content workload: AGS Quest's
AutoPilot, **now** (it exists today and is fully scripted). Known gap,
stated up front: that makes Gates 2 and 3 **the same 16-bit fixture**;
there is NO 8-bit moving-content fixture until the self-authored BENCH8
game exists. 8-bit moving content is therefore **inferred, not measured**,
until then."

*Why it was made:* BENCH8 did not exist. The operator named the cost at
the time -- two gates on one fixture, and 8-bit moving content unmeasured.

*Why it is superseded:* **BENCH8 exists and resolves precisely the gap the
operator themselves flagged.** Gate 2 is now 8-bit moving content,
measured; Gate 3 remains AGS Quest at 16-bit. The two gates test different
colour depths and different cost profiles, which is what the original
decision wanted and could not have.

*Recorded because the ambiguity was real:* the plan's own wording said
"moving on-screen content" with no depth, and no decision had ever changed
what Gate 2 **is**. That was flagged rather than resolved by assuming the
likely intent.

### 2. Gate 2 is judged at 12 objects -- the hardest case, chosen knowingly

**Two things a future reader needs, recorded with the bar itself:**

- **12 is the maximum BENCH8 supports as authored** (`MAX_SPINNERS`,
  `objects=N`, default 4). **It is not a figure derived from real
  gameplay.** The bar is a **deliberate stress test**, so **failing it
  must not be read as "adventure games do not run"** -- it is the
  hardest case our own fixture can pose, not a typical load.
- **`objects=4` is kept as a recorded secondary datum** wherever it is
  cheap to take. Not a gate -- evidence. **The 4-vs-12 difference IS the
  per-sprite cost**, which is the number that will matter the moment
  optimisation starts.

### 3. STANDING RULE: every Gate 2 cell runs `hold_ticks=4960`

BENCH8 scenes run for `hold_ticks`, not for the gate window. Measured on
one binary, one scene: **36.39 at the default 1040-tick run against 39.24
at 5000 ticks.** A **2.8-point artefact of window length alone -- large
enough to pass or fail a gate by itself.**

**Enforced, not remembered** (see the harness guard below): the same
reasoning as the pre-build stamp check, which turned diagnosing a problem
after the fact into preventing it beforehand.

### Not banked

The marginal whole-run figures (39.24 and 39.23, single cells, 0.04 and
0.03 over the bar) are **at the line, not past it**. They need proper
four-cell ABBA treatment once `fps_p50` is in range.

## Gate 2 / `anim12` fps: what I expect to dominate, written BEFORE looking

`fps_p50` is 14.99 against 40, with 3106 of 5000 frames skipped. Stated
before reading the per-tick breakdown, so the check is real:

**Expected, most to least:**

1. **`scene_construct` dominates.** It is where each object's sprite is
   transformed and composited into the frame, so it is the term that
   scales with sprite count -- and sprite count is the only thing `anim12`
   changes relative to `walk`, which holds 40 fps. On Trilby's idle it was
   already the largest non-wait term (3.24 ms mean).
2. **`render_backbuffer`** second -- more changed pixels per frame means
   less of the present path can be skipped.
3. **`script_vm` small** -- BENCH8's AutoPilot does almost nothing per
   tick in `anim`; the spinners animate via the engine's own object
   animation, not script.
4. **`wait_next_frame` collapses toward zero.** At 14.99 fps the frame is
   already over budget, so there should be little idle left to wait out --
   and if it is NOT near zero, my model is wrong and the problem is
   pacing rather than throughput.

**The falsifiable part:** if `scene_construct` is not the largest real
term, the per-sprite hypothesis is wrong and Gate 2's fps problem is
something other than sprite compositing cost.

*Note the instrument already exists* -- `tickstats_*` from the earlier
tick-timing work covers all of this, so no new patch is needed to answer
it. **The 5000-tick `anim12` cell already taken (TNG2A5) contains the
answer**; this prediction is written before reading it.

## Gate 2 / `anim12`: the prediction was WRONG. It is the PRESENT path, not sprite work.

*Measured from the TNG2A5 cell (5000 ticks, 12 objects), against the
expectation written above it:*

| term | mean ms | total ms | share of frame time |
|---|---|---|---|
| **`render_to_screen`** | 44.29 | **83,885** | **67%** |
| -- `present_blit` | **28.54** | 53,112 | 42% |
| ---- **`fastblit_hreplicate`** | **18.16** | **33,799** | **27%** |
| ---- `fastblit_vmemcpy` | 8.29 | 15,431 | 12% |
| -- `present_update_window` | 9.46 | 17,600 | 14% |
| -- `present_dirty_check` | 4.53 | 8,582 | 7% |
| `scene_construct` | 8.72 | 16,522 | **13%** |
| `script_vm` | 0.64 | 6,371 | 5% |
| `render_backbuffer` | 1.77 | 3,349 | **3%** |

### Scoring my own prediction: wrong on the substance

| predicted | actual |
|---|---|
| `scene_construct` **dominates** | **13%** -- not dominant |
| `render_backbuffer` second | **3%**, near the bottom |
| `script_vm` small | correct, 5% |

**The falsifier I wrote down fired.** I said: "if `scene_construct` is not
the largest real term, the per-sprite hypothesis is wrong and Gate 2's fps
problem is something other than sprite compositing cost." It is not the
largest term, and the hypothesis was wrong.

### What it actually is, and why `walk` passes while `anim12` fails

**`present_blit` costs 28.54 ms, and it is IDENTICAL in both scenes** --
28.54 in `anim12` and 28.54 in `walk`, with `fastblit_hreplicate` at 18.16
in both. **It is a fixed cost per present, independent of sprite count.**

What differs is **how often it is paid**:

| scene | presents_real | presents_skipped | skipped | fps |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `walk` | 982 | 3988 | **80%** | 40.00 |
| `anim12` | 1861 | 33 | **2%** | 14.99 |

**`walk` reaches 40 fps only because the dirty-rect check skips four
presents in five.** `anim12` cannot skip -- twelve spinners change pixels
across the frame -- so it pays the fixed 28.54 ms on nearly every frame.

**The decisive arithmetic: 40 fps allows 25 ms per frame, and the present
path alone costs 28.54 ms. The present path exceeds the entire 40 fps
budget before any game work happens at all.** A frame that must present
therefore cannot hit 40 fps on this machine by any amount of sprite
optimisation.

**So the sprite count was a red herring in the way I framed it.** It is
real, but it acts by controlling *how often a present can be skipped* --
not by making each frame's compositing expensive. Optimising sprite
compositing would move 13% and leave the gate unreachable.

### The target

**`fastblit_hreplicate` -- 18.16 ms, 27% of all frame time, and the single
largest term.** It is the horizontal pixel-doubling that turns the
320x200 surface into the 640x400 display mode. `fastblit_vmemcpy` (8.29 ms)
is the copy that follows it.

**Not yet investigated, and not to be assumed:** whether the replication
can be avoided (a real 320x200 mode on the Mach64), made cheaper, or
folded into the copy so the pixels are only touched once. **That is the
next thing to read from source -- measurement first picked the target, and
the same discipline applies to the fix.**

## Gate 2 at Mode 13h: the replication is GONE, and it is still not enough

One cell, TNG2M13, `binary_sha12=ccdc4269a903`, `build_dirty=0`,
`--gate` enforced (5000-tick window), `exit_code=0`, no criticals or
warnings. Only change from the baseline: `fullscreen = native` instead of
`full_window`.

| | full_window (baseline) | **Mode 13h** | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `fastblit_hreplicate` | 18.16 ms | **0.00 ms** | **eliminated** |
| `present_blit` | 28.54 ms | **4.17 ms** | **-85%** |
| `scene_construct` | 8.72 ms | 7.01 ms | -- |
| `fps_p50` | 14.99 | **38.87** | +23.9 |
| `tick_rate_steady` | 40.04 | 40.10 | pass |
| whole-run `tick_rate` | 39.23 | **38.94** | **FAIL** |

**The mechanism is confirmed exactly: `fastblit_hreplicate` goes to zero,
because Mode 13h is a true 320x200 mode and there is nothing to
replicate.** `present_blit` falls from 28.54 ms to 4.17 ms.

### But Gate 2 does NOT pass at 12 objects

**`fps_p50` 38.87 against a bar of 40, and whole-run `tick_rate` 38.94
against 39.2. Both short.** `tick_rate_steady` passes at 40.10.

The present path is no longer the constraint -- at 4.17 ms it is
comfortably inside budget. What remains is ordinary per-frame work:
`render_to_screen` 13.79 ms plus `scene_construct` 7.01 ms puts the frame
at roughly 25.7 ms against a 25.0 ms budget. **About 0.7 ms per frame
short.** That is now a sprite-work problem -- which is what I originally
and wrongly predicted the *present-bound* case to be.

### A discrepancy with the bake-off that I am NOT waving away

The presentation bake-off recorded Mode 13h on this same scene at
**`fps_p50` 40.00 with a 7.84 ms present**. This cell measures a **faster
present (4.17 ms) but a LOWER fps (38.87)**.

**Faster present, slower frame rate -- those cannot both be improvements,
so something else differs.** Candidates, none yet checked: a different
binary (many patches have landed since), a different window (this cell is
5000 ticks under `--gate`; the bake-off's length is unrecorded here), or a
different `objects` count. **Flagged as an open discrepancy to explain
before either number is relied on.**

### `presents_real` -- the metric is rewarding NOT displaying frames

**`fps_p50` counts render passes, not presents**, and on this fixture the
gap is large enough to invert the ranking:

| cell | `fps_p50` | render_passes | **presents_real** | actually displayed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `walk`, full_window | **40.00** | 4970 | **982** | **~7.9 / s** |
| `anim12`, full_window | 14.99 | 1894 | 1861 | ~14.8 / s |
| `anim12`, **Mode 13h** | **38.87** | 4817 | **2474** | **~19.6 / s** |

**`walk` scores a perfect 40.00 while displaying under 8 frames a second.
`anim12` at full_window scores 14.99 while displaying nearly twice as
many.** The scene doing more visible work scores worse.

**So "38.87 fps" at Mode 13h means 38.87 render passes per second and
about 19.6 displayed frames per second** -- half its render passes skip
the present. It is genuinely the best of the three by displayed frames,
but **the gate figure and the visible result are different quantities**,
and a pass achieved by skipping is not the same result as a pass achieved
by displaying. **Stated before any Gate 2 pass is claimed.**

### Implication for the DEFERRED presentation default -- reported, not acted on

The operator deferred the presentation default pending the
direct-framebuffer work, when the three fast rungs were tied at 40.00.
**They are no longer tied on this fixture: Mode 13h turns `anim12` from
14.99 into 38.87.** That is new evidence for the deferred decision.

**Not changing the default.** That is the operator's call, and this is
reported as evidence for it rather than folded into a gate result.

### Mode 13h secondary datum: `objects=4`, and the per-sprite cost

Cell TNG2M4, same binary, same gate window, `--gate` enforced.

| | Mode 13h, **4 objects** | Mode 13h, **12 objects** |
|---|---|---|
| `fps_p50` | **40.00** (PASS) | 38.87 (fail) |
| `tick_rate_steady` | 40.15 (pass) | 40.10 (pass) |
| whole-run `tick_rate` | **39.06 (FAIL)** | **38.94 (FAIL)** |
| `scene_construct` | 4.33 ms | 7.01 ms |
| `present_blit` | 4.17 ms | 4.17 ms |
| `presents_real` | **2474** | **2474** |

**Per-sprite cost, the number the operator asked to keep: `scene_construct`
goes 4.33 -> 7.01 ms for 4 -> 12 objects, so ~2.68 ms for 8 sprites =
about 0.335 ms per animating sprite.** Extrapolating back, the fixed part
of `scene_construct` is roughly 3.0 ms and each sprite adds a third of a
millisecond.

### Two findings that complicate the Mode 13h picture

**1. Whole-run FAILS at Mode 13h even at 4 objects -- and it PASSED at
full_window.**

| | whole-run | stall_ticks | stall_ms |
|---|---|---|---|
| full_window, 12 obj | **39.23** | 2 | 898 |
| Mode 13h, 12 obj | 38.94 | **4** | **1596** |
| Mode 13h, 4 obj | 39.06 | **4** | **1342** |

**Mode 13h roughly doubles the stall time and the stall-tick count.** That
is why whole-run gets *worse* while `fps_p50` gets dramatically better.
**So Mode 13h is not a strict improvement on the gate's terms** -- it
trades a large fps gain for a small whole-run regression, and the gate
requires both. Cause not investigated; the mode set itself is the obvious
suspect but that is a guess, not a finding.

**2. `presents_real` is 2474 in BOTH Mode 13h cells -- identical.**

Two different workloads (4 and 12 animating sprites), different render-pass
counts (4973 and 4817), and **exactly the same number of presents.** That
is not what dirty-rect-driven skipping would produce; it looks like a
**fixed cadence of roughly one present per two render passes** (~19.6
presents/s in both). **Flagged, not explained.** It matters because it
means the displayed frame rate at Mode 13h is ~19.6/s regardless of how
much changes on screen, and because an instrument that returns the same
number for two different workloads deserves suspicion before it is relied
on -- the same reasoning as the clock cross-check that read identically
across cells.

### Gate 2 status

**Not passed at either object count.** At 12 objects both `fps_p50` and
whole-run fail; at 4 objects `fps_p50` passes and whole-run still fails.
**The gate requires both figures, so Mode 13h alone does not close Gate 2
even at the easier object count.**

## The four Gate 2 measurement questions, answered (2026-09-18)

### 1. The 2474 is NOT an instrument artefact -- it is the content's own rate

**`anim12` generates exactly 20 distinct frames per second.** From our own
fixture's source: `AutoPilot.asc:238` is
`o.Animate(0, 1, eRepeat, eNoBlock, eForwards)`, and
`ac/roomobject.cpp:103` sets `wait = vfptr->speed + overall_speed` with
`:89` `if (wait>0) { wait--; return; }` -- so delay 1 advances a frame
every **2** ticks, i.e. **20 frames/s at 40 ticks/s.**

Measured `presents_real` at Mode 13h: **2474 over 126.2 s = 19.6/s**, and
2474 over 125.8 s = 19.7/s in the 4-object cell.

**So the skip decision IS content-driven and the dirty check is working
correctly.** The two cells report the same number because **all spinners
animate at the same delay and therefore change on the same ticks** -- the
count of *changed frames* is 20/s whether 4 sprites change or 12. The
suspicion was reasonable and the check was right to make; the instrument
is sound.

**The consequence is larger than the question:** at Mode 13h `anim12`
displays **19.6 of a possible 20 frames per second -- about 98% of the
ceiling this content can produce.** At full_window it managed only
14.8/s, i.e. genuinely present-bound below the content rate. **Mode 13h
does not merely speed up the present; it removes the present as a
constraint entirely for this fixture.**

### 4. Therefore a 40-fps DISPLAYED bar is unreachable by construction here

**`anim12` can never display more than 20 distinct frames/s**, because
that is all it generates. `fps_p50` counts render passes, so the engine
can score 40 by rendering 40 passes/s while only 20 can ever differ.

**Stated plainly, as asked: the 12-object bar needs rethinking regardless
of how fast the port gets** -- if "40 fps" is meant as displayed frames,
this fixture cannot reach it at any speed, and the limit is a property of
our own authored content, not of the port.

### 2. The bake-off "discrepancy" was two different metrics -- and underneath it is a REGRESSION

**There was never a present discrepancy.** The hub's "7.84 ms present" is
`present_update_window`, which BKAAN reports as exactly 7.84 -- a
*different term* from my `present_blit`. On `present_blit` the two runs
agree: **4.22 (bake-off) vs 4.17/4.22 (mine).**

`objects=12` is confirmed in the bake-off's own log
(`AUTOPILOT config scene=anim hold_ticks=1000 objects=12`), so my
objects=4 hypothesis was **wrong**.

**The fps difference is real and it is a regression.** Re-run at the
bake-off's exact 1040-tick window, same mode, same object count:

| | bake-off `9279767270b5` | current `ccdc4269a903` |
|---|---|---|
| `fps_p50` | **40.00** | **38.96** |
| `present_blit` | 4.22 | 4.22 |
| `game_tick_outer` | 25.85 | **27.24** |
| `render_to_screen` | 13.02 | **14.04** |
| `present_dirty_check` | 4.74 | **5.45** |
| `scene_construct` | 6.86 | 7.03 |

**About +1.4 ms per tick, spread across several unrelated terms rather
than concentrated in one** -- which is not the signature of a single patch
adding work. Not attributable from this data; it would need bisection.

**This matters because it is currently the whole difference between
passing and failing.** At the bake-off, `anim12` at Mode 13h **passed**
the fps bar at 40.00. On today's binary it does not.

### 3. The Mode 13h stall regression is BOTH one-off and recurring

Stall indices are logged individually:

| cell | stalls |
|---|---|
| Trilby (Gate 1) | `index=1 ms=497` -- startup only |
| `anim12` full_window | `index=1 ms=587`, `index=2671 ms=310` |
| **`anim12` Mode 13h** | `index=1 ms=768`, **`603 ms=277`, `1807 ms=277`, `2811 ms=272`** |
| **`anim4` Mode 13h** | `index=1 ms=529`, **`603 ms=270`, `1807 ms=273`, `4811 ms=268`** |

**Both, and the recurring part is the important half.** The startup stall
is larger at Mode 13h (768/529 against 587) -- a one-off mode-set cost,
and noisy between runs. But there are also **recurring ~270-280 ms stalls,
and Mode 13h has roughly 2.7x more recurring stall time than full_window**
(826 ms against 310 ms).

**They are deterministic: ticks 603 and 1807 appear in BOTH Mode 13h
cells, at both object counts.** Same indices, different workloads. Cause
unknown -- not the mode set, since these are thousands of ticks into the
run. **That is the thing to find before Mode 13h is recommended as a
default**, and it is a real recurring cost, not an artefact of paying for
the mode transition once.

## Two investigations: the instrumentation hypothesis is REFUTED, the stalls are still unexplained

### The +1.4 ms regression is REAL, not our instrumentation

The hypothesis -- that the diffuse spread across unrelated terms is the
signature of bracket overhead rather than a patch adding work -- was a good
fit for the shape of the evidence. **It is refuted on three independent
grounds.**

**1. The arithmetic falls four times short.** Counting every bracketed call
in the cell: **34,704 bracket entries over 1040 ticks = 33.4 per tick.** At
the measured ~11 us per bracket that is **0.367 ms/tick**, against a
measured regression of **1.4 ms/tick**. Checked before accepting the
hypothesis, as instructed -- and it does not reach.

**2. The bake-off binary has the IDENTICAL bracket set.** Both binaries
report **36 `tickstats_*` types**, and the set difference is **empty** --
**zero brackets were added between them.** So per-tick bracket overhead
cannot differ at all, let alone by 1.4 ms.

**3. Everything instrumented since is OFF the per-tick path.** 0109 brackets
room loads, 0110 the pre-loop, 0112 per light-table call -- none per tick.
0114's counters sit in `TransBlendBlt`/`LitBlendBlt`, and this cell reports
**`colormap_consumers transblend=0 litblend=0`**: they execute **zero
times**.

**So the regression is genuine and needs bisection.** The consequence the
hypothesis would have had -- that every gate figure in this campaign is
systematically pessimistic by ~1.4 ms/tick -- **does not follow**, because
the instrumentation is the same on both sides of the comparison. Gate 1's
numbers are unaffected by this.

### The 603/1807 stalls: two hypotheses tested, both wrong

**Not scripted events.** `AUTOPLT.LOG` for the cell shows the `anim` phase
running unbroken from tick 0 to 4960 -- **no phase boundary or scripted
action at 603, 1807 or 2811.** The fixture does nothing at those ticks.

**Not log-flush stalls to the CF card.** `STDOUT.TXT` is 9,456 bytes in the
Mode 13h cell (4 stalls) and **9,466 bytes in the full_window cell (2
stalls)** -- **more bytes, fewer stalls.** The hypothesis predicts the
opposite.

**Still unexplained, and the facts to explain are:** deterministic
(603 and 1807 identical across both object counts), Mode-13h-only,
thousands of ticks into the run so not the mode set, ~270-280 ms each, and
independent of sprite count.

**Next step is a targeted instrument rather than more hypotheses** -- log
what the engine is inside when a tick exceeds the stall threshold. Guessing
has now cost two wrong hypotheses; the campaign's own pattern says measure.

### Correction for the hub's bake-off entry: two distinct metrics, not one

`present_blit` and `present_update_window` are **different things** and the
hub's table conflates them. Both, per rung:

| rung | `present_blit` | `present_update_window` | `fps_p50` |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Mode 13h** | **4.22** | **7.84** | 40.00 |
| 512x384 centred | 4.22 | 15.95 | 26.89 |
| 640x480 centred 1x | 4.23 | 21.60 | 19.72 |
| 640x480 2x | **28.22** | **24.31** | 11.83 |

**The 7.84 figure the hub records as "present" for Mode 13h is
`present_update_window`.** My 4.17/4.22 is `present_blit`. There was never
a disagreement between the two runs.

**A cleaner reading falls out of seeing both columns:** `present_blit` is
**4.22 for the first three rungs** and only explodes at 640x480 2x, because
**only that rung does horizontal replication**. What separates the first
three from each other is entirely `present_update_window` -- 7.84 -> 15.95
-> 21.60 -- the push to the display, scaling with output pixel count. **So
"the blit is the cost" is only true of the 2x rung; for the others the cost
is the surface update, and it is proportional to output resolution.**

## Reusable: "is our instrumentation contaminating the gate figures?"

This will be asked again on the ViRGE and Cirrus rounds. **The cheap
answer is a set comparison, not an arithmetic estimate.**

**Systematic pessimism requires the instrumentation to DIFFER across the
compared pair.** If both binaries carry the same brackets, bracket cost
cancels in the comparison -- however large it is. So the check is:

```
comm -13 <(grep -ho "tickstats_[a-z_0-9]*" A/*.LOG | sort -u) \
         <(grep -ho "tickstats_[a-z_0-9]*" B/*.LOG | sort -u)
```

**An empty difference settles it with no estimate of per-bracket cost
required.** That is stronger than the arithmetic route, which needs a
per-bracket figure that is itself measured and arguable.

*Applied here:* both binaries report 36 `tickstats_*` types, difference
empty, so the +1.4 ms regression cannot be bracket overhead and **Gate 1's
figures are unaffected**. The arithmetic agreed (0.367 ms/tick against
1.4 ms) but was the weaker of the two checks.

**Caveat the set check does not cover:** instrumentation that is *not* a
`tickstats_*` bracket -- a counter, a log line, a hook. Those have to be
argued separately by where they sit. Here: 0109/0110/0112 are off the
per-tick path, and 0114's counters measured **zero executions** in the
cell.

## Gate 2 -- REDEFINED by operator decision, 2026-09-18. TWO bars, both must pass.

| bar | threshold | what it proves |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Render throughput** | `fps_p50` >= **40** render passes/s | the engine keeps up with 40 Hz logic |
| **2. Display completeness** | >= **95%** of the distinct frames the content generates | the port actually SHOWS them |

*Why two.* `fps_p50` alone lets a cell score a perfect 40.00 while
displaying under 8 frames a second -- **the `walk` cell does exactly
that.** And a 40-*displayed*-frames bar is unreachable for a fixture that
authors only 20 by design. **One bar is gameable from each end; two close
the loophole from both.**

*On this definition, completeness is what separates the presentation
rungs* -- and it is the distinction the single number was hiding:

| | `fps_p50` | displayed/s | content/s | **completeness** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mode 13h, 12 obj | 38.87 | 19.6 | 20 | **98%** PASS |
| full_window, 12 obj | 14.99 | 14.8 | 20 | **74%** FAIL |
| `walk`, full_window | 40.00 | 7.9 | -- | (content rate not yet measured) |

**Gate 2 status under the new definition: bar 2 PASSES at Mode 13h (98%),
bar 1 FAILS (38.87 against 40) -- and bar 1's shortfall is entirely the
unexplained regression**, since the same fixture and mode scored 40.00 on
the bake-off binary.

### Measuring completeness: the cheap way now, the general way next

**Now, for BENCH8 only:** the content rate is known *analytically* --
`Animate(0, 1, ...)` is a new frame every 2 ticks, so **20 distinct
frames/s by authorship**. Completeness = `presents_per_sec / 20`, scoreable
today with no new code.

**That is fixture-specific and useless for Gate 3 or for real games on the
ViRGE/Cirrus rounds.** The general instrument is **a count of ticks on
which the scene content actually changed, independent of whether a present
occurred**; completeness is then `presents / content-dirty-ticks`.

**The trap, recorded before building it: if the counter is derived from the
same dirty check that gates the present, it reads 100% by construction and
measures nothing.** It has to count content change **at the point the
content changes**, upstream of any coalescing or skip decision. That is
the same class of error as an instrument that returns the same number for
two different workloads -- it looks like a measurement and is a tautology.

## Regression BISECTED: it is patch 0104 -- one of Gate 1's own chain

Mode 13h, `anim12`, 1040-tick window (the bake-off's), same fixture and
config throughout:

| binary | `fps_p50` | `present_dirty_check` | `present_blit` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0102 (bake-off) | **40.00** | 4.74 | 4.22 |
| **0103** | **40.12** | 4.86 | 4.23 |
| **0104** | **38.91** | **5.46** | 4.22 |
| 0118 (current) | 38.96 | 5.45 | 4.22 |

**Patch 0104 is the regression, and essentially all of it lands at once**
-- 0118 is no worse than 0104, so nothing since has added to it.

**The cost is localised: `present_dirty_check` +0.60 ms per render pass**,
with `present_blit` (4.23 -> 4.22) and `present_sync_palette` (0.28 -> 0.28)
unchanged. `render_to_screen` rises 13.24 -> 13.77, consistent.

### What 0104 changed there

```
- const bool unchanged = same_geometry && !palette_changed &&
-                        FramesEqualFast(...);
+ const bool pixels_same = same_geometry && FramesEqualFast(...);
+ if (pixels_same && !palette_changed)
```

**The cheap test moved from BEFORE the expensive one to after it.** In
0103 `!palette_changed` could short-circuit the full-frame comparison away;
in 0104 `FramesEqualFast` runs whenever the geometry matches. A 64,000-byte
frame comparison is ~0.6 ms at this machine's memory bandwidth -- **the
right order of magnitude for the measured delta.**

**Stated as the limit of what is measured:** the magnitude matches and the
ordering change is real, but `presents_palette_only=0` in these cells,
which does not obviously fit a story where `palette_changed` is true often
enough to have short-circuited. **The exact path needs one targeted
measurement -- a count of `FramesEqualFast` calls in each arm -- and I am
not guessing past the bisect.** What is established: **0104, +0.60 ms in
`present_dirty_check`, nothing before it and nothing after it.**

### Why this matters beyond Gate 2

**Patch 0104 is in Gate 1's claimed chain.** It won the palette-only
present that Trilby's idle benchmark needed. **The same patch costs
~1.2 fps on 8-bit moving content at Mode 13h.**

**So it is not a regression to revert -- it is a trade between fixtures**,
and it was invisible until Gate 2 had a moving-content fixture to measure
on, which is exactly the gap the original Gate 2 decision named. Gate 1's
numbers are not affected: they were measured with 0104 present, on a
fixture where it helps.

**The fix should preserve both** -- keep the palette-only present where it
pays and restore the short-circuit where it does not -- rather than
choosing one fixture over the other. Not designed yet; the targeted
measurement comes first.

## Patch 0104's cost: BOTH hypotheses disproven. Cause still unidentified.

**Your case analysis was right and my attempted rescue of it also fails.**

*The reorder hypothesis (mine):* 0104 moved `FramesEqualFast()` ahead of
the `!palette_changed` test, so it could only cost anything on passes where
`palette_changed` is **true while the frames differ** -- the one branch the
original case analysis did not cover, and which `presents_palette_only=0`
does not rule out.

**Measured, with a probe on `palette_changed` itself:
`palchg true=2 of 1000`.** It is false essentially always. So 0103's
`!palette_changed` was true, `FramesEqualFast` ran in both arms, and **the
reorder is free.** Hypothesis dead.

*The heuristic-replacement hypothesis (coordinator's):* that making
palette-only presents correct required replacing a sampled/checksum
comparison with an exact one. **`FramesEqualFast` does not appear as a
changed line anywhere in patch 0104 -- the function is untouched.**
Hypothesis dead.

*What 0104 actually changes, in full:* a `bool` declaration; the
`unchanged` condition split into `pixels_same` plus a separate
`palette_changed` test; the frame memcpy moved into an `else` (same
execution for a changed frame); an `if (palette_only_present)` branch
around the push; and a 1x1 `dac_rect` built only on the palette-only path.
**None of that plausibly costs 0.60 ms per pass.**

### Where that leaves it, honestly

**The bisect stands -- 0104 is where fps drops, reproducibly (0103 40.12,
0104 38.91, 0118 38.96).** What is NOT established is why.

**One possibility worth testing before assuming a large hidden cost:** at
Mode 13h the engine sits right at the 40 fps cap. 0103 makes the frame
budget and 0104 misses it. **A small real cost can produce a
disproportionate fps drop by tipping a frame over the 25 ms line**, so the
underlying cost may be much less than 1.2 fps suggests -- and
`present_dirty_check`'s +0.60 ms may be partly attribution drift if the
bracket now encloses slightly different code.

**Not guessing further.** Three hypotheses have now died here (two on this
question, plus the stall hypotheses), and each died to a cheap measurement.
The next step is a targeted A/B of the remaining pieces of the 0104 diff,
not a fourth story.

**Process note worth keeping: `presents_palette_only=0` was used by both of
us as evidence about `palette_changed`, and it is not.** It reports the
conjunction "frames equal AND palette changed". Reasoning from a
conjunction counter to one of its conjuncts is unsound, and it took a
direct probe on the conjunct itself to settle a question two people had
already reasoned about confidently.

## NAMED RULE: never reason from a conjunction counter to one of its conjuncts

`presents_palette_only` counts **"frames equal AND palette changed"**. Both
coordinator and fork reasoned from it to a claim about `palette_changed`
alone -- **in opposite directions, and both wrong.** One asserted a
conjunct was false; the other argued a branch was still open. **Neither is
derivable from a conjunction counter.**

A zero conjunction tells you the two conditions never held *together*. It
says nothing about how often either holds *separately*. It took a direct
probe on the conjunct (`palchg true=2 of 1000`) to settle a question two
people had already reasoned about confidently and incorrectly.

**Rule: if a counter's name contains an "and", it cannot be evidence about
either half. Probe the half you care about.**

## Codegen investigation on patch 0104: no smoking gun -- and it invalidates the magnitude argument

Compiled `ali3dsw.cpp` to assembly at both revisions with the build's own
flags and extracted `Present()`:

| | instructions in `Present()` |
|---|---|
| 0103 | 2937 |
| 0104 | **2969** |

**+32 instructions.** The disassembly differs widely by register
allocation and scheduling, but there is **no structural bloat, no
un-inlined call, and no new loop**: `FramesEqualFast` is inlined in both,
neither calls `memcmp`, and both contain exactly one `rep movsl` (the cache
memcpy).

**32 extra instructions of straight-line code cannot cost 0.6 ms.** On a
66 MHz 486 that is ~40,000 cycles. It could only matter inside a loop
running tens of thousands of iterations -- and the loop structure is
unchanged.

### The correction that matters: FramesEqualFast EARLY-EXITS

```c
for (size_t i = 0; i < nwords; i++)
    if (wa[i] != wb[i]) return false;
```

**It returns on the first differing dword.** On `anim12` the frames always
differ, so **the comparison never scans the full 64,000 bytes** -- it stops
at the first changed pixel. The spinners' top row is at y=54 of 200, so a
row-major scan reaches a difference about 27% in: **~17 KB, roughly
0.15 ms, not 0.60 ms.**

**So the "64,000 bytes at ~107 MB/s = 0.60 ms" arithmetic that made both
hypotheses look plausible was never applicable to this fixture.** It
described a full scan that does not happen here. Both of us used that
number to judge magnitude; it was the wrong number.

### Where this leaves patch 0104

**The bisect stands. The cause is still unidentified, and I am not
offering a fifth hypothesis.**

Four have now died to cheap measurements: the reorder (killed by
`palchg 2/1000`), heuristic-replacement (killed by the function being
untouched), the tipping point (killed by the arithmetic being proportional,
not amplified), and codegen bloat (killed by +32 instructions with
unchanged loop structure).

**Next step is direct measurement, not inference: bracket the
`FramesEqualFast` call itself and build it into BOTH arms**, so the
comparison's actual cost is measured in each rather than reasoned about.
That is the instrument that should have been reached for two hypotheses
ago -- every one of the four died to a measurement, and none needed the
story that preceded it.

## Direct measurement of FramesEqualFast and the memcpy -- and a problem with the bisect

**Instrumented rather than argued.** `FramesEqualFast` is byte-identical
in 0103 and 0104, so the probe is literally the same code in both arms.
Split by outcome, because an equal frame scans all 64,000 bytes to prove it
while a differing frame early-exits -- one mean over both would describe
neither population (the same error shape as the conjunction counter).

| arm | equal-frame | differing | memcpy calls |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0103 | **5.38 ms** x504 | 0.85 ms x496 | **498** |
| 0104 | **5.67 ms** x503 | 0.90 ms x497 | **498** |

### Three findings

**1. The coordinator's correction was right and my claim was wrong.**
Frames are equal on about half the passes -- 504 of 1000 here -- exactly as
the content rate predicts. **"On anim12 the frames always differ" was
contradicted by `presents_skipped=2343` in the very cell I was quoting.**

**2. The magnitude was wrong by an order of magnitude, in the other
direction.** The equal-frame full scan costs **5.38 ms, not 0.60 ms** --
64,000 bytes at **11.9 MB/s**, because it is a dword compare loop with a
branch per word, not a `rep movs`. **Both of us calibrated against memcpy
bandwidth for a comparison loop.** The 0.60 ms figure was never the right
yardstick for either hypothesis it was used to support.

**3. The memcpy hypothesis is REFUTED by direct measurement: 498 calls in
both arms.** Its execution frequency is identical, so its relocation into
an `else` costs nothing. That was the one item in the 0104 diff whose
frequency could differ, and it does not.

### The problem: `fps_p50` near the cap is noisier than the effect being chased

| binary | unprobed | probed |
|---|---|---|
| 0103 | 40.12 | 40.00 |
| **0104** | **38.91** | **39.84** |

**Probed 0104 reads 0.93 FASTER than unprobed 0104** -- with strictly more
work in it. That cannot be a real improvement, so **`fps_p50` at the 40 cap
carries at least ~1 fps of run-to-run or build-to-build variation -- which
is the same size as the 1.21 fps bisect delta being chased.**

**Consequence, stated plainly: the bisect result is not safe.** "0103 40.12,
0104 38.91" looked clean and reproducible, and 0118 agreed at 38.96 -- but a
single perturbation of the same binary moved it 0.93 in the wrong
direction. **Before anything is concluded about patch 0104, the bisect needs
repeat cells per arm to establish whether the 1.21 gap survives replication
at all.** It may be a real effect; it is currently indistinguishable from
one.

**What IS solid**: the equal-frame scan costs 5.38 ms and runs ~20x/s
(~108 ms/s, ~8.6% of a 1.25 s budget per second). That is a large, real,
previously unmeasured cost **present in both arms** -- and a much better
optimisation target than a 1.21 fps difference that may not be real.

## METHOD FAILURE: we had the A-to-A rule and did not apply it

`shared/skills/dos-hardware-validation/references/abba-methodology.md`
**mandates an A-to-A spread check** before any A/B delta is trusted --
precisely to catch an unstable target. **That file has been cited all
campaign. It was not applied to the bisect.**

**We have never measured this campaign's noise floor.** Every delta acted
on -- the 0103/0104 bisect, the bake-off rung ordering, arguably the gate
margins -- was a **single-shot comparison read as signal.**

*Corrected standard, to go into the shared reference and not only here:*

> **An instrument can be cheap and still perturb what it measures. When a
> delta is near the noise floor, replicate before explaining.**

*And the correct first cells are NOT 0103-vs-0104 repeats* -- that
conflates noise with effect. **Same binary against itself, several times**,
so the spread defines what a real delta must exceed.

### Consequence for Gate 1, stated before the measurement

**Gate 1's whole-run figure is 39.54 against a 39.2 bar -- a margin of
0.34.** If the A-to-A spread is anywhere near the ~1 fps suggested by
probed-vs-unprobed 0104, **that margin sits inside the noise and the claim
rests on one run.**

**This is NOT a retraction.** It is the next thing to measure. Once the
noise floor is known, Gate 1's cell gets re-run enough times to say whether
it **clears the bar reliably or cleared it once.** The operator signed it
off and is owed a straight answer either way.

### Corrections to the 5.38 ms diagnosis -- both change the fix

**1. The share is larger than I said.** 504 equal x 5.38 ms = 2711 ms plus
496 differing x 0.85 ms = 422 ms, so the check totals **3133 ms over 1000
passes = 12.5% of a 25 ms budget** (equal-frame half alone: 10.8%). I said
8.6%.

**2. It is bandwidth-bound, NOT branch-bound -- my "branch per word" was
wrong.** The scan reads **two** 64 KB buffers: **128,000 bytes in 5.38 ms =
23.8 MB/s**, which is about what a 486DX2-66 sustains from main memory.
Both buffers blow through an 8 KB L1, so every dword is a main-memory read.
**Unrolling or `rep cmpsd` will buy almost nothing. The only real fix is to
stop reading 128 KB.**

### The prize: at Mode 13h, is the dirty check worth having at all?

It spends **5.38 ms to avoid a 7.84 ms present**. Net **+2.46 ms** on the
equal half, minus **0.85 ms** wasted on the differing half -- about
**+32 ms/s, ~3.2% of budget. It barely pays for itself.**

At 640x480 (21.60 ms present) it pays handsomely. **So its value is
mode-dependent** -- which maps onto the operator's "fastest by default,
tunable options" instruction: **a knob whose correct default may differ per
rung and per card.**

**The better fix, if reachable: AGS already knows which objects moved.**
Comparing 128 KB of pixels to rediscover that is doing the work twice.
Engine-level dirty tracking would replace a 5.38 ms scan with near-zero.
**Scope before committing.**

*Unaffected by any of this:* the **603/1807 stalls are ~275 ms**, far
outside any plausible noise floor. That finding stands.

## A-to-A noise floor MEASURED -- and my ~1 fps claim was wrong

Same binary (0103), same config, three cells, Mode 13h `anim12`:

| cell | `fps_p50` | whole-run |
|---|---|---|
| NF1031 | 40.00 | 30.93 |
| NF1032 | 40.12 | 31.15 |
| NF1033 | 40.24 | 30.93 |
| **spread** | **0.24** | **0.22** |

**The run-to-run noise floor is 0.24 fps, not ~1.** I inferred ~1 fps from
a single probed-vs-unprobed pair and generalised it to run-to-run
variation. **That inference was wrong, and it was exactly the single-shot
reasoning this whole exercise is about** -- I diagnosed the error and then
committed a version of it in the diagnosis.

### What that changes

**1. The bisect SURVIVES.** The 0103-vs-0104 delta is **1.21 fps, five
times the 0.24 spread.** Patch 0104's regression is real. My "the bisect is
not safe" was over-corrected -- I should have measured before withdrawing
it, the same discipline I had just demanded.

**2. The probed-vs-unprobed anomaly is NOT noise -- it is a real finding.**
0104 unprobed 38.91, probed 39.84: a **0.93 difference, four times the
spread**, from adding instrumentation to `ali3dsw.cpp`. Run-to-run
variation cannot explain it.

**So perturbing that translation unit moves its performance by ~1 fps.**
That is a codegen/layout sensitivity -- and it **revives the codegen
hypothesis for 0104 that my instruction count seemed to rule out**. +32
instructions with different register allocation can plainly do this on a
486 with an 8 KB cache and no branch prediction, because the effect is
alignment and scheduling, not instruction count. **My instruction-count
check tested the wrong quantity**: it asked "is there more code?" when the
question was "is the same code laid out worse?".

**3. Gate 1's 0.34 margin exceeds this 0.24 spread -- but only just, and
this spread was measured on the WRONG fixture.** It is `bench8` at Mode
13h, not Trilby's at 5000 ticks. **Gate 1 needs its own replication before
anything is concluded about it**, which is running.

## TWO noise floors, and our ABBA standard only ever measured one

### Rule 1: noise floors are PER-FIXTURE

| fixture | A-to-A spread (`fps_p50`) |
|---|---|
| Trilby's idle, 5000 ticks | **0.12** |
| `bench8` `anim12`, Mode 13h | **0.24** |

**Twice the spread on the busier fixture.** A floor measured on one
fixture must never be applied to another -- the mistake nearly made by
carrying `bench8`'s 0.24 onto Gate 1's 0.34 margin and concluding the
claim was at risk. **Measure the floor on the fixture the claim is made
on.**

### Rule 2: there is a SECOND floor -- build-to-build LAYOUT variance -- and A-to-A is structurally blind to it

**A-to-A repeats measure run-to-run variance of ONE binary.** They cannot
see layout variance, because the binary is byte-identical across every
repeat. **Our ABBA standard has never looked at this.**

*The evidence it exists:* probed-vs-unprobed 0104 differs by **0.93 --
with strictly MORE work in the faster build.** Not run-to-run (4x the
0.24 floor), not semantics (the probe only adds counters). **That leaves
code layout.**

**Every A/B in this campaign has been exposed to it.** A single-build A/B
whose delta is smaller than the layout floor is **unattributable to the
patch's semantics, full stop.**

*How to measure it -- a layout-perturbation ensemble:* build 3-4
**semantically identical** variants of the **same** revision (vary
`-falign-functions`/`-falign-loops`, pad ahead of the hot function, or
reorder two independent functions) and run a cell on each. **The spread
across that ensemble is the layout floor.** We already have an ensemble of
two, spanning 0.93.

**If 3-4 variants of 0104 alone span anything near 1.21, the 0103/0104
delta is not attributable to the patch at all** -- and four dead
hypotheses are explained without a fifth.

**This belongs in the hub standard beside the A-to-A check**, because it
sets a floor under every conclusion the campaign can draw.

## Layout floor MEASURED: 0.19. The bisect is attributable to the patch.

Four **semantically identical** builds of patch 0104, differing only in
alignment flags:

| build | flags | `fps_p50` |
|---|---|---|
| baseline | (none) | 38.91 |
| L1 | `-falign-functions=32` | 38.92 |
| L2 | `-falign-functions=64 -falign-loops=32` | 39.02 |
| L3 | `-falign-loops=16 -falign-jumps=16` | 38.83 |
| **spread** | | **0.19** |

**The layout floor is 0.19 -- comparable to the 0.24 run-to-run floor, not
~1 fps.**

### Consequences

**1. The 0103/0104 delta IS attributable to the patch.** 0104's entire
layout ensemble spans 38.83-39.02; 0103 sits at 40.12. **The 1.21 gap is
six times the layout floor and every layout variant of 0104 is far below
0103.** Layout variance does not explain it. **The regression is real and
it is patch 0104's semantics.**

**2. The 0.93 probed-vs-unprobed difference is NOT generic layout
variance** -- generic perturbation produces 0.19, not 0.93. So the probe
did something specific.

**Most likely: the probe un-inlined `FramesEqualFast`.** It added
`uclock()` calls at entry and before each return, which plausibly pushed
the compiler off inlining a function it otherwise inlines -- and a
dedicated out-of-line loop can get better register allocation than one
inlined into a large function. **That would mean un-inlining the scan is
itself worth ~0.9 fps**, which is a cheap standalone optimisation --
though largely moot if the scan is replaced outright.

**Recorded rather than pursued**, because the dirty-rect work would delete
the scan entirely. Worth revisiting only if that work does not land.

**3. The layout floor belongs in the standard anyway.** It is 0.19 here,
not negligible, and no A/B smaller than ~0.2 on this fixture is
attributable to a patch's semantics. **That it turned out smaller than
feared does not make the check unnecessary -- it makes it calibrated.**

## Dirty-rect feasibility: the system ALREADY EXISTS and is live. Scope is narrow-medium.

**This is not "build a new system."** AGS's upstream software dirty-rect
system is present, compiled and **running in this tree right now**, and the
DOS port has never touched it -- no patch in `patches/ags/` modifies
`draw_software.cpp` or any `invalidate_*` site.

- Span-based rects per room camera: `Engine/ac/draw_software.cpp:72-97`,
  overflowing to `WHOLESCREENDIRTY` past 25 regions (`:264-267`).
- **Active here:** `RequiresFullRedrawEachFrame()` returns false
  (`gfx/ali3dsw.h:178`), so `drawstate.FullFrameRedraw == false` and the
  dirty-rect branch is the one taken (`ac/draw.cpp:2845`). It already
  repaints the room background over dirty spans only.

### The invalidation set for the normal draw path is ALREADY COMPLETE

`put_sprite_list_on_screen()` invalidates **unconditionally for every DDB
it pushes** (`draw.cpp:2759`), so objects, characters, overlays, speech,
GUIs, the cursor and the FPS counter are all covered by construction.
Walk-behinds carry no independent area in software mode (cropped into the
sprite, `draw.cpp:2117`). Animated backgrounds, camera scroll, tint, shake,
room changes and all 13 script `DrawingSurface` sites invalidate
explicitly. **There is no "some contributors have flags, others don't"
problem.**

### The risk is a BOUNDED list of ~10 bypass sites, not an open audit

Sites that write `GetMemoryBackBuffer()` directly and call
`render_to_screen()` without invalidating: **screen transitions**
(`ac/screen.cpp:186,290,294,412,481,491,564,613` -- the highest risk, a
tight loop of direct writes), video playback (`video.cpp:187,225,341`),
startup/splash (`engine.cpp:630,647`), `draw.cpp:2975/760/1048`, and
**plugin render hooks** (`draw.cpp:2764-2768`, which invalidate nothing and
whose `mark_dirty` argument this driver ignores at `ali3dsw.cpp:1333`).

Two subtle traps worth recording: `invalidate_rect_ds/global` iterate
`RoomCamRects`, which is **empty between rooms**, so an accumulator placed
inside that loop is **silently inert** there; and `WHOLESCREENDIRTY` is a
sentinel *value* (30) of `NumDirtyRegions`, not a boolean.

### Why the payoff is bigger than deleting the 5.38 ms scan

**The same bbox scopes the upscale blit and the VESA flush**, both dearer
than the compare. And the backend **already honours partial rect lists** --
`SDL_dosframebuffer.c:1662` with per-rect loops, landed by
`patches/SDL/0033`. `ali3dsw.h:388-393` says it outright: the backend
"never receives a real partial rect list because AGS never provides one."
**The receiving half is already built and unused.**

### Sizing and the de-risking shape

| piece | size |
|---|---|
| accumulate + plumb a screen-space bbox | **small** (two functions, a getter, one branch in `Present()`) |
| scope the blit and update rect | small-medium; `_lastPresentedPixels` and the margin logic mostly get **removed** |
| close the ~10 bypass sites | **medium -- this is where the correctness lives** |

**De-risking, and this is the important design decision: default to a FULL
present and require a positive signal to narrow it.** Latch "full" at the
top of `Present()` unless the frame went through `construct_game_scene()`.
**That inverts the failure mode -- a missed contributor costs performance,
not corruption** -- which matters because the DOSBox gate cannot catch a
corruption that only appears on a path it never executes, the same
structural blindness recorded for the light table.

**Verdict: feasible, narrow-medium, and the risky half is a bounded
enumerable list rather than an open-ended audit.** Recommend proceeding,
with the full-present-by-default latch as the first thing built.

## Patch 0104's mechanism: PARKED (may become moot, not abandoned)

**State: effect real and attributable, cause unknown after five dead
hypotheses** -- reorder, heuristic-replacement, tipping-point, codegen
bloat, memcpy frequency. Each died to a cheap measurement.

**Parked because the dirty-rect work may DELETE the code path entirely**,
which would dissolve the question. **Not parked because we gave up** --
**if the scan survives that work, this gets revisited.**

*Asymmetry in the bisect evidence, recorded so nobody later reads it as
symmetric:* the layout ensemble was built for **0104 only** (four builds,
spread 0.19) and compared against a **single** 0103 figure (40.12).
Strictly the floor should be established on both sides. At **6x the
floor** the conclusion is not in doubt and the cells are not worth
spending -- but the evidence is one-sided and should be described that way.

*In the bank:* un-inlining `FramesEqualFast` appears worth **~0.9 fps**
standalone. **Fallback if dirty rects do not land.**

## Patch 0119 latch: NOT a no-op. And it reproduces patch 0104's signature exactly.

Verifying the latch on its own -- before any narrowing -- was the right
call, because **it costs about 1 fps for bookkeeping that should be
free.**

| build | `fps_p50` |
|---|---|
| **pre-latch (0118) ensemble** | 38.83, 38.91, 38.92, 39.02 |
| **latch (0119) ensemble** | **37.70, 37.92, 38.00** |

**The two ensembles do not overlap.** Latch 37.70-38.00 against pre-latch
38.83-39.02, a gap of ~0.83 with no intersection. **So the cost is real,
not the layout lottery** -- an alignment ensemble was built for the latch
specifically to test that, and it clusters tightly ~1 fps below.

### What the latch actually does per frame

`adds=999` over 1000 frames -- **about one accumulator call per frame** --
plus a dozen `dos_port_dirty_set_full()` calls that early-return after the
first, a bool store in `construct_game_scene()`, and a `Debug::Printf`
twice per 1000 presents. **That is nanoseconds. It cannot be 0.65 ms.**

### The signature is patch 0104's, and that is the finding

| patch | what it adds | cost |
|---|---|---|
| 0104 | a bool, a split condition, a moved memcpy, two branches | **-1.21** |
| 0119 | a bbox union, a latch, three counters | **-1.04** |

**Two unrelated patches, both adding small amounts of cheap logic to this
render path, both costing ~1 fps, neither with a mechanism that survives
scrutiny.** Five hypotheses died on 0104 precisely because they were
looking for a mechanism in *what the code does*.

**New hypothesis, and it explains both: the cost is incurred by ADDING
CODE to this path at all, not by what the code does.** Something here sits
on a cliff -- plausibly an I-cache boundary on the 486's 8 KB cache, or an
inlining decision in `Present()`/`construct_game_scene()` that flips once
the function grows. **That would dissolve 0104's mystery entirely**: there
is no semantic mechanism to find because there never was one.

**It is testable and I have not tested it:** add a *deliberately inert*
block of code of similar size to the same functions -- work that computes
something unused -- and see whether it also costs ~1 fps. **If inert code
costs the same as functional code, the hypothesis holds.**

### Consequence for the dirty-rect plan, stated before proceeding

**If any addition to this path costs ~1 fps, the dirty-rect work must
REMOVE more than it adds to net out.** The projected win is large enough
(~3.13 ms/frame from deleting the scan, plus a scoped blit and flush) that
it should still clear comfortably -- **but the latch alone is a 1 fps
liability with zero benefit until narrowing lands**, so it must not be
left in place on its own.

**Also: the alignment-flag ensemble (0.19) understates the build-to-build
floor for patches that ADD code.** Alignment reshuffles; adding code
changes inlining and function size. Two code-adding perturbations measured
+0.93 (the probe) and -1.04 (the latch). **The 0103/0104 delta of 1.21 is
only marginally above that, so the bisect's attribution is weaker than the
6x-over-0.19 figure suggested** -- recorded as a correction to my own
earlier conclusion.

## INERT-CODE TEST: the size hypothesis is REFUTED. And so is my "+/-1 fps floor".

Dead-but-emitted code in `Present()`, gated on a `volatile` the compiler
cannot prove zero, so it is **emitted but never executed**. Emission
verified by instruction count, not assumed -- the compiler did not fold it.

| build | `Present()` instructions | `fps_p50` | delta vs baseline |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0118 baseline ensemble | 2969 | 38.83-39.02 (mean **38.92**) | -- |
| inert, +28 | 2997 | 38.73 | **-0.19** |
| **inert, +54 (= the latch's size)** | 3023 | **38.69** | **-0.23** |
| inert, +158 | 3127 | 38.65 | **-0.27** |
| **LATCH, +52 (functional)** | 3021 | **37.87** | **-1.05** |

### 1. Size is NOT the cause

**Inert code of the same size as the latch costs 0.23. The latch costs
1.05.** Same instruction growth (+54 vs +52), **4.6x different cost.** The
hypothesis that adding code to this path costs ~1 fps regardless of what it
does is **dead** -- and it was my hypothesis, offered as the explanation
for five dead predecessors.

### 2. There is no cliff

**0.08 fps across a 5.6x size range** (+28 to +158 instructions), smooth
and monotone. **No I-cache step function at these sizes**, so there is no
boundary to stay under -- and the `-Os` idea loses its stated rationale.
(It may still help for other reasons, but not this one.)

### 3. My "code-adding floor is ~1 fps" was WRONG, and the correction I sent was worse than the claim it corrected

I told the coordinator the alignment ensemble understated the floor and
that code-adding perturbation was ~1 fps in either direction, implying a
**spread near 2** that 0104's 1.21 sat inside. **Measured, the code-adding
size effect is 0.19-0.27 -- indistinguishable from the 0.19 alignment
floor and the 0.24 run-to-run floor.**

**So the floor is ~0.25, and 0104's 1.21 delta is about 5x it. The bisect
is attributable after all.** I reversed a correct conclusion on the basis
of two data points I had not tested, then reported the reversal. **The
ensemble I should have built to check it took one round.**

### 4. What that leaves

**The latch's 1.05 fps is REAL EXECUTION COST**, not size, not layout --
from roughly fifteen cheap-looking calls per frame. That is ~43 us per
call, which is absurd on its face, so **something in that path is far more
expensive than it looks.** Mechanism unknown; it now needs its own
brackets rather than another hypothesis.

**And the same is true of 0104.** Both remain real, attributable, and
unexplained -- but they are no longer explained *away* by size.

**The within-build hint method stands regardless**, and is now the clear
next step: it removes layout, size and inlining from the comparison
entirely, and the operator already asked for the tunable it requires.

## Repaint-work test: also refuted. But everything now fits ONE hypothesis.

Counters on `update_invalid_region()`, present in **both** arms, counting
spans and pixels repainted rather than time:

| arm | calls | whole | spans | pixels | `fps_p50` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0118 + counters | 500 | 1 | 128030 | 5,497,408 | **37.85** |
| 0119 + counters | 500 | 1 | 128030 | 5,497,408 | **36.93** |

**Byte-identical repaint work.** The latch does not make AGS repaint more.
The hypothesis that its cost was extra work in AGS's own code is dead --
and the latch still costs ~0.92 with counters in both arms.

### The accidental control that makes the picture

**Adding the counters cost ~1 fps on the BASELINE too** -- 38.92 without,
37.85 with. So that is now **three independent small additions to this
render path, each costing about a frame**:

| change | cost |
|---|---|
| patch 0104 (bool, split condition, branches) | **-1.21** |
| patch 0119 latch (bbox, counters) | **-1.05** |
| repaint counters (span walk) | **-1.07** |
| **inert code, same size, NEVER EXECUTED** | **-0.23** |

### The hypothesis that fits all of it: I-CACHE PRESSURE, not work

**Executed additions cost ~1 fps. Never-executed additions cost 0.23.**
The difference between them is not size -- the sizes were matched -- it is
**whether the code occupies cache lines at run time.**

On a 486DX2-66 with an **8 KB unified cache**, any code that actually runs
inside this path evicts part of the hot blit/compare loops. **The cost is
the cache footprint, not the instructions retired** -- which is why three
additions doing wildly different amounts of work all cost about the same.

**It also explains the one result that never fitted anything: the
`FramesEqualFast` probe made 0104 ~0.93 FASTER.** Adding `uclock()` calls
plausibly un-inlined the scan out of `Present()`, *shrinking* the hot
function's footprint. **Same mechanism, opposite sign** -- which is exactly
what a cache-pressure effect predicts and what a "tax" model cannot.

**Not yet directly confirmed** -- a 486 gives us no cache-miss counter, so
this is a hypothesis that fits six observations rather than a measurement.
The falsifiable prediction: **a change that REDUCES this path's executed
footprint should GAIN ~1 fps**, and the un-inlining result is already one
instance.

### Three consequences

1. **The dirty-rect work must shrink the executed footprint, not merely do
   less work.** Deleting the 5.38 ms scan removes a large hot loop, so it
   should win on both counts -- but **the win must be measured, never
   projected**, because adding the bookkeeping costs a frame by itself.
2. **Cross-build A/B on this path is unreliable below ~1 fps, for a reason
   we now understand.** The within-build hint is not a convenience, it is
   the only sound method here.
3. **0104's mystery is plausibly closed** without a sixth semantic
   hypothesis: it added executed code to `Present()`. Five hypotheses
   failed because they all looked for a mechanism in *what the code does*.

## noinline ensemble: +1.20 fps confirmed, and it CLEARS Gate 2's bar 1

Testing the cache-footprint model's own prediction -- reduce the hot
function's executed footprint, gain ~1 fps.

| build | `fps_p50` |
|---|---|
| 0118 baseline ensemble | 38.83, 38.91, 38.92, 39.02 (mean **38.92**) |
| **`FramesEqualFast` noinline** | **40.12, 40.12** |
| `TryFastIntegerNearestBlit` noinline | 38.83, 38.96 (mean 38.90) |

**`FramesEqualFast` un-inlined gains +1.20 fps, and the two layout
variants returned the IDENTICAL value (40.12, 40.12)** -- a tighter
reproduction than the 0.19 layout floor would lead you to expect.

**40.12 clears 40.** That is Gate 2's bar 1, met by a compile attribute.

### The prediction held -- but only ONE of the two candidates actually tested it

`TryFastIntegerNearestBlit` gave nothing (-0.02, inside every floor).
**That is not evidence against the model, because the attribute changed
almost nothing there.** Symbol counts in the built binaries:

| build | `TryFastIntegerNearestBlit` | `FramesEqualFast` |
|---|---|---|
| baseline | **2 (already out-of-line)** | **0 (fully inlined)** |
| blit-noinline | 3 | 0 |
| feq-noinline | 2 | **1 (now out-of-line)** |

**The blit function was already out of line, so `noinline` was close to a
no-op and tested nothing.** Only `FramesEqualFast` was genuinely inlined,
and un-inlining it is the only real test performed. **One confirmed
prediction, one null that does not count -- recorded that way rather than
as "one of two".**

### It exactly cancels patch 0104

0104 cost **-1.21**; un-inlining `FramesEqualFast` gains **+1.20**, landing
at **40.12 -- the same figure 0103 measured before 0104 existed.** Under
the cache model that is what should happen: 0104 added executed code to
`Present()`, and this removes a large body from it. **Consistent, and
close enough to be worth noting as a coincidence only if the model is
wrong.**

### A harness failure worth recording, because it nearly produced a wrong conclusion

**Four consecutive cells failed to collect** -- stage dirs with only a send
witness, target idle at a prompt, input verified working. I suspected the
binaries. **They were fine**: the same binary later produced 40.12, and a
known-good binary run in between also succeeded (37.85, matching its
earlier value exactly). **Transient, not reproducible, cause unknown.**

**The isolation that settled it -- run a known-good binary between the
failures -- is the cheap move whenever a batch fails**, because "my change
broke it" and "the harness had a bad patch" look identical from the
output. Had I not run it, the honest conclusion available would have been
"noinline binaries do not run on hardware", which is false.

| | `fps_p50` | `tick_rate_steady` | whole-run |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gate 1 as claimed (5 cells) | 40.00 | 40.04 | 39.48-39.60 |
| **with 0119** (G1N1, G1N2) | **40.00** | **40.04** | **39.60, 39.60** |

*Also dropped from the series:* the 0119 dirty-bbox latch. It cost 1.05 fps

## Unexplained harness transient, 2026-09-18 -- recognise, do not re-diagnose

**Four consecutive cells failed to collect**: stage dirs containing only a
send witness, target idle at a DOS prompt, `vcctrl_verify_input`
confirming the target acknowledged a keystroke. **Not the post-FTP
keyboard hang** -- input was verified working.

**It was not the binaries.** A known-good binary run between the failures
succeeded (37.85, matching its earlier value exactly), and one of the
"failing" binaries later produced 40.12 twice. **Transient, not

**Recorded so it is recognised rather than re-diagnosed if it recurs.**
The isolation that settled it -- **run a known-good binary between the
failures** -- is the cheap discriminator, because "my change broke it" and
"the harness had a bad patch" are indistinguishable from the output alone.
**Four failures with a plausible common cause is exactly the shape that
produces a confident wrong conclusion**, and the conclusion available here
