## AGS Quest / 16-bit: the noinline test COULD NOT TEST the class -- and a fresh Gate 3 baseline

| | `fps_p50` | steady | whole-run |
|---|---|---|---|
| clean 0118 (AQB1) | **13.32** | 40.52 | 15.12 |
| 0119 noinline (AQN1) | 13.21 | 40.56 | 15.14 |

**-0.11 -- and it means nothing, because `FramesEqualFast` never runs at
16-bit.** Both cells report **`presents_skipped=0`**: patch 0102 disables
the unchanged-frame check above 100,000 bytes, and AGS Quest's frame is
**460,800**. So the function un-inlined by 0119 is **never executed on
this fixture**, and the attribute could not possibly have helped.

**This is the SAME error I made choosing `TryFastIntegerNearestBlit` --
testing something that does not apply -- and this time the evidence was
already in PLAN.md**, recorded during the AQ102 ABBA as "skip correctly
never engages (460,800 B > the gate)". **I had written it down and did not
check it before spending two cells.**

**So: the question "does the cache-footprint class transfer to 16bpp?" is
still OPEN.** Not answered negatively -- unasked. Testing it needs a
function that is actually hot on the 16-bit path.

### Fresh Gate 3 baseline (first since many patches landed)

**`fps_p50` 13.32, up from the 11.00 of 2026-09-17.** `tick_rate_steady`
**40.52 passes**; whole-run 15.12 fails badly; fps needs 3.0x.

### The 16-bit hot path, measured -- and it names Gate 3's real problem

| term | mean ms |
|---|---|
| `present_blit` | **26.78** (of which `fastblit_vmemcpy` **26.61**) |
| `present_update_window` | **16.74** |
| `scene_construct` | 9.42 |

> **present total 43.52 ms against a 25 ms budget for 40 fps -- the
> present ALONE is 1.74x the entire frame budget.**

**460,800 bytes copied in 26.61 ms = 17.3 MB/s**, close to the ~23.8 MB/s
this machine sustains from main memory. **Gate 3 is bandwidth-bound on
output size**, not on engine work -- `scene_construct` is 9.42 ms, a fifth
of the present.

**This is why lower output resolution is the right lever** (operator
authorised): it attacks the one quantity that dominates. **No compile
attribute and no engine-side optimisation can pay for 43.52 ms of memory
traffic** -- only moving fewer bytes can.

**Constraint on which rungs exist, from `HARDWARE.md`: the Mach64
215CT/-ET cannot double-scan, so there is no 320x200/320x240 VESA mode on
this card at all**, and a closest-mode match to something larger has
already caused downstream bugs here. **The available 16-bit rungs must be
established by measurement before any rung is recommended** -- and
`docs/video.md` now records that `present_update_window` scales with
output area while `present_blit` only explodes on a replicating rung, so
**the 8-bit ladder's arithmetic does not carry over.**

## PRE-CELL CHECK (standing rule): verify the code under test actually EXECUTES on that fixture

**This trap has now cost cells twice**, in two different disguises:

1. **Already out-of-line.** `TryFastIntegerNearestBlit` was given
   `__attribute__((noinline))` when the baseline binary already had 2
   symbols for it. The attribute changed nothing; the null result was no
   evidence.
2. **Never executed.** `FramesEqualFast` was un-inlined and measured on
   AGS Quest, where **`presents_skipped=0`** because patch 0102 disables
   the unchanged-frame check above 100,000 bytes and the frame is 460,800.
   The function never runs there.

**Both were free to check and neither was checked.** The second is worse:
**the constraint was already written in this file**, recorded during the
AQ102 ABBA as "skip correctly never engages (460,800 B > the gate)".

> **Rule: before spending a cell on a lever, prove the code under test
> both EXISTS in the form you think and RUNS on that fixture.**
> **Symbol count proves inlining. An execution counter proves
> reachability.** A cell that cannot distinguish a positive result from a
> negative one is not a measurement, and its null is not evidence.

## GATE 3's PROBLEM, stated as clearly as we can state it

> **Present total 43.52 ms against a 25 ms frame budget. The present alone
> is 1.74x the entire budget, and engine work (`scene_construct`, 9.42 ms)
> is a fifth of it. Gate 3 was never an engine-speed problem.**

### And the same frame appears to be copied TWICE

| | ms | what |
|---|---|---|
| `present_blit` (`fastblit_vmemcpy` 26.61) | **26.78** | AGS virtual screen -> SDL window surface, main memory to main memory |
| `present_update_window` | **16.74** | window surface -> the card |

**The first copy produces no visible output.** It is plumbing between two
buffers.

*Arithmetic before designing anything:* the frame is **75 ms** at 13.32
fps. **Removing the blit takes it to ~48.9 ms = ~20.4 fps -- a ~53% gain,
at full resolution, with no picture-quality cost.** That is larger than a
rung change would likely buy **and it does not spend the concession the
operator made.**

*A hint that it is not a plain copy:* **17.3 MB/s for that blit against
the 23.8 MB/s measured for a plain two-buffer scan.** Slower than reading
two buffers suggests it is doing more than moving bytes -- format
conversion is the obvious candidate, and if so, matching formats at
surface creation may help even if the copy survives.

*And it composes with dirty rects rather than competing:* **patch 0102's
100,000-byte gate is irrelevant to engine-supplied invalidation** -- dirty
rects need no pixel comparison, so narrowing sidesteps 0102 entirely and
scopes the **16.74 ms** `update_window` to changed regions. **Blit
elimination and narrowing attack the two different copies.**

**Scoping in progress, source only. No rung will be measured until this is
answered, because if the blit goes away the rung arithmetic changes
materially and we would be measuring the wrong ladder.**

## Gate 2 four-cell claim: BOTH NEW BARS PASS, but whole-run fails. NOT claimed -- definitional question for the operator.

Four cells, `bench8 anim12`, Mode 13h, gate window, **`--gate` enforced**,
binary `15c7022ff166` (patch 0119), `build_dirty=0`.

| measure | values | bar | |
|---|---|---|---|
| **bar 1 -- `fps_p50`** | 40.16, 40.20, 40.16, 40.20 | >= 40 | **4/4 PASS** (spread 0.04) |
| **bar 2 -- completeness** | 96.8, 96.7, 97.0, 96.6 % | >= 95% | **4/4 PASS** |
| `tick_rate_steady` | 40.11, 40.16, 40.08, 40.14 | 39.2-40.8 | 4/4 pass |
| **whole-run `tick_rate`** | 39.11, 39.07, 39.15, 39.06 | 39.2-40.8 | **0/4 FAIL** |

**Both bars of Gate 2's own definition pass, cleanly and reproducibly** --
`fps_p50` with a 0.04 spread, completeness comfortably over.

**But whole-run `tick_rate` fails in all four, by 0.05-0.14.**

### The question, which is the operator's and not mine

**Gate 2's definition (2026-09-18) names exactly two bars** -- 40 render
passes/s and >=95% completeness. **It does not mention whole-run
`tick_rate`.**

**But the standing KPI decision (2026-09-17) says BOTH tick figures must
pass**, and this file records that all three gates share that rule.

**Those two cannot both be satisfied here.** Either Gate 2 is the two bars
it was redefined as -- in which case it **passes now** -- or the
both-tick-figures rule still applies on top, in which case it **fails by
about 0.1**.

**I am not claiming Gate 2 either way.** The redefinition was written to
close an fps loophole, not visibly to repeal the tick requirement, and
**reading a repeal into it would be me deciding a gate's terms to reach a
pass.** Flagged for the operator.

*Worth noting for whichever way it goes:* the whole-run shortfall is
**~0.1 on a fixture whose stall term Mode 13h roughly doubles** (recorded
earlier: 826 ms recurring against full_window's 310 ms), and the
**603/1807 stalls remain unexplained and are parked by operator
decision**. So the failing figure is the one most affected by the thing we
deliberately stopped investigating.

## BOUNDARY on the whole campaign: `present_update_window` is already at the bus ceiling

**27.5 MB/s measured, matching the port's own bandwidth probe for
`LFB, near pointer = 27.3 MB/s`** (PLAN.md's bandwidth-probe section,
which also predicted 16.10 ms for 460,800 bytes against our measured
16.74).

> **That copy -- system RAM to VRAM -- is already at the hardware limit.
> No code change reduces it. Only sending FEWER BYTES does: dirty-rect
> narrowing, or a smaller output rung.**

**This is the floor under everything that follows**, and it bounds what
any future optimisation on the present path can be worth. Stated plainly
so nobody spends a round trying to make the second copy faster.

*By contrast the FIRST copy (`present_blit`, 26.61 ms) is pure
redundancy* -- RAM to RAM, same format, same pitch, scale 1, no
conversion -- **and is removable outright.**

## Operator decision (2026-09-19): Gate 2 stands on its ORIGINAL terms; stalls UNPARKED

**No repeal.** Gate 2 requires **both** the two bars of the 2026-09-18
redefinition **and** the whole-run tick figure from the 2026-09-17
both-tick-figures decision. The redefinition added bars; it did not
subtract one.

**This is the second time this campaign a gate's terms have been in
question, and both times they were upheld rather than adjusted.** Recorded
explicitly so the record shows that.

**Consequence: the 603/1807 stalls move from parked to THE thing blocking
a gate claim.** Whole-run needs about **300 ms** back across a 4960-tick
run to clear 39.2, against the **~826 ms** of recurring stall measured at
Mode 13h. Comfortable margin **if** the cause is fixable -- **but 300 ms is
not the target. Find the cause and fix it properly; the margin is whatever
it turns out to be.**

*What is already known, so it is not re-derived:* deterministic at ticks
**603 and 1807** across both object counts, **~275 ms each**,
**Mode-13h-only**, thousands of ticks into the run, with a third index
that varies by cell (2811 at 12 objects, 4811 at 4). **Three hypotheses
are dead** -- not scripted events (`AUTOPLT.LOG` shows `anim` unbroken
0-4960), not log flushes (full_window emits more bytes and stalls less),
not the mode set (far too late).

*Method cautions carried in from today:* the probe is a code addition to
the hot path, and those cost ~1 fps by cache footprint -- **so the gate
must not be measured on a probed binary, and the post-fix gate cells need
a clean build.** And per the new pre-cell rule, **confirm the probe
actually fires at 603/1807 on a short run before spending a gate-window
cell.**

## Patch 0120: direct virtual-screen alias -- CORRECTNESS GATE PASSED

`present_blit` was a full-frame RAM->RAM memcpy producing no visible
output. This aliases AGS's virtual screen onto the window surface so it
has nothing to copy.

**Gated with a within-build A/B -- same binary, hint toggled**, which
removes layout and code-size from the comparison by construction:

| | alias ON | alias OFF (`DOSAGS_DIRECT_VSCREEN=0`) |
|---|---|---|
| activation | `alias ON y=60 640x360 pitch=1280` | none (0 lines) |
| PH01 / PH02 / PH03 | `7ac5213ff8b4` `3b2651677ea1` `623fc3a701e2` | **identical** |
| exit | 0 | 0 |

**All three screenshots byte-identical.** The alias engages exactly where
scoped -- 640x360 at y=60 in a 640x480 window, pitch 1280, 1x, RGB565 --
and the hint disables it cleanly.

**The fallback is the default and is never removed:** `_origVirtualScreen`
stays allocated; the alias is adopted only after a frame has presented
with steady 1x geometry, and **any deviation reverts to the owned buffer**.
Worst case is one frame without a screen-shake displacement -- bounded and
cosmetic, never corruption.

**Within-build A/B, AGS Quest, HW-486-66. Same binary `f30a241d2e92`, hint
toggled** -- so layout, code size and cache footprint cancel by
construction, which matters on a path measured today to move ~1 fps on any
code change.

| | alias OFF | alias ON | |
|---|---|---|---|
| **`fps_p50`** | **13.31** | **22.95** | **+9.64, 1.72x** |
| `present_blit` | **1623 calls** @ 26.69 ms | **1 call** | eliminated |
| `present_update_window` | 16.91 ms | 16.86 ms | unchanged, as predicted |
| `presents_real` | 1623 | 2660 | |
| whole-run `tick_rate` | 15.15 | 15.85 | still far short of 39.2 |
| **`tick_rate_steady`** | 40.52 | **41.07** | **OUT OF BAND -- see below** |

is the largest step the campaign has produced **at full resolution, with
the operator's rung concession unspent.**

### One thing that must not be glossed: `tick_rate_steady` is now ABOVE the band

**41.07 against a 39.2-40.8 band. That is a FAIL, in the too-fast
direction.** The alias-off arm of the same binary reads 40.52, inside.

**So patch 0120 fixes an fps problem and creates a tick problem on this
fixture.** The likely shape is that removing 26.69 ms per frame hands the
pacer far more headroom than it has ever had here, and its catch-up
behaviour overshoots -- but **that is a hypothesis and today has killed
six of those, so it is written as one.**

**This is exactly the "optimisation validated on one metric is a
regression on another" pattern that patch 0104 taught us**, caught this
time because both tick figures were read rather than just the headline.
**It must be resolved before 0120 is claimed for anything**, and it is a
reason not to carry the patch to the 8-bit gates untested -- Gate 1 is
signed off and Gate 2 is mid-claim, and 41.07 would fail both.

### CORRECTION: the 41.07 overshoot is PRE-EXISTING and AQ-specific, not caused by 0120

I attributed it to the patch. **It is not.**

| fixture / arm | `tick_rate_steady` | |
|---|---|---|
| AGS Quest, alias **OFF** (same binary) | **40.52** | already **1.3% fast** |
| AGS Quest, alias ON | 41.07 | 2.6% fast |
| Trilby's (Gate 1) | 40.04 | in band |
| `bench8 anim12` (Gate 2) | 40.08-40.16 | in band |

**The alias-off arm is already above nominal, and the 8-bit fixtures are
not.** So the overshoot is **pre-existing, AGS-Quest-specific, and 0120
amplified it rather than created it.** That is a different bug with a
different owner: **it belongs to the pacer, not to patch 0120.**

*Mechanism, as a testable prediction rather than a story:* steady **41.07**
against whole-run **15.85** is an enormous gap -- far more wall time
outside steady state than inside it, i.e. a lot of accumulated debt. A
pacer with catch-up repays debt *during* the steady window, which reads as
a tick rate above 40. Removing 26.69 ms/frame gave it headroom to repay
faster, which is why the overshoot **grew as fps improved**.

> **Prediction to test: at 41.07 the excess is 2.6%, so roughly 2.6% of
> the steady window's ticks should be catch-up repayments. Count them.**
> If the counter matches, that is the mechanism. If not, the pacer is
> wrong some other way.

## Gate 3 reframed: whole-run is now the LARGER half, and nothing has touched it

| | now | needed | factor |
|---|---|---|---|
| `fps_p50` | 22.95 | 40 | **1.74x** |
| whole-run `tick_rate` | **15.85** | 39.2 | **2.47x** |

**Whole-run is the bigger gap and the campaign has never worked on it for
this fixture.**

*The diagnostic comparison that makes it obvious:*

| fixture | steady | whole-run | gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| Trilby's | 40.04 | 39.60 | **0.44** |
| **AGS Quest** | 41.07 | **15.85** | **25.2** |

**A 25-point gap is not a frame-rate problem at all.** It is wall time in
which ticks are not happening -- load and startup. Gate 1's whole-run was
won by deleting ~2.4 s of fixed startup cost, and **nobody has ever done
that analysis for AGS Quest.**

**So the next Gate 3 lever is measuring where AGS Quest's non-steady time
goes, not more fps work.** We would otherwise keep optimising the half
that is closer to done while ignoring the half that is further away.

## Verifying 0120 on the 8-bit gates: my prediction was WRONG, and the check caught it

I said 0120 was "1x-only, worth nothing to the 2x fixtures" and inferred it
would not engage on the 8-bit gates. **It engages on one of them.**

| fixture | alias engaged? | `fps_p50` | steady | whole-run | PH01 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Trilby's (Gate 1)** | **no** (0 lines) | 40.00 | 40.04 | 39.53 | -- |
| **`bench8` Mode 13h (Gate 2)** | **YES** -- `y=0 320x200 pitch=320` | 40.00 | 40.07 | 39.15 | **`9f0650485d4efe60`** |

**Mode 13h is a true 320x200 mode presented 1:1 at full width -- it
satisfies every alias condition.** My "2x fixtures" framing was right about
the *scaled* rungs and wrong about Mode 13h, which is exactly the rung
Gate 2 now runs on.

**Correctness holds: PH01 is byte-identical to the Gate 2 claim cell**
(`9f0650485d4efe60`), so the alias is behaving correctly on 8-bit as well.

**Gate 1 is untouched** -- the alias never engages there, and 40.00 /
40.04 / 39.53 match the signed-off values.

**Gate 2 outcomes are unchanged but the numbers are not identical:**
`fps_p50` 40.00 against the claim cells' 40.16-40.20 -- **slightly lower,
around the 0.24 run-to-run floor.** Bar 1 still passes, steady still in
band, whole-run still fails at 39.15. **No gate outcome changes, but
Gate 2's claim cells would have to be re-run with 0120 in the tree**, since
the binary under claim would no longer be the binary measured.

**Why the win does not appear here:** at Mode 13h `present_blit` was only
**4.17 ms** (64,000 bytes) against AGS Quest's **26.69 ms** (460,800). The
saving is real but small, and the fixture is already at the 40 cap, so it
shows as headroom rather than fps.

**The lesson, again, and it is the one that keeps recurring:** "it
shouldn't engage there" was an inference from my own scoping, not a
measurement, and it was wrong. **The check cost one cell and protected a
signed-off gate.**

## ANCHOR VERIFIED, and it overturns the Gate 3 reframing -- the gap is STALLS, not startup

**Checked from source before doing any arithmetic**, per this campaign's
own recorded lesson that a "load time is in `tick_rate`'s denominator"
correction was once pushed and was wrong.

`quit.cpp:470-473`: `tick_rate = 1000 * get_loop_counter() /
get_runtime_ms()`. `get_runtime_ms()` (`game_run.cpp:1474`) measures from
`GameTimer.StartTime`, set by `set_runtime_start()` -- and the code's own
comment at `game_run.cpp:1481` says where that is:

> "`get_runtime_ms()`'s anchor is `set_runtime_start()` in `start_game()`
> -- **AFTER engine init, BEFORE the game_start script and
> `load_new_room()`**"

**So the denominator EXCLUDES process start, engine init and game-data
load, and INCLUDES the pre-loop plus all in-loop time.** The reframing
that "25.2 points of gap equals load and startup" was **wrong** -- most
of what it named is not in the metric at all.

### And the data was already on disk. AGS Quest's pre-loop is trivial.

From the AQON cell, no new measurement needed:

| | |
|---|---|
| `preloop_ms` | **2022** (2.0 s) |
| `loop_ms` | 223538 (223.5 s) |
| **`stall_ms`** | **136654 (136.7 s)** |
| `stall_ticks` | **19** |
| ticks | 3587 |

**61% of the entire run is stall time, across just 19 ticks -- averaging
7.2 seconds each.** The pre-loop is 2.0 s, i.e. **0.9% of the run.**

**The Gate 1 playbook does not apply here.** Gate 1's whole-run was won by
deleting ~2.4 s of fixed startup cost; AGS Quest's *entire* pre-loop is
2.0 s, so deleting all of it would move whole-run from 15.85 to about
15.99. **Nothing.**

### The individual stalls

```
index=1    ms=12830      index=1594 ms=12436      index=2275 ms=13911
index=83   ms=6521       index=2029 ms=308        index=2478 ms=6849
index=84   ms=7114       index=2033 ms=493        index=2487 ms=12392
index=85   ms=8003       index=2036 ms=10691      index=2663 ms=5648
index=503  ms=6321       index=2064 ms=12254      index=2719 ms=490
index=1205 ms=561        index=2089 ms=12197

```

**Fourteen of nineteen exceed 5 seconds.** Several cluster (83/84/85,

the balcony and back, so **room transitions are the obvious candidate** --
but that is a hypothesis and this campaign has killed six today, so it is

> **Gate 3's whole-run is a room-transition problem, not a startup problem
> and not a frame-rate problem. 136.7 seconds of a 225-second run is spent
> in 19 ticks.**

**This is the single largest unexplained cost the campaign has found, and
it was sitting in a log file we already had.** Fourth time today the

## Gate 3's whole-run, traced end to end -- FROM DATA ALREADY ON DISK, no new cells

**Applying the habit before designing anything**, the AQON cell already
contained the whole chain.

| link | measurement |
|---|---|
| whole-run `tick_rate` | **15.85** against a 39.2 bar |
| of a 225 s run, stall time | **136.7 s (61%)** in **19 ticks** |
| room transitions | **8, total 102.1 s, mean 12.77 s each** |
| of one transition, `load_new_room` | **1.85 s (14.5%)** |
| `roomload_lighttable_ms` | **0** -- 16-bit, guard is `color_depth == 1`, as expected |

> **Gate 3's whole-run is eight room transitions at ~12.8 seconds each.
> And `load_new_room` is only ~15% of one.**

*Per-transition times, from the engine's own `room_transition` events:*
13.22, 21.57, 12.30, 6.89, 11.95, 12.04, 11.99, 12.18 s.

### So ~85% of a transition is NOT room loading

**A corroborating figure from the same cell:** `preloop_ms` is 2022, yet
room 1 reports `ready` at **t_ms=12426**. That is **~10.4 s between the
pre-loop finishing and the first room being ready** -- time that is
neither engine init (outside the anchor) nor `load_new_room` (1.85 s).

**The leading candidate is the screen fades**, which is also the
coordinator's top-ranked guess and has form: Gate 1's patch 0106 found a
fade doing pointless work. At 16-bit a fade blends **460,800 bytes per
step** against 8-bit's 64,000, and at the ~17 MB/s measured for RAM-to-RAM
traffic even a modest step count runs to seconds.

**Written as a candidate, not a conclusion.** Today's record on confident
mechanisms is 0 for 6, and the specific thing still unmeasured is *which
phase inside the transition* holds the 10.9 s.

**Next instrument: bracket INSIDE the transition** -- fade-out, room load,
fade-in as separate terms. A single "transition took 12.8 s" bracket
restates what we already know; the fix for a fade is completely different
from the fix for a load, and one may be skippable while the other is
irreducible.

### Two stall phenomena, kept apart deliberately

**These are NOT the 603/1807 stalls**, and conflating them would be easy
later:

| | **AQ transition stalls** | **603/1807 stalls** |

| magnitude | **~7.2 s** average tick, 12.8 s per transition | **~275 ms** |
| fixture | AGS Quest, 16-bit | `bench8`, Mode 13h, 8-bit |
| pattern | ~3 consecutive ticks per transition | deterministic at fixed indices |
| blocks | **Gate 3** whole-run | **Gate 2** whole-run |

**Twenty-six times different in magnitude, on different fixtures, at
different depths, blocking different gates.**

## Patch 0121 on hardware: the transition is FADES. Fade-out is a fixed 5.25 s.

AGS Quest, HW-486-66, `binary_sha12=f5742942e37f`. Per-transition phases
from the four milestone stamps:

| room | fade-out | load | setup | fade-in + gameplay |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 5.21 | 1.82 | 0.01 | 6.53 |
| 3 | 5.20 | 1.91 | 0.03 | 51.64 |
| 4 | 5.25 | 1.79 | 0.02 | 25.96 |
| 4 | 5.51 | 1.51 | 0.92 | 7.74 |
| 3 | **0.01** | 1.57 | 0.01 | 6.15 |
| 4 | 5.17 | 1.46 | 0.01 | 10.01 |
| 3 | 5.18 | 1.52 | 0.02 | 18.96 |
| 4 | 5.21 | 1.51 | 0.01 | 9.84 |
| 3 | 5.25 | 1.65 | 0.01 | -- |

> **Fade-out is a FIXED 5.25 s** -- 5.17 to 5.51 across 8 of 9, exactly the
> near-identical signature predicted for fixed-cost work. **One transition
> shows 0.01 s**, i.e. a transition with no fade at all, which is itself
> useful: the engine can already skip it.

**`load_new_room` is 1.64 s (1.46-1.91)** -- steady, and only **13%** of a
12.77 s transition. The content-dependent variance the spread suggested is
**not in the load**.

### Fades are ~82% of a transition

**Fade-out alone is 42.0 s of the 102.1 s of transition time -- 41%.** The
`fade-in + gameplay` column cannot be separated by these four stamps (my
instrument's limitation, stated rather than papered over), **but its
minimum is 6.15 s**, and if the fade-in costs what the fade-out costs that
leaves a ~0.9 s gameplay floor -- entirely plausible for a scripted
autopilot.

**On that reading fades are ~10.5 s of a 12.77 s transition: 82%.**
**Marked as inferred by symmetry, not measured** -- separating fade-in
needs one more stamp at fade-in completion, which is the obvious next
increment.

### What this means for Gate 3

**Gate 3's whole-run is dominated by screen fades, and a 5.25-second fade
is not loading -- it is animation.** That makes it the *skippable polish*
case rather than the *irreducible work* case, which is the distinction the
operator question was waiting on.

**And there is precedent in this campaign's own record: patch 0106 won
Gate 1 ground by skipping a fade that was animating something invisible.**
This is a different fade doing visible work, so the answer is not
automatically "skip it" -- but **5.25 s per transition on a 486 is not a
crossfade anyone would choose**, and the operator's "tunable features that
could reduce fps/ticks as options" instruction is squarely about this
class of decision.

**Worth stating the arithmetic before any design:** removing fades
entirely would cut ~10.5 s from each of 8 transitions, i.e. ~84 s from a
225 s run. **Whole-run would go from 15.85 to roughly 25.4** -- still short
of 39.2, but it is by far the largest lever identified for Gate 3, and it
composes with everything else.

## Gate 3's whole-run bar: the arithmetic CHECKS OUT, and the bar is unreachable with 8 transitions

**Verified independently, all four figures reproduce:**

| | |
|---|---|
| runtime (`preloop` 2022 + `loop` 223538) | **225.6 s**, 3587 ticks -> 15.90 (reported 15.85) |
| to clear 39.2, the run must fit in | **91.5 s** |
| 3587 ticks at 40 Hz need | **89.7 s** |
| **total non-tick budget for the whole run** | **1.83 s** |
| **8 room loads alone** (8 x 1.64) | **13.1 s = 7.2x the entire budget** |

| scenario | runtime | whole-run |
|---|---|---|
| remove fades (84 s) | 141.6 s | **25.3** |
| remove fades **and every room load** | 128.4 s | **27.9** |
| **perfect run: ticks + irreducible loads only** | 102.8 s | **34.9** |

> **Even a perfect run -- zero fades, zero stalls, nothing but ticks and
> the loads themselves -- reaches 34.9 against a 39.2 bar. The bar is
> unreachable with 8 room transitions, by construction.**

### And the sharpest way to say why

**Gate 1 and Gate 2 both pass this bar on fixtures that never change
room.** Trilby's 5000-tick window loads room 1 once, inside the pre-loop,
and never transitions; `bench8` is a single room. **AGS Quest transitions
eight times.**

> **The 39.2 whole-run bar is, in practice, "your fixture must not load
> anything". It measures whether a fixture transitions, not how fast the
> port is.** That is the same shape as Gate 2's 40-displayed-frames bar,
> which our own fixture could only ever produce 20 of.

### But the transition count is OUR choice, which changes the question

**`tests/harness/packages/agsquest/overlay/AutoPilot.asc` is our own
overlay** -- we author AGS Quest's route. It reads **no config file**
(unlike BENCH8's `BENCH.CFG`), so the 18 phases and their ~8 transitions
are **hardcoded by us, not a property of the game.**

**So this is "the bar and the fixture disagree", not "the port cannot do
it"** -- and that is the easier conversation. Options, for the operator
rather than for me:

- **Change the fixture** -- fewer transitions, or a transition-free variant
  for the tick bar. Cheap, but a less representative workload.
- **Change the bar** -- judge whole-run on a fixture-appropriate basis, or
  exclude transition time as Gate 2's completeness bar excluded frames the
  content never generated.
- **Keep both and accept Gate 3's whole-run cannot pass**, treating fps as
  the real target.

**No recommendation from me on which.** It is the second time a gate's
terms have met arithmetic they cannot satisfy, and the first time that was
resolved by the operator upholding the terms -- so this is squarely their
call, and worth raising before a week is spent optimising toward a number
that cannot be reached.

## Operator decisions (2026-09-19): fades, and splitting Gate 3's whole-run

### 1. Fades: make them FAST, keep them VISIBLE

**Not skipped.** Target roughly **1 s** instead of 5.25, shipping fast by
default with **a tunable to restore the full-length fade** -- the standing
"fastest by default, tunable features that could reduce fps/ticks as
options" instruction applied directly.

### 2. Gate 3's whole-run SPLITS INTO TWO BARS -- the Gate 2 medicine

1. **A gameplay tick-rate figure with transition time excluded** -- does
   the port sustain 40 Hz during play?
2. **A separate per-transition time budget**, with its own number -- are
   transitions acceptable?

**The reasoning matters as much as the ruling, and is recorded so this is
never read later as a bar relaxed to reach a pass:** excluding transitions
and saying nothing more **would hide a real defect** -- 12.8 s room
changes are genuinely bad for a player. Folding them into a rate that
assumes zero loading **measures our own authored route rather than the
port**. Two bars measure both honestly.

**Precedent, stated explicitly: this is the SECOND gate whose single
number was hiding two different questions, and in both cases the fix was
to stop conflating them rather than to move a threshold.** Gate 2's
`fps_p50` was hiding "renders fast" from "actually displays frames";
Gate 3's whole-run was hiding "sustains 40 Hz" from "loads quickly".

## The fade is 13 steps at 404 ms -- and the present is only 4% of it

**Measured, not inferred** (patch 0122 counter): **13 steps** per fade, not
the 64 a default speed would give.

| per step | ms | share |
|---|---|---|
| `render_to_screen()` (with 0120's alias) | 16.7 | **4%** |
| **`Fill` + `TransBlendBlt`** | **387** | **96%** |
| total | 404 | |

**~1.4 MB of traffic per step in 387 ms is 3.6 MB/s** -- against 17.0 MB/s
measured for a straight RAM-to-RAM copy. **That gap is the per-pixel alpha
blend: it reads, computes and writes, where a copy only reads and writes.**

### This decides the route, and it is the one that costs the operator nothing

**The cheap-per-step route wins outright.** With only 13 steps, cutting
steps is the wrong lever -- it would have to go to ~3 to reach 1 s, which
is a visibly coarse fade for no good reason.

**Make the per-step operation cheap and all 13 steps survive.** If the
blend came down to copy speed the fade would be **~568 ms, comfortably
inside the ~1 s target, with the animation exactly as authored.** A fade
to black at 16-bit is a shift-and-mask per pixel, not a general alpha
blend, so there is real headroom.

**Still to verify before this is called done: a picture on the real
monitor.** This is a visible-quality change and no fps number can say
whether it still looks like a fade.

## Patch 0123 on hardware: fade 5.23 -> 2.30 s (2.27x). Real, but SHORT of the ~1 s target.

A/B on AGS Quest, arms `46e1d31a5ec2` (0122, counter only) and
`d0523a6c08e5` (0123, LUT), both carrying the counter:

| | stock blend | LUT | |
|---|---|---|---|
| fade-out, 8 transitions | 5.18-5.49, **mean 5.23 s** | 2.23-2.55, **mean 2.30 s** | **2.27x** |
| whole-run `tick_rate` | 15.85 | **20.47** | **+4.62 (+29%)** |
| `fps_p50` | 22.93 | 23.41 | +0.48 |
| steps | 13 | **13** | preserved |

**Stated against the number set in advance: the target was ~1 s and the
estimate 1.0-1.3 s. Measured 2.30 s. That is a miss, and it is reported as
one** -- the saving is real and large, but it did not reach what was
predicted.

### Why it fell short

Per step: **177 ms**, of which the present is ~16.7, leaving **~160 ms of
LUT work** for 0.92 MB -- **5.7 MB/s**, against 3.6 for the stock blend and
17.0 for a plain copy.

**So the LUT is 1.6x faster than the blend, not the 4-5x a copy-speed
assumption predicted.** At 230,400 pixels that is ~45 cycles per pixel for
unpack, three table reads and repack -- plausible on a 486, and the honest
reading is that **per-pixel work on 230,400 pixels is expensive whatever
the arithmetic**, because each pixel still costs a read, several
dependent lookups and a write.

**The coordinator's revised estimate was closer than my 568 ms and still
optimistic by ~2x. Both estimates assumed the bottleneck was arithmetic;
the measurement says a large part of it is the per-pixel access pattern
itself.**

### Where it leaves things

- **Whole-run 15.85 -> 20.47 is the single biggest movement Gate 3 has
  seen**, and it composes with 0120's fps win.
- **A transition is now ~2.30 + 1.64 + ~2.30 = ~6.2 s**, down from ~12.8 --
  which is the number bar 2's budget should be argued from, once fade-in
  is separately confirmed.
- **Not yet done, and required: a picture on the real monitor.** The LUT
  route's risk is **banding**, not coarseness, and no timing number can
  show it. The fade must be captured before this is called finished.
- **Further headroom exists but is not free**: two pixels per 32-bit word,
  or a single shared table where the fade colour makes red and blue
  identical. Whether 2.30 s is acceptable, or worth another round, is a
  judgement for the operator now that the cost of each increment is known.

### Banding risk, answered analytically -- the LUT is MORE precise than what it replaces

The concern with a table route is banding rather than coarseness. Settled
by comparing the two formulas rather than by eye.

**Allegro's `_blender_trans16` (`libsrc/allegro/src/colblend.c:163`)
quantises alpha to 32 levels** -- `n = (n+1)/8`, then `(x-y)*n/32 + y`.
**The LUT interpolates at full 255 precision.**

| | |
|---|---|
| endpoints (a=0, a=255) | **identical** in both -- fade start and end are bit-exact |
| max deviation, all 32 channel levels x 13 steps | **1 of 31**, and in the direction of *more* precision |

**So the LUT cannot band worse than the stock blend; where they differ it
is because the LUT is smoother.** That also explains why the settled
screenshots (PH01/02/03) are byte-identical across both arms while
intermediate frames are not required to be.

**The monitor capture is still outstanding** and remains the right final
check -- an analysis says what the pixels should be, a photograph says
what the monitor shows, and the two have come apart before on this
hardware. **But the risk it is checking is now known to be low, and the
failure mode it would catch is not banding.**

### Fades: BANKED at 2.30 s, closed by operator decision

**No further fade optimisation.** Another round might reach ~1.3 s, worth
~1 s across 16 fades, ~16 s of a 175 s run, ~1.7 whole-run points --
against fps sitting at 23.41 with **both its levers untouched.**

*Recorded for anyone who revisits it:* **~45 cycles per pixel measured**
for unpack, three dependent lookups and repack. A tight LUT loop should
manage 20-25, so **hand-optimising the inner loop is better value than
two-pixel packing or a shared table.** A note, not a task.

**And record the constant, because it prices every future per-pixel
operation on this machine: ~45 cycles/pixel for a dependent-lookup
transform at 230,400 pixels.** Both estimates today failed by assuming
arithmetic was the bottleneck when the access pattern dominates.

## The ~35 s of "hidden" stalls: characterised WITHOUT a cell, and both hypotheses die

**The sprite-cache hypothesis is dead, killed by the existing cell's own
startup log** -- and checking that cost nothing:

```
Sprite cache set: 16384 KB
Sprite cache: 4 -> 73 KB
memory_min_free_kb=144256
```

**A 16 MB cache that only ever grew to 73 KB cannot evict, cannot thrash,
and cannot miss.** And 141 MB free kills the swap variant of the same idea
(my own hypothesis, formed on seeing a 32 MB default on a 16 MB machine --
the engine had already capped it).

### What the stalls actually are: AutoPilot's own scripted phases

Correlating every stall tick against `AUTOPLT.LOG`'s phase boundaries:

> **All 19 stalls fall 0-3 ticks after a phase begin or ok. Every single
> one.**

| phase | stall time | count |
|---|---|---|
| **gem** | **33.99 s** | 6 |
| **splash** | **19.71 s** | 4 |
| interior | 9.99 s | 2 |
| **save** | **7.76 s** | 1 |
| settle | 5.96 s | 1 |
| unlock | 5.14 s | 3 |
| guimenu | 2.62 s | 1 |
| dialog | 0.50 s | 1 |
| **total** | **85.66 s** | 19 |

**So the ~35 s is not one hidden engine defect. It is distributed across
the fixture's scripted operations**, and the coordinator's hope that
removing it takes bar 1 from 30.3 to ~40 **does not hold** -- there is no
single thing to remove. Several of these are work the game legitimately
asks for, and a real player doing the same actions would pay the same
costs.

### But three of them are real player-facing costs worth their own look

- **`save` -- 7.76 s in ONE tick.** This is `SaveGame` at 16-bit, and it
  has **direct prior art**: patch 0108 found restart-point compression
  costing 494 ms at 8-bit on a 9 KB save. At 16-bit with a screenshot the
  payload is far larger. **A player saving the game waits nearly eight
  seconds.**
- **`gem` -- 33.99 s across 6 stalls**, the single largest group, and
  unexamined.
- **`splash` -- 19.71 s across 4**, at startup.

**None of this is a defect in the sense the 10991 ms stall suggested -- it
is the fixture doing expensive things -- but "the game takes 7.8 s to
save" is a finding worth having regardless of any gate.**

**Bounded as instructed: characterised, reported, not chased.** The save
cost is the one with prior art and a player-visible consequence; the rest
would each need their own investigation and this is exactly where the
603/1807 probe went wrong.

## Correction to my own framing: "legitimate" is not "acceptable"

I wrote that much of the stall time is "work the game legitimately asks
for" and that "a real player doing the same actions pays the same costs."
**Both true, and both describe what TRIGGERS a cost rather than whether the
cost is acceptable.**

> **A player clicking a gem and waiting 5.7 seconds is a bad port,
> however correct the script is.**

**`gem` is 33.99 s across 6 stalls -- the largest group in the table and
entirely unexamined.** Recorded so "legitimate" does not quietly file it
as "fine".

*Coordinator error recorded alongside the others:* the claim that removing
~35 s would take bar 1 from 30.3 to ~40 was the load-bearing reason for
redirecting a cell, and it was wrong -- the time is distributed scripted
work with no single thing to remove. (The cell was not spent; the
characterisation came from existing data.)

## FRAME for Gate 3, offered as a hypothesis: one cost class, several triggers

Every stall follows a phase boundary -- a discrete scripted action -- and
the pattern across what has been measured is consistent:

| operation | cost | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| screen fade | 5.25 s -> 2.30 s | per-pixel over 460,800 px |
| `save` | **7.76 s** | screenshot at 16-bit + compression (suspected) |
| `gem` | **33.99 s / 6** | unexamined |
| `splash` | 19.71 s / 4 | unexamined |

> **The emerging story for Gate 3 is not "rendering is slow" but "ANY
> full-screen operation at 16-bit costs seconds."** 460,800 pixels at the
> measured **~45 cycles/pixel** for a dependent-lookup transform is ~0.3 s
> *per pass*, and these operations make several passes.

**If that holds, these are not separate bugs -- they are one cost class
with several triggers, and patch 0123's LUT fade is a template rather than
a one-off.**

**It is a hypothesis and today's record is 0 for 6 on those, so it is
written as the frame for where to look next, not as a finding.** Its value
is predictive: it says to expect seconds from anything touching the whole
frame, and to check pixel count x passes before assuming a mechanism.

## Characterised, NOT chased -- recorded as defects, not measurements

**`save`: 7.76 s in a single tick.** `SaveGame` at 16-bit. **Direct prior
art: patch 0108 found restart-point compression costing 494 ms at 8-bit on
a 9,397-byte payload.** At 16-bit with a screenshot the payload is far
larger, making compression plus screenshot capture the obvious suspects,
and probably a short patch.

**Not a gate lever, and it should not jump the queue. But an eight-second
save is the kind of thing that decides whether someone finishes the game,
and it belongs in the record as a DEFECT rather than a measurement.**

**`gem`: 33.99 s across 6 stalls.** Largest single group. Unexamined. No
prior art, no suspected mechanism -- the frame above predicts a
full-screen operation, which is where to look first.

## Patch 0124 (narrowed present): +0.74 fps. Real, attributable, and SMALL.

Within-build A/B on AGS Quest, same binary, `DOSAGS_DIRTY_PRESENT`
toggled -- so layout and code size cancel by construction.

| | off | on | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `present_update_window` | 16.83 ms | **15.40 ms** | **-1.43 (-8.5%)** |
| `fps_p50` | 23.00 | **23.74** | **+0.74** |
| whole-run | 20.39 | 20.49 | +0.10 |

**Correctness first: all three AGS Quest screenshots byte-identical
between arms** under DOSBox, with the alias and narrowing both active.

**The measured saving matches the pixel arithmetic** -- 6.8% fewer pixels
pushed predicted ~-6.8%, measured -8.5%. **The instrument and the model
agree**, which is worth as much here as the gain.

### Why it is small: a single bounding box is coarse

**Only 407 of 3500 frames narrowed -- 11.6%.** The rest went full not
because anything demanded it (`reason="-"`, so the full latch never fired)
but because **the bbox was not smaller than the frame.** One sprite at
top-left and another at bottom-right make a full-screen union, and AGS
Quest has content spread across the frame most of the time.

**The headroom is real but needs finer granularity.** AGS's own
`draw_software.cpp` dirty system already tracks **spans -- up to 4 per
scanline** -- and this patch collapses all of that into one rectangle
before using it. **Pushing the spans through as a real rect list is where
the rest of the win is**, and the backend already accepts one
(`SDL_dosframebuffer.c` per-rect loops, patch SDL/0033). That is a larger
job than this was.

### Gate 3 standing

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| `fps_p50` | **23.74** | vs 40 -- **1.69x short** |
| bar 1 (gameplay ticks) | ~30.3 | vs 40 |
| whole-run | 20.49 | vs 39.2 |

**From 13.32 fps at the start of this work to 23.74 -- 1.78x -- via
0120 (blit elimination, +9.64), 0123 (LUT fade, +0.48) and 0124
(narrowed present, +0.74).** The overwhelming majority is 0120.

**Stated plainly: the remaining 1.69x on fps has no identified lever of
that size.** The present path is now 15.40 ms of a ~42 ms frame; the rest
is engine work spread across `scene_construct` and the tick phases, none
of which has shown a single dominant term. **Further fps gains on this
fixture look like many small wins rather than one large one** -- which is
worth saying before anyone budgets for another 0120.

## FULL 16-bit frame accounting -- and "17 ms unattributed" was an artefact

**The breakdown does exist; the brackets NEST, so per-call means cannot be
subtracted from a frame budget.** `update_game_once_total` alone totals
245 s of a 175 s run, which is only possible because it contains the
others. Comparing a 15.40 ms per-call mean against a ~42 ms frame and
calling the difference unattributed mixes two different denominators.

**Accounting properly, per TICK, over non-stall time** (runtime 175.1 s
minus 85.7 s of stalls = 89.4 s over 3587 ticks = **24.9 ms/tick**):

| term | total | per call | **per tick** | share |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `present_update_window` | 42.1 s | 15.40 ms | **11.73 ms** | **47.1%** |
| `scene_construct` | 21.7 s | 8.65 ms | **6.05 ms** | **24.3%** |
| `render_backbuffer` | 18.1 s | 6.60 ms | **5.04 ms** | **20.2%** |
| **accounted** | | | **22.82 ms** | **91.6%** |
| remainder | | | 2.10 ms | 8.4% |

> **Three terms account for 91.6% of a non-stall frame. There is no
> 17 ms hole.**

*And `script_vm` -- 103.7 s over just 497 calls -- is not per-frame work at
all.* It is the blocking scripted phases, i.e. **the stalls already
characterised** (gem, splash, save). Counting it as frame cost would
double-count what the stall table already reports.

### What this changes about "no lever of that size"

**My claim was right in substance but I could not have known it -- I
asserted a breakdown I did not have, and the coordinator was right to push
back.** Now it is measured, and it says something more useful than
"diffuse":

- **`present_update_window` is still the largest single term at 47%**, and
  it is at the bus ceiling. Only fewer pixels help -- span-level narrowing
  or a smaller mode.
- **`render_backbuffer` at 20.2% has never been examined.** It is the
  third-largest term in the frame and nothing in this campaign has looked
  at it.
- **`scene_construct` at 24.3%** is sprite composition, the term the
  8-bit work found was only 13% there.

**So there are two unexamined terms totalling 44% of the frame, which is a
better position than "many small wins".** The next measurement should be
inside `render_backbuffer` and `scene_construct`, not another present
optimisation.

## Letterbox hypothesis: ALREADY FIXED, by patch 0100. Both halves dead.

**Checked before bracketing, and it cost one read.**

`gfx/ali3dsw.cpp:1194-1205, 1307-1317` -- patch 0100 already does exactly
the proposed optimisation. Its own comment describes the bug it fixed:

> "The old rule cost every letterboxed game (AGS Quest 640x360, any true
> 320x200 game at 2x, any centred unscaled picture) the unchanged-frame
> skip, the fast blit AND a full-window black fill on every single
> present... On AGS Quest this fill was 614,400 bytes, ~15 ms, 1231 times
> a run."

**The margins are filled black ONCE**, tracked by `_marginsClean*`, and
thereafter `full_update = !has_border` is **false** -- so every subsequent
present pushes only `dst`, the 640x360 game area.

**My own measurement independently confirms it:** `present_update_window`
at 15.40 ms and the measured 27.5 MB/s ceiling is **~423 KB pushed**.
640x360x2 is **460,800 bytes**; 640x480x2 would be **614,400**. **We are
already pushing the game area.**

**And the second half dies too:** `render_backbuffer` operates on AGS's
*virtual screen*, which is 640x360 and **contains no letterbox rows at
all** -- the bars exist only in the window surface. So its 5.04 ms/tick is
not bar-painting either.

### Consequence for the 640x400 mode question: it is MOOT

**Since the letterbox is never pushed, a 640x400 mode would save nothing
on the present term.** The bars cost only VRAM that the CRT scans out,
which is not our time. **The rung question at 16-bit is therefore not
"fewer letterbox rows" -- it is only "fewer game pixels", which means
downscaling, which is per-pixel work at ~45 cycles/pixel and would cost
more than it saves.**

**So the 8-bit ladder's logic does not transfer, for a concrete reason:
Mode 13h won by removing an upscale, and there is no upscale here to
remove.** Recorded so the operator's resolution concession is not spent on
a change that cannot pay.

**Seventh time today the answer was already available** -- this one in a
patch comment describing the exact optimisation being proposed, plus a
byte count already in hand.

## `render_backbuffer` structure: no redundancy found. ~1 batch per sprite.

**Looked for structure before efficiency**, per the redundancy-first
principle (this campaign's biggest win, 0120's +9.64, came from redundancy
in an unexamined path; its best micro-optimisation was +1.20 -- **8x
apart**).

Measured over 3500 frames:

| | per frame |
|---|---|
| sprite batches | **6.59** |
| **`ClearTransparent` calls** | **0** |
| cleared pixels | **0** |
| sprites composited | **7.18** |

**The per-batch full-surface clear -- the obvious redundancy candidate --
never fires.** Every batch is opaque or has no surface. That hypothesis is
dead.

**And the blit itself looks efficient:** 5.04 ms/tick over 7.18 sprites is
**0.70 ms per sprite**, which for a ~100x200 sprite is **~2.3 cycles per
pixel** -- a fast masked copy, not the 45 cycles/pixel of a transform.

### The one structural observation: 1.09 sprites per batch

**6.59 batches for 7.18 sprites.** Whatever per-batch setup exists --
surface selection, transform preparation, the batch loop's own bookkeeping
-- is paid **once per sprite** rather than amortised across many.

**Whether that overhead is material is NOT yet measured**, and on today's
record I am not going to assert it. It needs one bracket around per-batch
setup versus per-sprite blitting. **But it is the only structural
irregularity in the term**, and it is where the next bracket goes.

**Honest interim read, flagged early as requested:** so far
`render_backbuffer` looks like **legitimate work done once** -- seven
sprite blits at a sensible cost per pixel. **If the batch bracket confirms
that, this term is close to irreducible and the operator should hear that
rather than have us grind at it.**

## `render_backbuffer` measured properly: memory-bound at the ceiling. My 2.3 cycles/pixel was wrong.

**The efficiency argument rested on a sprite size I assumed rather than
measured, and the coordinator's inversion was right: 0.70 ms at 17 MB/s is
~12 KB, which a 100x200 sprite is not.**

**Measured composited area, 3500 frames:**

| | |
|---|---|
| sprites/frame | 7.18 |
| **pixels/sprite** | **2,383** (~48x48, not 100x200) |
| **pixels/frame** | **17,117** = 34,234 bytes |

**So the sprites are small -- the coordinator's first branch -- and the
arithmetic now closes:**

| | |
|---|---|
| masked blit touches ~3 streams (read src, read dst, write dst) | **100 KB/frame** |
| in 5.04 ms | **20.4 MB/s** |
| measured RAM-to-RAM ceiling | 17.0 MB/s |
| per pixel | **19.4 cycles** at 6 bytes = **3.2 cycles/byte** |
| 20.4 MB/s at 66 MHz | 0.31 bytes/cycle = **3.2 cycles/byte** |

**Two independent routes agree at 3.2 cycles/byte, and the throughput is
slightly ABOVE the RAM-to-RAM figure** -- consistent with 2.4 KB sprites
being cache-resident so only part of the traffic reaches main memory.

> **`render_backbuffer` is memory-bound at this machine's ceiling. It is
> seven small sprite blits moving 100 KB, and the blit cannot go faster.**

**My earlier "~2.3 cycles/pixel, a fast masked copy" was wrong by 8x**, and
wrong in the direction that would have ended the investigation with a
false reassurance. **The real figure is 19.4 cycles/pixel -- and it is
still irreducible, but for the opposite reason: not because the code is
fast, but because the memory is slow.**

**That distinction matters for what comes next.** "The code is efficient"
invites micro-optimisation; "the memory is saturated" says the only levers
are **fewer pixels or fewer streams** -- and fewer streams is real, since a
masked blit reading the destination could in principle be avoided for
opaque sprites.

**Not asserted, not yet measured:** the batch bracket (`rb_sprite_time`)
still needs a hardware cell to separate per-batch setup from the blitting
half. **And `scene_construct` at 24.3% -- the LARGER unexamined term --
remains untouched. No outlook conclusion until both are measured.**

## CORRECTION AGAIN: the blit is TWO streams, and the term is COMPUTE-bound with headroom

**I inferred three streams. Source says two.**
`libsrc/allegro/src/c/cspr.h:68-73`, the masked blit's inner loop:

```c
uint32_t c = GET_MEMORY_PIXEL(s);      // read source
if (!IS_SPRITE_MASK(src, c))
    PUT_MEMORY_PIXEL(d, c);            // write destination
```

**The destination is never read.** At 16-bit every pixel is a whole word,
so there is no sub-word merge to justify one.

| stream count | KB/frame | throughput |
|---|---|---|
| 3 (my assumption) | 100 | 20.4 MB/s -- *above* the ceiling |
| **2 (from source)** | **67** | **13.6 MB/s** |
| 2, with ~60% of pixels non-mask | 53 | **10.9 MB/s** |
| **measured RAM-to-RAM ceiling** | | **17.0 MB/s** |

> **Below the ceiling. `render_backbuffer` is COMPUTE-bound, not
> memory-bound, and my "irreducible" conclusion was wrong.**

**19.4 cycles/pixel supports the same reading independently:** a tight
masked blit -- load, compare, branch, conditional store -- should manage
**6-10 cycles** on a 486. Nineteen points at per-pixel loop overhead: this
is a generic, non-unrolled C loop with two pointer increments and a
counter per pixel.

**If the loop reached 10 cycles/pixel the term goes 5.04 -> 2.60 ms/tick,
saving ~2.44 ms of a ~42 ms frame.**

### The same error twice in a row, in mirrored positions

**The sprite dimension was invented and sat in the DENOMINATOR. The stream
count was inferred and sat in the NUMERATOR.** Both produced a confident
bound; both were wrong; both would have closed the investigation.

> **Rule for this path: check every quantity you did not measure before
> drawing a bound from it.** A bound is only as good as its least-measured
> input, and neither of these inputs was measured.

### And the deeper lesson, which is the one worth keeping

**Both wrong numbers CONFIRMED what I already believed** -- that the term
was efficient, then that it was irreducible. **A number that agrees with
your prior gets less scrutiny than one that contradicts it, which is
exactly backwards: the confirming number is the one that ends
investigations.** Eight hypotheses died today to contradicting evidence
that got checked immediately; these two survived a round each because they
agreed with me.

## Write-only bandwidth measured -- the blit ceiling is 7.8 cycles/pixel

`HW-486-66-2026-09-19-bwprobe-writeonly-PRBOUT.TXT`. Both instruments
(this case and `rb_sprite_time`) were checked under DOSBox-X before the
cell, which is the rule I broke last time.

| loop | MB/s payload | flat across sizes? |
|---|---|---|
| CONTROL sysram->sysram `movsl`/`memcpy` | **17.0** | yes, 64KB..614KB |
| WRITEONLY sysram `stosl`/`memset` | **40.9** | yes, 64KB..614KB |

`stosl` and `memset` agree to three digits, as do `movsl` and `memcpy`,
so this is the bus, not a code-generation artifact.

### What it does NOT do: raise the masked blit's ceiling

**I asked for this number while entertaining the idea that it would.**
It does not, and the reason is the thing I had already established and
then failed to carry forward: **the masked blit reads as well as writes.**
`cspr.h:68-73` loads every source pixel because the mask test needs it.
So the ceiling that governs it is the **copy** ceiling, 17.0 MB/s
payload, not the write-only one.

At 2 bytes/pixel and 66 MHz:

    17.0 MB/s payload = 8.5 Mpx/s = 66e6 / 8.5e6 = 7.8 cycles/pixel

**7.8 cycles/pixel is the hard floor** for any 16-bit read-plus-write
inner loop on this machine, measured rather than reasoned. My earlier
"6-10 cycles achievable" was a guess that happens to bracket it; 6 was
never reachable and I should not have written it.

### Sanity check: the model reproduces the measurement

At the measured 19.4 cycles/pixel and 17,117 sprite px/frame:

    17,117 x 19.4 = 332,070 cycles = 5.03 ms  (measured: 5.04)

The model lands on the measurement to within a percent, which is the
first time this frame budget's arithmetic has closed on itself. So the
saving is calculable rather than hoped for:

| target | cycles/px | ms/tick | saving |
|---|---|---|---|
| today | 19.4 | 5.03 | -- |
| realistic (`rep movsd` runs + mask test) | 10 | 2.59 | **2.44 ms** |
| bus floor (pure copy, no mask test at all) | 7.8 | 2.02 | 3.01 ms |

**2.4 ms/tick is the honest number to plan against**, not 3.4.

### What the write-only number IS good for

It prices a read against a write, which nothing else here has:

    write byte:  66e6 / 40.9e6 = 1.61 cycles
    copy byte:   66e6 / 17.0e6 = 3.88 cycles
    => read byte: 3.88 - 1.61  = 2.27 cycles

**A read costs 1.4x a write on this machine** (write posting, as
expected on a 486). Two consequences for the tighter blit:

1. **Skipping the write on a transparent pixel saves only 41% of that
   pixel**, not 100% -- the read is unavoidable because it IS the mask
   test. A transparency-heavy sprite is therefore much less of a win than
   the "skip the work" framing suggests.
2. **An opaque run is the whole prize.** A run handled by `rep movsd`
   pays the copy ceiling, 7.8 cycles/pixel, against today's 19.4 -- a
   2.5x improvement on that span. The coordinator's run-based suggestion
   is the right shape, and this says why: the win comes from the opaque
   spans, so run *detection* only pays for itself where runs are long.
   **Run-length distribution is the next thing to measure, before writing
   the loop** -- if the sprites are speckled, run detection costs more
   than it saves.

### Pre-registered: batch bracket cell RBB2 (re-run, emitter now wired)

**Question:** of `render_backbuffer`'s ms/tick, how much is the sprite
blitting and how much is the per-batch scaffolding around it? 1.09
sprites/batch has been unpriced since the structure measurement.

**Prediction:** `rb_sprite_time` >= 90% of `render_backbuffer`. Under
DOSBox-X it was 4607/4624 = **99.6%**, and the scaffolding is fixed CPU
work while the blit is bus-bound -- on a machine where the bus is 20x
slower relative to the core, the blit's share should go UP, not down.

**Threshold:** if `rb_sprite_time` < 80% of `render_backbuffer`, there is
a real per-batch overhead term and it gets its own investigation. At
>= 90% I close the batch question and spend nothing further on it.

**Invalidity:** `rb_sprite_time` absent or `calls=0` (the failure mode
that wasted RBB1); `render_backbuffer calls` not within 10% of RBB1's
2731, which would mean a different workload rather than a cleaner
measurement.

**Note on what this cell cannot settle:** a high ratio says the
scaffolding is cheap, NOT that the blit is efficient -- efficiency is the
19.4-vs-7.8 cycles/pixel question above, and this cell does not touch it.

## scene_construct measured on its own terms -- it is not scaffolding

The coordinator's ordering was right and my framing of this term was
wrong. I had been carrying `scene_construct` as "draw-LIST building",
which is what patch 0081's own comment in
`dos_port_tick_timing.h` calls it and what the bracket's own comment in
`ac/draw.cpp` asserts: *"everything in this bracket only walks room/UI
objects and appends to gfxDriver's draw list, nothing here touches the
back buffer or the video hardware."*

**That comment is false**, and upstream says so three hundred lines
away. `construct_game_scene` -> `construct_room_view` ->
`prepare_room_sprites` reaches `update_room_invreg_and_reset`, and
directly above that call in `ac/draw.cpp:2481-2484` sits a comment by
AGS's own author:

    // TODO: (by CJ)
    // the following line takes up to 50% of the game CPU time at
    // high resolutions and colour depths - if we can optimise it
    // somehow, significant performance gains to be had

**640x360x16 is exactly "high resolutions and colour depths."** The line
is the background restore: it repaints the room background over every
dirty rect to erase last frame's sprites. That is pixel work, inside the
bracket I had labelled as containing none.

I wrote that bracket comment myself in patch 0081 and never followed the
call chain past `construct_game_scene`'s first line. **The 24.3% was
never unexplained -- it was mislabelled**, and a comment I wrote made it
look explained.

### Patch 0126: both instruments, both verified before any cell

`bg_restore` (timing) to `RUNMANI.LOG`, `bgstruct` (pixel counters) to
`STDOUT.TXT` -- the same split `rbstruct` already uses, checked in both
files rather than one. DOSBox-X structure, 3,699 restores:

| quantity | value |
|---|---|
| `slow_px` (non-memcpy Blit arm) | **0** -- always the fast arm |
| `whole` (full-surface Blit frames) | 23 of 3,699 = **0.6%** |
| mean restored px/frame | **32,514** |
| late-phase px/frame (last 199 frames) | **142,105** |

### What that costs on the target

The restore is an unmasked `memcpy` per span, so it runs at the copy
ceiling measured this morning, 17.0 MB/s payload:

    32,514 px x 2 bytes = 65,028 bytes / 17.0 MB/s = 3.83 ms/tick

**That is not far off `render_backbuffer`'s whole 5.04 ms, and it is a
term I had written off as list-walking.** Two consequences:

1. **The background restore moves ~1.9x the pixel volume the sprite blit
   does** (32,514 vs 17,117 px/frame). Every optimisation argument I have
   made about the sprite blit applies with more force here -- except that
   this loop is *already* at the copy ceiling, so unlike the masked blit
   there is no cycles-per-pixel win available. **The only lever here is
   moving fewer pixels.**
2. **Each of the 23 whole-surface frames costs 460,800 bytes = 27.1 ms**,
   a guaranteed dropped frame. Rare enough not to matter for a mean, but
   it is exactly the kind of event the Gate 2 display-completeness bar is
   built to catch, so it is now named rather than lurking.

### The redundancy, stated without overclaiming

The restore paints background across the dirty area; the sprite blit then
paints sprites over part of it. **Every pixel where an opaque sprite
pixel lands was written twice.** That is real redundancy and it is the
shape my own `docs/optimization` note predicts ("redundancy in unexamined
code beats efficiency in known code").

**But I am not claiming it is recoverable.** Skipping the restore under a
sprite requires knowing which sprite pixels are opaque, which is the mask
test, which requires the source read -- the same read the blit already
pays for. A merged restore-and-composite pass could in principle pay that
read once instead of twice, but that is a rewrite of two loops on the
strength of an argument, not a measurement, and the measurement to make
first is **how much of the restored area is actually covered**. Unmeasured.

### Outlook stays held

The coordinator's condition was `scene_construct` measured on its own
terms before any outlook. It is measured structurally under DOSBox-X;
**it is not yet measured on the target**, and DOSBox's CPU-to-memory
ratio is nothing like a 486's, so the 20% bg_restore share of
`scene_construct` seen there should rise sharply on hardware and the
3.83 ms above is arithmetic, not observation. Outlook still held.

### Patch 0127: measure opaque run length BEFORE writing the run-based blit

The bandwidth probe says all the win in a tighter masked blit is in the
opaque spans (a transparent pixel still costs its read, which IS the mask
test). So `rep movsd` over runs only pays if the runs are long, and
**speckled sprites would make run detection cost more than it saves.**

`cspr.h`'s inner loop now counts opaque *runs* -- transparent-to-opaque
transitions -- alongside total and opaque pixels. Mean run length falls
out of runs vs opaque pixels, and that single number decides whether the
loop is worth writing.

**Gated behind `AGS_SPRITE_RUN_STATS=1`, not always on.** Three adds and
a branch inside the engine's hottest loop is exactly the shape this
port's own cache-footprint observations price at ~1 fps. **A stats binary
is for structure only and must never be used for a timing comparison** --
writing that here because the temptation to read an fps number off a
convenient run is precisely how the last several retractions started.

Decision rule, written before the number exists:

| mean opaque run | verdict |
|---|---|
| >= 16 px | write the run-based blit, the 2.5x on those spans is real |
| 6-16 px | marginal; `rep movsd` setup eats it, consider 4-px unrolling instead |
| < 6 px | **do not write it** -- sprites are speckled and detection loses |

was in flight, and the stamp proves the cell was unaffected; that was luck,
not care, and the rule is **do not rebuild while a cell is on the wire**).

batch question is closed.** Validity checks: 2,732 calls against RBB1's
2,731 (within 10%), `rb_sprite_time` present and non-zero.

### The whole-frame table, which is what actually matters here

`fps_p50=23.98`. Every per-tick phase, largest first:

| phase | calls | total ms | ms/call |
|---|---|---|---|
| `render_to_screen_pertick` | 2,502 | 57,626 | 23.0 |
| ... of which `present_update_window` | 2,723 | **42,326** | **15.5** |
| ... of which `render_backbuffer` | 2,732 | 18,263 | 6.69 |
| `scene_construct` | 2,502 | **21,647** | **8.65** |

**Two things here contradict what I have been working on.**

1. **`scene_construct` (8.65 ms) is larger than `render_backbuffer`
   (6.69 ms).** The coordinator ordered it ahead of the blit and was
   right; my mislabelled bracket comment was hiding the bigger term.
2. **`present_update_window` at 15.5 ms/call is larger than both of them
   put together** -- 42.3 s of the run, and I have spent the day tuning a
   6.69 ms term.

### Why the present is still costing a full screen

640x360x16 = 460,800 bytes; at the measured 27.5 MB/s LFB rate that is
16.8 ms, against 15.5 measured. **The present is pushing the whole screen
every frame.** Patch 0124 was supposed to stop that. Its own counters:

    narrow=376 full= 124   px_narrow=34549375  px_full= 28569600
    narrow=376 full= 624   px_narrow=34549375  px_full=143769600
    narrow=376 full=1124   px_narrow=34549375  px_full=258969600
    narrow=376 full=1624   px_narrow=34549375  px_full=374169600
    narrow=376 full=2124   px_narrow=34549375  px_full=489369600

**`narrow` is frozen at 376 and `full` grows by exactly 500 per report.**
After roughly frame 500, every single frame presents full. The narrowing
worked, then stopped, and nothing reported it -- `reason` prints `-`
because `full_reason` is cleared by the per-frame reset while the counters
accumulate, so the one field meant to explain this explains nothing. That
is an instrument bug of the same family as the two I hit today.

### The mechanism, read from source rather than guessed

The alias log says `vscreen alias ON y=60 640x360`: a 640x360 game
letterboxed into a 640x480 window, so `dst = {0, 60, 640, 360}`.

The bbox is accumulated in `invalidate_rect_ds`/`invalidate_rect_global`
in **game/virtual-screen coordinates**, y in 0..359. The gate at
`ali3dsw.cpp:1441-1444` then tests it against **window coordinates**:

    b.x >= dst.x && b.y >= dst.y && b.x+b.w <= dst.x+dst.w && ...

`b.y >= dst.y` is `b.y >= 60`. **Any frame whose dirty region reaches into
the top 60 rows of the game viewport fails the test and presents full.**
Once something at the top of the screen redraws every frame -- a GUI bar,
a status line -- the narrowing is off permanently. That is exactly the
"worked for 376 frames, then never again" shape.

### And the 376 frames that DID narrow were presenting the wrong region

Same mismatch, other direction. Under the patch 0120 alias the virtual
screen IS the window surface offset by 60 rows, so game row `y` lives at
window row `y+60`. `_dp_push = b` hands SDL a rect in game coordinates,
which SDL reads as window coordinates -- **the update lands 60 rows too
high**: the actually-dirty region is never refreshed, and a clean region
above it is pushed instead.

**This is a correctness bug, not only a performance one**, and it has been
invisible because the `PH0N.BMP` baselines are `SaveScreenShot()` captures
of the game's own back buffer -- they never look at the window surface, so
no screenshot check in this project could have caught it. **A present-path
bug needs a capture of the screen, not of the buffer.**

I am stating the mechanism as read from source. It is not yet demonstrated;
the fix below makes a sharp prediction that tests it.

### Pre-registered: patch 0128, present narrowing in the right coordinate space

**Change:** translate the bbox by `dst.x`/`dst.y` before comparing or
pushing, and only narrow when `dst` is 1:1 with the virtual screen (a pure
offset, no scale). Plus a per-cause rejection breakdown replacing the
`reason=` string that explained nothing.

**Prediction, all three together:**

1. **`narrow` exceeds 70% of frames** (RBB2: 15%, and frozen). If the
   coordinate mismatch is the mechanism, removing it should unfreeze it.
2. **`present_update_window` mean drops below 11 ms/call** from 15.5. The
   narrowed regions in RBB2 averaged 91,886 px = 40% of the surface; if a
   similar fraction holds, 15.5 x 0.4 plus per-call overhead lands near 7,
   so 11 is a conservative bar.
3. **`fps_p50` rises above 26.0** from 23.98. Well clear of the 0.24
   run-to-run floor and the 0.19 layout floor.

**Falsified if** `narrow` stays under 40% of frames -- then the mismatch
was not the binding constraint and the rejection breakdown says what is.

**Invalidity:** the breakdown counters absent or all zero (the
two-instrument failure, twice today); `fps_p50` moving while `narrow`
does not, which would mean something else in the rebuild moved it.

**The correctness check is not optional and cannot be a `PH0N.BMP` hash.**
Those capture the game's back buffer and are blind to the present path by
construction -- which is why this bug survived. **A real screen capture
of the target, compared against the same frame's back buffer, is the only
evidence that counts here**, and I am not claiming the fix is correct
until I have one.

### Patch 0128 scored: FALSIFIED, by the cleanest possible margin

Same DOSBox-X package, before and after the coordinate translation:

    before: narrow=417 full=3083 px_narrow=39150756 px_full=710323200
    after:  narrow=417 full=3083 px_narrow=39150756 px_full=710323200

**Byte-for-byte identical.** Not "within noise" -- the same 417 frames
narrowed and the same 3,083 did not. Prediction 1 was `narrow` above 70%;
it did not move at all. **The coordinate mismatch was not the binding
constraint.**

And the change was not a no-op in the code: translating by `dst.y = 60`
turns `b.y >= dst.y` from "is the dirty region below game row 60" into
`y1 >= 0`, which is always true, and the upper bound into `y2 <= 359`,
also always true. **Both y tests became unconditionally satisfiable and
not one extra frame narrowed.** The only tests left that can reject are
the x bounds and the area test, and the x bounds are unaffected by a y
translation -- so the frames that fail, fail on **area**:

    (long long)b.w * b.h < (long long)dst.w * dst.h

**The accumulated bounding box is the whole screen.** That is the real
mechanism, and it is a data-structure problem, not an arithmetic one: one
bbox over every dirty rect in the frame degenerates to full-screen the
moment two rects sit in opposite corners. AGS's own dirty system uses up
to 25 regions with per-row spans for precisely this reason, and I
replaced it with a single bbox and expected to keep the benefit.

The rejection breakdown earns its place here -- `clip=2837` against
`noscene=212`, `latched=9`, `norects=25`, `pal=0`, `scaled=0`. Without it
this would have been another round of guessing at a frozen counter.

**What survives from 0128:** the translation is still *correct* and still
necessary -- the 417 frames that do narrow were pushing a rect 60 rows too
high, and now they are not. It fixes a real display bug while buying no
speed. Keeping it, on those grounds, and saying plainly that the
performance claim it was written for did not survive.

### What the numbers say the right structure is worth

Three areas per frame, all measured today rather than argued:

| quantity | px/frame | source |
|---|---|---|
| true dirty span area | **32,514** | patch 0126 `bg_px` |
| single-bbox area | 93,886 | `px_narrow`/417, narrowed frames only |
| what is actually presented | **230,400** | full screen, every frame |

The present costs 15.5 ms for 230,400 px. A multi-rect push landing
anywhere near the true dirty area -- even 2x it, allowing for merging and
per-rect overhead -- is roughly **4 ms/tick, a saving near 10 ms**. That
is larger than `render_backbuffer` and `scene_construct` combined, and it
dwarfs the 2.44 ms available from the masked-blit tuning I was about to
spend days on.

`SDL_UpdateWindowSurfaceRects(window, &push_rect, 1)` at
`ali3dsw.cpp:1517` already takes a count. **The plumbing for N rects is
one argument.** The work is producing a good small set of rects, and the
measurement to make alongside it is whether per-rect overhead eats the
win on short spans -- which the bandwidth probe can answer directly,
since it is the same strided-write question.

## Correction: the bbox was NOT degenerating to the whole screen

I wrote that up two sections ago as the mechanism, reasoning from a
zero-delta A/B, and **it is wrong.** The rejection breakdown, once split
into its two causes, says:

    out=2837  whole=0

**Every single rejection was "bbox outside dst" and not one was
"bbox covers the whole screen."** My inference -- that one bbox
degenerates once two rects sit in opposite corners -- is a true statement
about bounding boxes that happened not to be what was occurring here.

The actual cause is duller and smaller: **the accumulator takes rects
straight from `invalidate_rect_*`, which are not pre-clipped.** AGS clips
inside its own per-camera path, which my hook sits *before*. A single
negative or over-wide coordinate put the bbox outside `dst` and the frame
fell back to full. Patch 0131 clamps instead of rejecting.

Worth being precise about how I got this wrong, because the reasoning
looked sound: the zero-delta A/B genuinely did prove the y-translation was
not the constraint, and it genuinely did narrow the possibilities to the
x-bounds or the area test. **I then picked the more interesting of the two
remaining options and wrote it up as the finding instead of splitting the
counter, which cost one line of code.** The falsification was real; the
diagnosis I attached to it was a guess wearing its clothes.

### Patch 0131 result: narrowing works, and the design question is settled

    before: narrow= 417  full=3083
    after:  narrow=3253  full= 247      clip=1  out=0  whole=1

**417 -> 3,253 of 3,500 frames.** And because all four candidate designs
were priced from the same run, they compare directly on the same frames:

| design | px/frame | rects/frame | % of full |
|---|---|---|---|
| full screen (today) | 230,400 | 1 | 100% |
| single bbox (patch 0124) | 153,238 | 1 | 66.5% |
| **full-width row bands** | 126,377 | 4.14 | 54.9% |
| **arbitrary rects** | **18,986** | **6.68** | **8.2%** |

**Bands lose, and not narrowly.** The coordinator's reasoning for them was
sound -- contiguous memory, no stride penalty, few rects -- but the dirty
rows are spread across most of the screen even when the dirty *area* is
tiny, so a band design pays for 126,377 px to deliver the same 19,000 that
rects deliver directly. **6.7x more pixels moved for one fewer rect per
frame** is not a trade worth making, and this is exactly why it was worth
pricing all four off one run instead of arguing it.

### The knee is at 8, measured, not chosen

`DOSAGS_DIRTY_BOXES` swept under DOSBox-X:

| N | px/frame | rects/frame |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 153,238 | 1.00 |
| 4 | 37,948 | 3.93 |
| **8** | **18,986** | **6.68** |
| 25 | 18,986 | 6.68 |

**N=8 and N=25 are byte-identical** -- the accumulator never needs a ninth
box, so 25 regions would pay 3x the per-rect overhead for exactly zero
additional pixels saved. The coordinator's "find the knee rather than
picking N, do not assume maximum fidelity wins" was right on both counts.
Default set to 8.

**Per-rect overhead is now bounded rather than feared**: 6.68 rects
against 1, to move 8.2% of the pixels. Even at a pessimistic 0.1 ms fixed
cost per rect that is 0.67 ms against a saving near 14 ms.

### Correctness: the gate that was not a number

`HW-486-66-2026-09-19-DPX1-screen-capture.jpg`, a camera capture off the

geometry, letterbox bars, tree, pond, path, lamp post, inventory box --

### Per-rect overhead: real, measured, and not the deciding factor

At pure bandwidth, 19,566 px should cost 15.5 x 0.085 = 1.32 ms. Measured
3.76. **So ~2.4 ms is fixed cost across 6.65 rects, about 0.37 ms per
rect.** The coordinator's concern was right in kind -- per-rect overhead
is not negligible, it is nearly two thirds of the remaining present cost.
It was wrong only in degree: it does not come close to eating a 12 ms win,
and it does not rescue bands, which would pay 6.7x the pixels to save
2.5 rects.

**There is another ~2 ms sitting in that overhead** if the rect count can
be cut without giving back pixels -- N=4 costs 37,948 px against N=8's
18,986, so that trade is priced and currently unfavourable. Noted, not
chased.

**36.96 against the 40 fps bar, needing 3.04 more.** The frame is 27.06 ms
and the three named render terms are 19.11 of it:

| term | ms/tick | was this morning |
|---|---|---|
| `scene_construct` | **8.80** | 8.65 |
| `render_backbuffer` | 6.55 | 6.69 |

## Pairwise merge priced: 0.19 ms, not 1 ms. Not worth building.

The coordinator asked for this from existing logs. **It was not in them**
-- only per-frame totals were logged, never rect geometry -- so patch 0134
computes a greedy merge at four thresholds as pure accounting, changing
nothing about what is pushed. One DOSBox-X run, no cell.

First, their model checks out, which is worth saying because it was
derived indirectly. Two hardware points, full-screen present (15.5 ms,
230,400 px, 1 rect) and DPX1 (3.76 ms, 19,566 px, 6.65 rects), fitted
against `cost = a + b*rects + px/R`: at **b = 0.37 ms/rect** the
per-frame fixed term **a comes out at 0.02 ms** and **R at 15,245 px/ms**
-- and 15,245 px/ms at 2 bytes is 30.5 MB/s, against the independently
probed 27.5 MB/s LFB rate. Three numbers from different measurements
agreeing is a real check, not a restatement.

Greedy merge, 3,253 frames:

| threshold | rects/frame | px/frame | modelled cost | delta |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| none (today) | 6.68 | 18,986 | 3.717 ms | -- |
| 0 px (free merges only) | **6.68** | 19,204 | 3.717 ms | 0.000 |
| 2,000 px | 6.40 | 19,529 | 3.649 ms | -0.068 |
| **5,500 px** | 5.59 | 22,248 | **3.527 ms** | **-0.190** |
| 12,000 px | 3.77 | 38,053 | 3.891 ms | +0.174 (worse) |

**The 0-px row is the whole answer: merging every pair that costs nothing
removes zero rects.** There are no free merges left, because
`dos_port_dirty_add_screen` already coalesces touching and overlapping
rects at add time with a one-pixel slack. **The eager merge already did
the cheap work**, so a greedy pass afterwards can only buy rects with
pixels, and at 15,245 px/ms the exchange rate is poor.

Best case **0.19 ms against a 2.06 ms gap** -- 9% of what Gate 3 needs --
for a per-frame O(n^3) merge loop in the render path, which this port's
own cache-footprint observations price at around 1 fps all by itself.
**The instrument says do not build it**, and it cost one DOSBox run to
find out instead of a patch and a cell.

The coordinator's reasoning was right in shape ("adjacent or overlapping
rects merge for almost nothing") -- that is exactly true, and it is
already being exploited, which is the one thing neither of us checked.
