## For whoever picks up the deferred sound work: read this first

Sound is deferred by operator decision until the fps gates pass, so this
note is filed here rather than only in `tests/harness/RUNNER-DEFAULTS.md`,
where someone starting audio work would not look.

**Sound Blaster autodetection has never been validated under DOSBox-X.**
`dosbox-run.sh` hardcodes `SDL_DOS_AUDIO_SB_SKIP_DETECTION=1`, which is
`patches/SDL/0001`'s escape hatch from the detection path. `run-hw.sh`
does not set it, so the target exercises detection and the emulator never
has. **Every emulator run that appeared to cover audio startup skipped the
part most likely to be wrong**, which is the same shape as the
`DOSAGS_FIXED_TIMESTEP` divergence found the same day: not a wrong result,
a vacuous one.

**And `BLASTER` differs, unverified.** `dosbox-run.sh` hardcodes
`A220 I5 D1 H5 T6`; `run-hw.sh` sets nothing, so on the target the value
comes from the machine's own `AUTOEXEC.BAT` -- which per
`reference_sibling_repos_and_rig_config` is the real authority for that
box, and which carries a **real DreamBlaster S2 on the WaveBlaster header
at 330h**. So the two environments are very likely parsing *different
BLASTER strings*, and the emulator's is the invented one.

**I have not checked the target's actual AUTOEXEC.** That is the first
thing to do, and it is a `get-file`, not a cell.

Neither affects the 40/40 gates, which is why they are recorded rather
than fixed. Both would bite an audio task silently.

## FIVE1 scored: four of five predictions wrong, and the useful one reverses the plan

Binary `e157a1619b70`. `sumcheck_fail=0`, 3 SUSPECT flags (the same three
explicable ones), `frames_skipped=381`, `fps_p50=37.55`.

| # | prediction | result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | bar 1 above 41.35, fails high | **UNRESOLVED -- my tool is wrong** |
| 2 | catch-up ticks 100-150 | **FALSIFIED: 489** |
| 3 | `gem` script-dominated | **FALSIFIED: 11-13% script** |
| 4 | the 19 operations are NOT one shape | **CONFIRMED: three shapes** |
| 5 | skips script/event-dominated, render under 20% | **FALSIFIED: 85.8% render** |

### 1. Bar 1: my own tool emitted an impossible number

    transitions AND blocking ticks excluded  <= BAR 1   3558 / 33222 ms = 107.10

**107 ticks/s on a 40 Hz pacer.** Transitions and blocking ticks
**overlap** -- a transition is largely *made of* blocking ticks, since the
load and the fade are the stalls -- so subtracting both double-counts the
same 52,930 + 84,778 ms out of a 170,930 ms run.

I built `gate3-bars.py` two hours ago **specifically so bar 1 would stop
being computed wrongly by hand**, and it got it wrong in a new way. Taking
the union needs a **timestamp on each stall record**, which does not exist
yet. Until it does the tool now **refuses** rather than printing a figure,
and bar 2's list is de-duplicated the same way (19 blocking operations,
not 19 + 8 transitions counted twice).

**An impossible number that looks like a measurement is worse than no
number**, and the only reason this one was caught is that 107 is absurd on
its face -- the same luck that covered two of the five instrument bugs.

### 2. Catch-up: 489, not ~120

`catchup ticks=489 events=177 clamped=23`, against a pre-registered
100-150 from two independent routes. **3.3x the upper bound**, and the
prediction is falsified rather than merely imprecise. 489 of 3,577 ticks
is 13.7% excess, which would put the rate at 45.5 -- but
`tick_rate_steady` reads **41.30**. So **not all catch-up ticks land
inside the steady window**, and the epoch resync absorbs some. The
mechanism is confirmed as present and large; its arithmetic does not yet
close, and I am not claiming it does.

### 3. `gem` is NOT script -- the fixture question is answered

The cleanest `gem` ticks (small `children_ms`):

    tick=2057 self_ms=6321 children_ms=465 script_us=809620  events_us=6781509
    tick=2469 self_ms=4142 children_ms=80  script_us=473934  events_us=4219680

**Script is 11-13% of the tick. Event dispatch is essentially all of it.**
So `gem`'s six-second ticks are **AGS's own event-processing machinery**,
not script execution -- which means **not our `AutoPilot` overlay, and not
the game's script either.** The fixture hypothesis is dead, bar 2 is
priced against the port, and the remaining question is what
`processallevents()` does for 5.5 seconds outside `RunScriptFunction`.

### 4. Three shapes, not one -- and one of them is a surprise

Cleanly attributable stalls (`children_ms=0`):

| tick | self_ms | dominant term | shape |
|---|---|---|---|
| 82, 83 | 3510, 4085 | `events` 99.7%, 99.9% | event dispatch |
| 2022, 2026 | 320, 498 | `script` 99%, 96% | script |
| **148, 2991** | **256, 265** | **`present` 96%, 95%** | **LFB** |

**Two stalls are 95% `present_update_window`** -- a quarter-second inside
one push to the framebuffer, on a path whose mean is 3.84 ms. Nothing
predicted that and it does not resemble the others at all.

Bar 2 as a single budget is the wrong instrument for three populations a
player experiences differently: a transition they expect to wait through,
a six-second freeze mid-puzzle, and a quarter-second video hitch.

### 5. The tail is render-bound, and I had conceded this only halfway

41 clean skip frames split into two populations that barely overlap:

| population | n | mean | render three | script | events |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **under 100 ms (ordinary play)** | **37** | **79.2 ms** | **85.8%** | 0.0% | 0.0% |
| 100 ms and over (blocking) | 4 | 8,790 ms | 2.7% | 53.7% | 98.9% |

**The ordinary-play tail -- the 13.2%, the 4.35 fps -- is 85.8% render and
literally zero script or events.** My prediction was the opposite. In
aggregate across all 41 the render share is 9.1%, which is how I would
have read it if I had not split the populations: **four monsters drown 37
ordinary frames, and the aggregate describes neither.**

So the masked blit's 2.44 ms and the restore's headroom are **not**
deferred work -- they are the direct attack on the thing costing 4.35 fps.
The coordinator argued this and I conceded it as a caveat; it is the main
finding. And the tail frames average **79.2 ms against a 25 ms budget**,
3x over, so this is a fat tail with a large cause, not marginal overruns.

## Patch 0150: `gem` decomposed -- it is ROOM events, and not the obvious ones

`process_events_dispatch` is six things behind one bracket, exactly as
`scene_construct` was. Same treatment: bracket `process_event` by
`AGSGameEventType`, and split `kAGSEvent_Object` by its own sub-type.
DOSBox-X:

| event type | n | us |
|---|---|---|
| `object` | 284 | **49,539,591** |
| `script` | 135 | 34,486,055 |
| `fadein` | 9 | 3,145,408 |
| `none`, `gui`, `newroom` | 0 | 0 |

| object sub-type | n | us |
|---|---|---|
| **1 = `kObjEventType_Room`** | **153** | **49,538,566** |
| 2 = `kObjEventType_Hotspot` | 131 | **1,025** |

**Room events are 49.5 seconds across 153 dispatches -- 324 ms each.
Hotspot interactions are 1,025 microseconds across 131.** A factor of
48,000 between two sub-types of the same event kind.

**I would have guessed hotspots**, because the `gem` phase's visible
action is `RunHotspot("hBackDoorway", eModeInteract)` and I had read that
line hours earlier while checking whether the fixture was at fault. The
enum settles it: `kObjEventType_Room` is 1, `kObjEventType_Hotspot` is 2,
and **checking the enum rather than assuming the switch's source order
matched the numbering is the only reason this is right.**

**Still open, and it is the interesting part:** `gem`'s ticks were 11-13%
`script_vm`, so a room event is **not** spending its 324 ms inside
`RunScriptFunction`. Something in the room-event path costs that outside
script execution. That is the next bracket, and the same argument that
found `draw_preroom_background` applies: the name says one thing and the
measurement says another.

## Patch 0151: it is `AfterFadein`, 4.56 seconds per event

Room events decomposed by `AGSRoomEventType` (DOSBox-X):

| room event | n | us | per event |
|---|---|---|---|
| **`afterfadein`** | **9** | **41,059,241** | **4.56 s** |
| `firstenter` | 4 | 8,300,058 | 2.08 s |
| `beforefadein` | 9 | 1,744 | 0.2 ms |
| `repexec` | 131 | 4,640 | 0.04 ms |

**`kRoomEvent_AfterFadein` is 41.1 of the 49.5 seconds**, across nine
dispatches. `repexec` -- the one that fires every tick and the one anybody
would suspect -- is 4.6 milliseconds across 131 dispatches, total.

So the blocking operation behind `gem`, and behind the room-change stalls
generally, is **the event AGS fires once the fade has completed**. And
with `script_vm` at 11-13% of those ticks it is **not the room's
AfterFadein script handler**. Next bracket goes inside that path.

### Patch 0152: print the name, not the code

The `evobj` line printed `subtype=1` and I read it as Hotspot, because
`process_event`'s switch lists Hotspot first. The enum says
`kObjEventType_Room = 1`, `kObjEventType_Hotspot = 2`.

**Reading the enum is a discipline; printing the symbolic name is a fix.**
It removes the downstream mapping that can be got wrong, rather than
relying on the next reader to be careful. All three event instruments now
emit names.

### Why the three-in-one cell has to be two cells

The coordinator asked for one cell carrying bar 1, the room-event bracket
and patch 0127's run-length counter. **The first two can share a binary.
The third cannot share with the first.**

Patch 0127 adds three increments and a branch **inside Allegro's masked
blit inner loop**, per pixel. At 17,117 sprite pixels a frame that is
~68,000 extra operations per frame, which is not the ~0.23 fps an inert
addition costs -- it is on the order of a millisecond a frame, 4% of a
27 ms frame.

**Bar 1 is judged against 40 +/- 2%.** A 4% perturbation can flip the
verdict on its own, which is exactly the outcome a gate figure must not
have. That is why 0127 was built opt-in behind `AGS_SPRITE_RUN_STATS=1`
and why its own header says a stats binary is for structure and never for
a timing comparison. **Carrying it into the bar 1 cell would violate the
rule written when it was built.**

So: **two cells, back to back.**

- **BAR1A** -- clean binary. Bar 1 via the union, plus the room-event
  decomposition on the target. Both are counts and per-phase times, which
  the instruments already carried in FIVE1 without measurable cost.
- **RUNLEN1** -- `AGS_SPRITE_RUN_STATS=1`. **Its fps and tick rate are
  discarded by construction**; the only output that matters is the run
  length distribution. It does not need to be a full-length run.

### Pre-registered: BAR1A

1. **Bar 1 computable and between 39 and 45.** FIVE1's data gave 41.30 for
   `tick_rate_steady` (blocking ticks excluded, transitions not), and
   excluding transitions on top removes low-tick wall time, so bar 1
   should come out at or above that. **Falsified if the tool refuses**
   (union still exceeding bounds) or if bar 1 lands below 39 -- which
   would mean transitions carry *more* ticks than ordinary play, the
   opposite of everything measured.
2. **`evroom afterfadein` is the largest room-event term on hardware**,
   as it was on the emulator. Falsified if `repexec` or any other room
   event exceeds it.
3. **`script_vm` is under 30% of the `afterfadein` time**, consistent with
   the 11-13% seen in `gem`'s stalls. If it is over 50%, the blocking is
   script after all and the next bracket goes somewhere else entirely.

### Pre-registered: RUNLEN1

**Decision rule, unchanged from when patch 0127 was written and quoted
here so it cannot drift:**

| mean opaque run | verdict |
|---|---|
| >= 16 px | write the run-based blit |
| 6-16 px | marginal; consider 4-px unrolling instead |
| < 6 px | **do not write it** |

**Prediction: 12-30 px.** Sprites at ~2,383 px and ~48x48 are mostly solid
with transparent margins, so a scanline through one should be a short
transparent run, a long opaque run, and a short transparent run.
**Falsified below 6**, which would mean the sprites are speckled and the
whole run-based approach is dead.

**`fps_p50` and every tick rate from RUNLEN1 are void** and must not be
compared with anything.

## BAR1A: the room-event answer is decisive. Bar 1 is not, and I am stopping.

Binary `1edff2f51e58`, `fps_p50=36.60`, `sumcheck_fail=0`.

### Prediction 2 CONFIRMED, and larger on hardware than on the emulator

| room event | n | us | per event |
|---|---|---|---|
| **`afterfadein`** | **9** | **67,741,019** | **7.53 s** |
| `firstenter` | 4 | 8,564,996 | 2.14 s |
| `repexec` | 130 | 80,631 | 0.6 ms |
| `beforefadein` | 9 | 38,604 | 4 ms |

| object sub-type | n | us |
|---|---|---|
| `room` | 152 | 76,425,250 |
| `hotspot` | 130 | **14,483** |

**`AfterFadein` is 7.53 seconds per event on the target**, 67.7 s of a
170.8 s run -- **40% of the whole run in nine dispatches.** `repexec`, the
per-tick one, is 0.6 ms.

### The reconciliation the coordinator asked for, and it is worse than framed

**Only 2 of 19 blocking ticks fall inside a `fadeout_begin`..`fadein_end`
window. 17 fall outside, carrying 74,833 of 84,882 ms.**

So `AfterFadein`'s seconds sit **outside** the interval we call a
transition -- by its name it fires once the fade has completed, and the
measurement agrees. Consequences, all real:

- **A player waits ~6.7 s for the transition and then several seconds
  more before anything responds**, as one unbroken wait. Our transition
  interval describes the first part only.
- A bar 2 budget priced on the transition interval would call a room
  change 6.7 s when the actual wait is closer to 14.
- **88% of blocking time is currently outside the interval meant to
  capture it.**

The excluded interval needs extending to cover the post-fade work, and
that is a question for the operator alongside the categorisation.

### Bar 1: three answers from one run, so the honest output is none

| method | bar 1 |
|---|---|
| sum of transitions and blocking ticks | **107.10** (impossible) |
| union, ticks interpolated from the series | **26.24** |
| union, samples partitioned by window | **21.98** |

**That spread is five times the bar's entire tolerance.** It is not three
refinements converging; it is three reconstructions of a quantity the data
does not contain.

**The specific defect:** a blocking tick's window is built as
`[t_ms, t_ms + self_ms)`, and `self_ms` **excludes nested game loops**
while the wall span does not. So every window is too short and misplaced,
and every sample-to-window assignment inherits that. 21.98 for ordinary
play against a 40 Hz pacer is independently implausible.

**I built `gate3-bars.py` so bar 1 would stop moving when computed by
hand. It now moves when computed by tool.** Same failure, better coat.
The tool prints the working and then refuses, naming the defect and what
would fix it: **the wall-clock start and end of each excluded region,
recorded directly, rather than reconstructed from a self-time and a
per-second series.**

**Bar 1 is an open instrument gap, not a measurement.** I am not quoting
21.98 and neither should anyone else.

## RUNLEN1: 57 px mean opaque run. Write the blit. And it needed no cell.

    px=115473216  opaque_px=74606797  runs=1309835

| quantity | value |
|---|---|
| opaque | 74,606,797 px, **64.6%** |
| transparent | 40,866,419 px, 35.4% |
| opaque runs | 1,309,835 |
| **mean opaque run** | **57.0 px** |

Against the rule written when patch 0127 was built and quoted before the
data existed: **>= 16 px, write the run-based blit.** 57.0 is 3.6x the
threshold. Prediction was 12-30; the answer is above that range, so the
prediction was wrong in the direction that makes the work more worthwhile.

**A `rep movsd` over a 57-pixel run replaces 57 iterations of
load-test-store with one string instruction**, and the bandwidth probe
already priced the ceiling: an opaque run copied that way pays 7.8
cycles/pixel against the current loop's 19.4.

### This did not need a hardware cell, and saying so is the point

**Run length is a property of the content, not the machine.** The
autopilot is deterministic -- `PH01/02/03` hash identically across
independent runs, which this project verified before committing them as
baselines -- so DOSBox-X blits exactly the sprites the target does, in the
same order. The emulator's *timing* is worthless here and its *counts* are
the same counts.

I had planned RUNLEN1 as a hardware cell and pre-registered it as one.
**It should never have been one**, and the reason is visible from the
question itself: nothing in "how long is an opaque run" depends on how
fast the machine is.

**The cell saved is worth less than the habit**: the pre-registration
asked what the measurement needs, and the answer was "not this machine".

### One caveat on the figure

The counters are shared across every colour depth's instantiation of
`cspr.h` (8/15/16/24/32), so an 8-bit blit contributes on equal terms. AGS
Quest is 16-bit throughout, so the contamination should be nil, **but it
is unverified** and a 57 px mean is longer than a ~48x48 sprite's widest
possible run -- which says some of these blits are of considerably larger
sprites than the 2,383 px average, not that the number is wrong. Worth
splitting per depth if the figure ever needs to be exact; it does not, to
clear a 16 px threshold by 3.6x.

## Patch 0153: bar 1 becomes computable, by measuring the span instead of deriving it

`DosTickStallScope` now records `begin_ms` and `end_ms` from the same
clock the transition milestones use, at entry and exit. `ms` (the
self-time) stays -- **bar 2 wants the tick's own cost and bar 1 wants its
wall span, and those are genuinely different questions**, which is part of
why conflating them went unnoticed.

**The first stall in the verification run shows how wrong the derivation
was:**

    tick_stall index=1 ms=927 t_ms=2210 begin_ms=285 end_ms=3137

**Self-time 927 ms; measured wall span 2,852 ms. Three times wider.** Every
bar 1 attempt built on `[t_ms, t_ms + self_ms)` was working with windows a
third of their true size, misplaced by the difference.

With measured spans, DOSBox-X gives a physically sensible **38.75**,
correctly flagged FAILS LOW. The union caught 7,921 ms of overlap.

### And one guard had to be relaxed, deliberately

The exclusion now covers 74% of the run, which tripped the >70% check. **I
wrote that check as a proxy for the overlap bug** -- summing two
overlapping sets -- and taking the union of *measured* spans removes that
bug at its source. A fixture that genuinely spends most of its run inside
blocking operations, which AGS Quest's autopilot does, is a fact about the
fixture and not an arithmetic error.

So it is now a printed note rather than a refusal. **Excluding more than
the run remains impossible and remains a hard failure**, as does a rate
above 45.

**Relaxing a guard needs a reason, not a result.** The reason here is that
the condition it was proxying for is gone; if the guard had been left
blocking it would have suppressed a correct answer, which is the worse
failure of the two.

## Patch 0155: `AfterFadein`'s 7.53 seconds is OUR OWN LOGGING

    afterfadein gui_n=9 gui_us=25   log_n=9 log_us=38395917
    evroom afterfadein n=9 us=40754690

**`GUIE::MarkSpecialLabelsForUpdate` is 25 microseconds across all nine
dispatches. The logging block is 38.4 of the 40.8 seconds -- 94%.**

That block is **ours**: patch 0078's startup-timing report and patch
0121's `room_transition` milestone, both `debug_script_log()` calls added
by this port for instrumentation, inside an event the engine fires on
every room entry.

### What this means, stated carefully

**The largest single cost this campaign has measured is an artefact of the
campaign's own instrumentation.** 40% of the AGS Quest run, the thing I
was about to propose as the biggest actionable defect, and the thing the
coordinator called "bigger than the double copy was."

Arithmetic, if a `debug_script_log` call has a roughly constant cost: the
one-shot startup report is ~40 calls and the per-dispatch milestone is 1
call x 9, so 49 calls for 38.4 s puts a single log line near **0.78
seconds**. That is absurd on its face and is exactly why it needs
measuring rather than assuming -- but the total is not in doubt.

### Why this was invisible

`run-hw.sh` and `run-dosbox.sh` both pass `--log-stdout=+mgs:all`, so
**every measurement this campaign has taken includes it**, and nothing
ever compared against a run without it. The cost sits inside
`process_events_dispatch`, which is why it looked like engine event
machinery -- and `script_vm` was 11-13% precisely because **it is not
script, not the engine, and not the game.**

### What I got wrong along the way, in order

1. Guessed **hotspots** -- the enum said room.
2. Guessed the **room's AfterFadein script** -- `script_vm` said 11-13%.
3. Guessed the **interaction run** -- patch 0154 said 10.7 s across all
   281 object events against 40.9 s for these nine.
4. Guessed **`MarkSpecialLabelsForUpdate`** -- 25 microseconds.

**Four wrong guesses, each eliminated by a bracket rather than by
argument.** The chase only converged because every step measured instead
of reasoning from the name of the thing.

### Immediate consequences

- **`gem`, `menu`, `interior`, `exit` and the other blocking stalls need
  re-examining** -- if they share this cause, bar 2's whole distribution
  is contaminated.
- **Gate 2 and Gate 1's figures were taken with the same logging enabled.**
  Gate 1 is 8-bit Trilby and does not fire these room events nine times,
  but that is an assumption and needs checking rather than asserting.
- **The fix is not to delete the instrumentation** but to find why a log
  line costs what it does -- and until that is known, to measure with and
  without it so the size of the artefact is on the record.

**This is the fourth time today the win was our own redundant work rather
than slow engine code, and the first time it was actively corrupting the
measurements.**

## RETRACTION: AfterFadein is NOT our logging. My bracket was mis-scoped.

    BEFORE (patch 0155, mis-scoped):  log_n=9 log_us=38497286
    AFTER  (patch 0157, corrected):   log_n=9 log_us=1865
                                      onevent_n=9 onevent_us=38357470

**The logging is 1.9 milliseconds across all nine dispatches.** The 38.4
seconds is `run_on_event(kScriptEvent_RoomAfterFadein, displayed_room)` --
**the game's own on-event dispatch**, which sat *after* the `#endif` and
therefore inside a scope I opened before the `#ifdef` and never closed.

**I reported "the largest single cost this campaign has measured is an
artefact of the campaign's own instrumentation" to the coordinator, who
had already relayed it to the operator. It is false.** Nothing about the
port's measurements is contaminated by this logging, and the operator's
decision between the render tail and `AfterFadein` does not dissolve.

### The contradiction that exposed it, and why I should have seen it sooner

Patch 0156 timed one `debug_script_log` line: **48 microseconds**
(`line_us=456` over nine). I wrote in the same breath that the arithmetic
implied ~0.78 seconds per line and that this was "absurd on its face". The
coordinator independently said the same thing from a second direction --
that 40 such calls would be 31 seconds against Gate 2's entire 2.7 s
excess.

**Two people called the number absurd and I still shipped the conclusion
that rested on it.** The corrected figure closes exactly: ~40 calls at
48 us is 1.9 ms, and `log_us` reads 1,865. **An arithmetic check that
fails should block the conclusion, not be noted beside it.**

### The actual mechanism of the mistake

`DosPortNamedScope _dp_log` was declared just before an `#ifdef __DJGPP__`
block and destructed at the end of the enclosing `else if` -- which
includes `run_on_event()`. **A scope measures to the end of its block, not
to the end of the thing it is named after**, and I named it `_dp_log`.
Patch 0157 makes the scope closable so it can end where its subject ends.

**Fifth wrong guess in this chase, and the only one I published.** The
previous four were killed by brackets before they left my hands; this one
was killed by a bracket after I had already sent it.

### Where this leaves the real finding

`AfterFadein` at 7.53 s/event on hardware **stands as a genuine defect**,
and it is `run_on_event(kScriptEvent_RoomAfterFadein)`. That is the game's
own event dispatch, so the fixture question reopens in a new place -- and
`script_vm` reading 11-13% while this is 94% needs explaining before
anything is concluded about it. **I am not guessing what `run_on_event`
does. The next bracket goes inside it.**

## Resolving the "contradiction": there wasn't one

The coordinator asked for a bracket designed to discriminate between
`run_on_event` reaching script by a path `script_vm` does not bracket, and
its 7.53 s not being script at all. **Neither. The premise was false.**

`script_vm` brackets `curscript->Inst->CallScriptFunction(...)` -- the VM
bytecode call itself. Our overlay's `on_event` runs inside that, and so do
the engine API calls it makes. **So AfterFadein's time IS inside
`script_vm`**, and on BAR1A `script_vm` totals 102.5 s against
`afterfadein`'s 67.7 s, which is consistent rather than contradictory.

**The 11-13% figure came from `gem`'s stall ticks (2057, 2469). The 94%
came from the AfterFadein dispatches. Different ticks.** I put two numbers
side by side that measure different things, called the result a
contradiction, and the coordinator built an instruction on it. Reading the
bracket site settled it without a cell.

## Patch 0158: the screenshots are 3.1%, so the fixture is not the artefact

    screenshot n=3 us=1181771      (394 ms each)
    afterfadein onevent_us=38569289

**1.18 s of 38.6 s.** Our `SaveScreenShot` calls -- the one piece of pure
fixture overhead in that path -- are 3.1% of it.

The remaining 37.4 s is the rest of our `on_event`: principally
`RunHotspot(...)` calls, which run the game's own hotspot interactions
synchronously. **That is the autopilot playing the game, and a player's
click would cost the engine the same work.**

### What that means for bar 2, provisionally

If the blocking operations are largely **scripted interactions responding
to input**, then bar 2 is substantially measuring *how long the game takes
to respond to a click* -- which is a real player-experience number and
exactly what a blocking-operation budget should measure. **It is not an
artefact and it is not the port being slow at something avoidable.**

**Marking this provisional deliberately.** It rests on one DOSBox run and
on reading our overlay rather than on bracketing `RunHotspot` itself, and
I have been wrong five times in this chase. The bracket that would settle
it goes inside the interaction path, separating the walk from everything
else. **I am not concluding bar 2's character from a source read after
today.**

### The scope bug, recorded as its own class

**A scope opened before an `#ifdef` and never closed runs to the end of
the enclosing block, not to the end of the thing it is named after.**
`_dp_log` measured a call sitting after the `#endif`.

**The sum-check assertion cannot catch this**: the parts still added up.
They were parts of the wrong whole. That is a third distinct instrument
failure mode, alongside "the decomposition does not add up" (sum check)
and "the interval is not the intended one" (plausibility floor). This one
needs a scope that ends where its subject ends -- patch 0157 made
`DosPortNamedScope` closable for exactly that.

## Patch 0159: AfterFadein animates. gem's stall ticks freeze. Two different things.

    afterfadein onevent_n=9 onevent_us=38592594 nested_us=33198877

**86% of `run_on_event`'s time is nested ticks.** The game loop keeps
running throughout, so the screen is animating -- a character walking after
the autopilot's `RunHotspot`, which is what a player's click would also
cost. Only 5.4 s across nine dispatches (0.6 s each) is self-time with the
loop stopped.

So the provisional reading holds: **that part of bar 2 is measuring click
responsiveness, not a freeze.** The coordinator's challenge was the right
one to make and it confirmed rather than overturned.

### But stating the denominators, per the rule just recorded

**These are not the same population as `gem`'s stall ticks, and the two
answer differently:**

| population | measured over | self vs nested |
|---|---|---|
| AfterFadein dispatches | 9 room-entry events | **86% nested** -- animating |
| `gem`'s stall ticks (2057, 2469) | individual game-loop iterations | **93% self** (465 ms children of 6,321 ms) -- frozen |

**Both are real and they are different defects.** Room entry runs a long
animated sequence; `gem`'s blocking ticks stop the loop for seconds. The
first is a game taking its time, the second is a freeze.

**This is the fourth time in this chase that two figures described
different populations**, and the first time I noticed before comparing
them rather than after. Writing the denominators down is what did it.

### What it means for bar 2, now non-provisionally for one half

Bar 2's 19 blocking operations contain **at least two kinds**:

- **Animated waits** -- the loop pumps, the screen moves, the player sees
  the game working. A budget should price these generously.
- **Frozen ticks** -- the loop stops. `gem`'s five ticks averaging 6.6 s
  each are here, at 93% self.

**A single budget cannot price both**, which is the fifth instance of one
number conflating two things this campaign. The self-versus-nested split
is the discriminator and it is now instrumented, so bar 2's distribution
can be reported as two distributions rather than argued about.

**What is still not measured**: which of the 19 fall in which bucket. The
split exists for AfterFadein and for the two clean `gem` ticks; the other
seventeen need the same treatment before anyone proposes a budget.

### Pre-registered: RUNBLIT1, within-build A/B on `DOSAGS_RUNBLIT`

Patch 0160 copies opaque runs with one `memcpy` instead of storing pixel
by pixel. **One binary, both arms**, so layout and code size cancel --
`DOSAGS_RUNBLIT=0` falls back to the original loop.

**Correctness already established under DOSBox-X**: `PH01/02/03` are
byte-identical between arms and match the long-standing baselines.
Unlike the present-path change, a back-buffer hash IS sufficient evidence
here -- the masked blit writes *into* the buffer those hashes cover, so a
wrong pixel would appear in them. The 0124 defect was invisible to them
because it corrupted *which region was pushed*, not the buffer contents.
**A screen capture will still be taken on the target**, because that
argument is mine and the operator's rule is not.

**Predictions:**

1. **`frames_skipped` falls by more than 40** from ~381. This is the
   metric, not mean frame time -- the engine is pacer-limited and a saving
   on an early frame goes into `wait_next_frame`. FIVE1 put the ordinary
   tail at 85.8% render across 37 frames averaging 79.2 ms against a 25 ms
   budget, so cutting the blit should pull some of those under.
2. **`fps_p50` rises above 38.0** from 36.60-37.55.
3. **`render_backbuffer` mean falls below 5.2 ms** from 6.55. At 57 px
   runs the loop should approach the copy ceiling on opaque spans; 19.4 ->
   ~12 cycles/pixel would give 4.0 ms, so 5.2 is conservative.

**Falsified if** `render_backbuffer` does not move by more than the 0.24
run-to-run floor -- which would mean the loop's cost was never the
per-pixel bookkeeping and the 19.4-vs-7.8 gap is something else.

**Invalidity:** `PH0N.BMP` differing between arms; either arm failing to
run; `sumcheck_fail > 0`.

**Also riding along:** patch 0153's `begin_ms`/`end_ms`, so bar 1 becomes
computable from this cell without needing its own.

## Bar 2 gets a principled structure, from one measurement

The coordinator argued `AfterFadein` was a freeze; I argued it was the
game responding to a click. **It is both, in different places**, and the
self-versus-nested split separated them where neither argument could:

| kind | signature | example | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| **animated blocking** | mostly nested -- loop pumps, screen updates | `AfterFadein`, 86% nested | a **pacing** question, not a defect |
| **frozen blocking** | mostly self -- loop stops, screen dead | `gem`, 93% self | a **defect at any duration** worth measuring |
| **transitions** | authored wait | the 8 segments | own case; the player expects it |

**Three budgets with different numbers and different justifications,
because a player experiences them differently** -- and the discriminator
is measured rather than asserted. That is a far better proposition than
"no budget in a defensible range passes", which was true and useless.

**When `AfterFadein` comes back round, re-price it as animated blocking.**
7.53 s of a character walking may still be too long, but that is a
different argument and it may not be the port's fault at all.

## Two multi-depth traps, for every port in this hub

Both found while writing patch 0160 into a template instantiated at
8/15/16/24/32 bpp.

### Run length from pointer difference, never `sizeof`

At 24 bpp `PIXEL_PTR` is `unsigned char*` while a pixel is **three
bytes**, so `sizeof(*p)` is 1. A byte count computed as `n * sizeof(*p)`
is correct at four instantiations and silently copies a third of each run
at the fifth.

**That is the worst possible failure distribution** -- four arms of a test
pass, one is quietly wrong, and nothing in the shared header hints that
the depths disagree. `(const char *)end - (const char *)begin` is correct
at every depth by construction.

### A pointer-valued macro in a multi-declarator declaration

    PIXEL_PTR rs = s, rd = d;     /* rd is NOT a pointer */

`PIXEL_PTR` expands to `unsigned short*`, and C binds the `*` to the first
declarator only, so `rd` is a plain `unsigned short` holding a truncated
address. **The compiler caught this one** with an int-conversion warning
-- but the same shape with a compatible type would compile clean, and the
failure is memory corruption rather than a wrong number.

**A `typedef` removes the class entirely and is worth doing rather than
remembering.** Deferred until the current cell's two arms are done, since
it means a rebuild and the binary under test must not change mid-cell.

## Reading RUNBLIT1 against the right ceiling

**The ceiling is `tick_rate_steady` (~41.3), not 40.** So:

- skips fall **and** fps rises toward 41.3 -> the tail is closing.
- skips fall **and** fps does not move -> the pacer picture needs
  revisiting before anything else, because the model says it should.

## RUNBLIT1 scored: all three predictions falsified. The blit is worth ~0.45 ms, not 2.44.

Within-build A/B, one binary, `DOSAGS_RUNBLIT`:

| metric | ON | OFF | delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| `render_backbuffer` mean | **6.14** | **6.62** | **-0.48 ms** |
| `rb_sprite_time` mean | 2.15 | 2.33 | -0.18 ms |
| `frames_skipped` | 378 | 386 | -8 |
| `fps_p50` | 36.31 | 36.38 | -0.07 |
| `tick_rate_steady` | 41.51 | 41.47 | +0.04 |

`PH01/02/03` byte-identical across arms. `rb_sprite_time` calls 9,595 vs
9,580, within 0.16%, so both arms did the same work.

| prediction | bar | result |
|---|---|---|
| `frames_skipped` falls by >40 | 40 | **fell 8 -- FALSIFIED** |
| `fps_p50` above 38.0 | 38.0 | **36.31 -- FALSIFIED** |
| `render_backbuffer` below 5.2 ms | 5.2 | **6.14 -- FALSIFIED** |

**The effect is real and it is small.** 0.48 ms against OFF arms that
cluster at 6.55-6.69 across four cells, so it is well outside run-to-run
variation -- but it is a fifth of the 2.44 ms the model predicted, and
`fps_p50` moved less than the 0.24 noise floor in the *wrong* direction.

### Why the model was wrong, and I flagged the reason before the cell

**The 57 px mean opaque run was measured across every colour depth's
instantiation and is inflated by large blits.** I wrote that caveat into
PLAN.md when I recorded the figure -- *"a 57 px mean is longer than a
48x48 sprite's widest possible run, which says some blits are of
considerably larger sprites"* -- and then priced the work as if 57 px were
the sprites' runs anyway. **AGS Quest's sprites average 2,383 px, so their
runs cannot exceed 48**, and a `memcpy` of ~96 bytes carries enough call
overhead to eat most of what the loop bookkeeping saved.

**The caveat was correct, recorded, and ignored by me one section later.**
That is the same shape as the 0.78 s/line arithmetic: the disqualifying
fact was written down and then not applied.

**What would have caught it:** splitting the run-length counter per colour
depth, which I explicitly declined as unnecessary "to clear a 16 px
threshold by 3.6x". The threshold was cleared by a number that did not
describe the sprites being blitted.

### Keeping it, and why

0.48 ms/tick for a behaviour-identical change, hint-gated, with both arms
proven pixel-identical, is worth keeping. **It is not worth the second
optimisation pass** the 2.44 ms figure would have justified.

## Bar 1, computed at last: 37.54, FAILS LOW

Patch 0153's measured spans rode along on this cell, so bar 1 is a figure
for the first time:

    exclusion: union 153186 ms, naive sum 207480 ms (overlap 54294 ms)
    remaining 841 ticks / 22402 ms  =  37.54     target 39.2-40.8: FAILS LOW

**Caveat that has to travel with it: the exclusion is 90% of the run.**
A blocking tick's measured span covers the nested ticks inside it, so
excluding a ten-second `AfterFadein` removes every animated tick it
contained. That is arguably right for "sustained tick rate during play" --
ticks that happened *during* a blocking operation are not ordinary play --
but it leaves bar 1 resting on **22.4 s of a 171 s run**.

**So bar 1 fails low, and the figure is thin.** It is the first one
computed from measured rather than reconstructed spans, and it is a
starting point for the operator's discussion rather than a verdict.

## Bar 1 is not well-defined, and that is the finding

The coordinator asked me to compute bar 1 both ways and verify their
arithmetic rather than take it. **Verified, and it does not hold.**

| definition | result | base |
|---|---|---|
| **A** -- exclude each blocking tick's full wall span, and the ticks inside it | **37.54** | 13% of the run |
| **B** -- exclude transitions, and blocking ticks' *self* time only | **67.81** | 23% of the run |
| (`tick_rate_steady`: blocking self-time excluded, transitions **not**) | 41.51 | 50% |

**67.81 is impossible on a 40 Hz pacer.** Definition B removes 85,326 ms of
denominator for the stalls' self-time while only 21 ticks leave the
numerator -- and the nested ticks that ran during those spans stay counted.
**Same double-count shape as the 107.10, mirrored.**

The coordinator's reconstruction of B as "3,558 ticks / 86,048 ms = 41.35"
is in fact just `tick_rate_steady`, which **does not exclude transitions**
and so is not bar 1 as the operator defined it. Adding transition exclusion
on top is what breaks it.

### Why, and it is a definitional problem rather than an arithmetic one

**The coordinator's substantive point is correct**: patch 0159 showed
`AfterFadein` is 86% nested, those nested ticks rendered, the screen
animated -- **that is play**, and definition A excludes it.

But the repair does not work, because a blocking operation's self-time is
**interleaved with** the nested ticks, not contiguous with them. You cannot
subtract it as an interval. And you cannot keep the play inside a
ten-second operation while excluding the operation, because the ticks and
the wall clock they ran in are the same seconds.

**So: "sustained tick rate during play, excluding transitions and blocking
ticks" is not well-defined when a blocking operation *contains* play.**
Definition A is the only internally coherent reading, and it answers a
question nobody wants -- the tick rate during the 13% of the run when
nothing at all is happening.

**This is the sixth time this campaign a single number was conflating two
things**, and the first time the conflation is in a definition the
operator has already ruled on twice.

### What I would put to the operator

**A gate figure resting on 13% of a run is not a figure.** I relaxed my own
70%-exclusion guard earlier with a reason -- the union was of measured
spans, so a large exclusion was a fact about the fixture. **90% is past
where that reasoning holds**, and the right response is to question the
definition, not the guard.

The measurable, coherent alternatives:

- **`tick_rate_steady` = 41.51** -- exclude blocking ticks by self-time,
  keep transitions. Rests on 50% of the run. Fails **high**, which puts
  the catch-up question back on the critical path.
- **Render rate during animated play** -- count only ticks that actually
  rendered, over the wall time they occupied. Not yet instrumented, and it
  is closest to what a player perceives.

**I am not choosing between these.** The definition is the operator's and
they have ruled on it twice; what I can say is that the current wording
does not survive contact with a blocking operation that animates.

## The bar 1 repair works, and transition exclusion is redundant for a stronger reason

The coordinator proposed dropping transition exclusion, on the grounds
that a transition's non-blocking content is ordinary ticks at the pacer
rate. **Checked against the records: there is no such content.**

Partitioning the per-second series by "inside a transition AND outside
every blocking span" returns **no samples at all**. And the union of
transitions plus blocking spans is **153,186 ms against 154,218 ms of
blocking spans alone** -- transitions add essentially nothing.

**So transitions are, to measurement resolution, made entirely of blocking
operations.** Excluding blocking ticks already excludes them; the separate
transition exclusion was always a no-op that happened to be applied
inconsistently.

**That is what produced 67.81.** Definition B was coherent until I applied
a redundant exclusion on top of it -- the redundancy double-counted, the
same shape as 107.10 and for the same underlying reason.

**With transitions dropped, bar 1 is `tick_rate_steady` = 41.51**, on 50%
of the run, coherent, already measured, needing no new instrument. **It
fails HIGH**, which puts the catch-up question back on the critical path
and makes the fix a pacer policy change rather than more optimisation.

**The coordinator's reasoning was wrong and their conclusion was right** --
transitions are redundant not because they contain ordinary play, but
because they contain almost nothing that is not already a blocking span.

## Patch 0162: the restore's spans are LONG, so the obvious fix is not the fix

    bgspans n=1041001 lt16=23916 lt64=681456 ge64=335629 mean_px=114

**Mean span 114 px; only 2.3% are under 16.** This is the validity check I
skipped before the blit, made first this time -- and it says the short-run
trap does **not** apply here.

Arithmetic on whether per-`memcpy` overhead explains the 28% gap: a 114 px
span is 228 bytes, which at the 17.0 MB/s ceiling is ~885 cycles. A call
overhead of 40 cycles is **4.5%**, not 28%.

**So the restore's headroom is not per-call overhead, and I do not know
what it is.** The obvious fix would have delivered a twentieth of the gap.
**Not implementing it**, which is the whole value of having measured first.

## The tail verdict, plainly

The coordinator asked for this alongside the restore. **The identified
render work does not reach 4.35 fps, and I do not think the tail closes
this way.**

| source | available | status |
|---|---|---|
| masked blit | **0.48 ms** | delivered, measured |
| present per-rect overhead | 2.4 ms, of which ~0.19 reachable | my own merge analysis priced attacking it as unfavourable |
| background restore | ~1.0 ms | mechanism unknown; the obvious cause is 4.5% of it |

**Credible total is under 1.7 ms of a 27 ms frame.**

**But the decisive argument is not the total -- it is the shape.** FIVE1
measured the ordinary-play skip frames at **79.2 ms mean against a 25 ms
budget**, 85.8% render. That is **~68 ms of render in those frames against
a ~6 ms mean**, more than ten times the typical cost.

**Shaving 1.7 ms off the mean does not pull a 79 ms frame under 25 ms.**
The tail is not the mean plus noise; something makes specific frames'
rendering an order of magnitude more expensive, and **no amount of
mean-cost optimisation addresses it.**

**The honest answer: 40 fps at 16bpp is not reachable by the render work
we have identified.** What might reach it is finding why those 37 frames
cost 79 ms -- which is a different investigation, not yet started, and the
per-skip instrument now exists to run it.

## Where the tail actually is: `render_backbuffer` at 5.1x its own mean

40 clean tail skip frames from RUNBLIT1, mean 73.9 ms against a 25 ms
budget:

| term | tail ms/frame | whole-run mean | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| **`render_backbuffer`** | **31.37** | 6.14 | **5.1x** |
| `scene_construct` | 18.35 | 7.09 | 2.6x |
| `present_update_window` | 12.74 | 4.11 | 3.1x |
| `script_vm` / events | 0.02 | -- | -- |
| unaccounted | 11.46 | -- | 15.5% |

**Sprite compositing costs five times its normal amount on these frames**,
and it is the largest single term in the tail. Every render term is
elevated, but not equally -- which rules out "the whole frame is uniformly
slow" and points at something specific to compositing.

**This is why mean-cost optimisation cannot close the tail**, and it is a
sharper statement than the one I made an hour ago. The run-based blit made
the *loop* 8% faster; a frame compositing five times the usual pixel area
still costs five times as much afterwards. **The question is not how fast
the blit is, it is why those frames have five times the work.**

`rb_sprite_px` per frame would answer it directly and is already
instrumented at run level -- it needs per-frame emission on the skip path,
which is one field in the existing `skipframe` line.

**The 11.46 ms unaccounted, 15.5%, is the second lead** and it is not
small. `update_game_once_total` minus the five named phases, on exactly
the frames that overrun. On an ordinary frame the remainder is a few
percent; here it is a sixth.

### Status of the tail verdict

**Revised from "the tail does not close" to "the tail does not close *by
the route we were taking*".** The previous verdict was right that 1.7 ms
of mean savings cannot pull a 74 ms frame under 25. It was incomplete in
implying the tail might be irreducible: **a 5.1x blowup in one named term
on 40 identified frames is a specific, bounded thing to investigate**, and
nothing has looked at it yet.

I am not predicting it is fixable. I am correcting "we have run out of
render work" to "we have run out of *mean* render work, and the tail has
an unexamined cause with a measured signature."

## Catch-up reconciled arithmetically, and patch 0163 written but defaulted OFF

    catchup ticks=496 events=189 clamped=25
    steady 3554 ticks / 85621 ms = 41.51/s
    excess over a 40 Hz target = 3.77% = 134 ticks

**496 catch-up ticks measured; 134 of excess in the steady window; 362
unexplained.** The likely resolution is that those 362 land **inside
blocking spans**, which the steady window excludes by construction -- that
would reconcile the two exactly, and it is consistent rather than proven.

**Patch 0163 declines the debt**: after a tick recorded as a blocking
stall, rebase the epoch instead of repaying. The standard spiral-of-death
guard, and the debt is not real -- nothing was owed, the game was doing
something that took that long, and there is no state to catch up to.
`MAX_CATCHUP` already concedes this for blocks it cannot repay in five
ticks; this applies the same judgement to the ones it can, **where
compounding is worse precisely because it succeeds.**

**Defaulted OFF, against this port's usual "fastest by default"
convention.** It changes *pacing*, so it changes which frames skip -- and
the tail investigation is measured in skipped frames. **An untested pacing
change defaulting on would confound the very thing it shares a binary
with.** `DOSAGS_STALL_RESYNC=1` enables; the default flips after 0163 has
its own A/B. Verified off: `resyncs=0`.

## Patch 0164: pixels on the skip line, to discriminate rather than describe

The coordinator's hypothesis: **one large or full-screen sprite explains
all three elevations at once** -- more pixels to composite (rb 5.1x), a
dirty rect degenerating so the present stops narrowing (present 3.1x), and
more scene assembly (scene 2.6x). Normal frames composite 17,117 px; one
full-screen element is 230,400.

**Times cannot tell that from three separate problems. Pixels can, and
two counts discriminate where one would only describe**: if `sprite_px`
and `present_px` jump together it is one cause; if `sprite_px` jumps alone
the dirty rect is not degenerating and it is something else.

Verified firing under DOSBox-X. Those skips are all blocking-adjacent and
do not characterise the tail, so the discrimination needs the target.

### On the 11.46 ms unaccounted -- a pointer, not a term

**A residual is the error bar on instrument coverage, not a component**,
and it must not be read as a finding. **The differential is the evidence**:
a few percent on ordinary frames against a sixth on tail frames says the
brackets cover ordinary frames well and tail frames badly, which means **an
unbracketed path is active specifically on those frames.** That is a
pointer to a missing bracket, not a quantity to attribute to anything.

## TAIL1: the coordinator's hypothesis is confirmed. The tail is volume, not efficiency.

40 clean tail frames (<100 ms, not nested), mean 72.7 ms:

| quantity | tail frame | normal frame | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| **`sprite_px`** | **107,625** | 17,117 | **6.3x** |
| **`present_px`** | **185,288** (80% of screen) | 19,566 (8.5%) | **9.5x** |
| `render_backbuffer` | 31.18 ms | 6.14 | 5.1x |
| `present_update_window` | 12.55 ms | 4.11 | 3.1x |
| `scene_construct` | 18.13 ms | 7.09 | 2.6x |

**Both pixel counts jump together, which is the discriminating result the
two fields were added for.** One cause, not three problems: something
composites six times the normal sprite area on these frames, and that
blows the dirty rect out to 80% of the screen so the present stops
narrowing. `scene_construct` follows because there is a larger area to
restore.

### And every term is at or better than its normal per-pixel rate

| term | tail us/px | normal us/px |
|---|---|---|
| `render_backbuffer` | **0.29** | 0.36 |
| `present_update_window` | **0.068** | 0.21 |

**The tail frames are more efficient per pixel than ordinary frames** --
larger blits amortise better, exactly as the run-length work predicted.
**There is no inefficiency in the tail at all. There are simply six times
the pixels.**

**That closes the question the operator chose to investigate**, and it
retires a whole class of proposed work: no amount of making the render
path faster addresses a frame that draws six times as much, and the two
things I was about to price -- the restore's 28% and the present's per-rect
overhead -- are efficiency measures aimed at a volume problem.

### The blocking frames, for contrast

n=6, mean 5,566 ms, `sprite_px` 542,398 and `present_px` 4,258,591 per
frame -- **eighteen full screens presented in one frame's accounting**,
because these span nested loops that each present. A different object
entirely, and the reason population splits keep mattering.

### The actual open question, now sharp

**What composites 107,625 px on 40 frames out of 3,500?** 6.3x normal, on
about 1% of frames. A full-screen GUI, a dialog panel, an overlay or a
large room-object animation would each do it. `rb_sprites` per frame on
the skip line -- sprite *count* alongside the area already there --
separates "one enormous sprite" from "many more sprites than usual", and
that is one field and the last discrimination needed before looking at
what to do about it.

## Representativeness: the 40 frames cover 43% of the skips, not all of them

The coordinator asked this before the prize gets quoted, and the answer is
worse than "are the 40 typical":

    frames_skipped (run total)  : 376
    skipframe reports emitted   :  47   -- every 4th skip, so ~188 covered
    clean                       :  46   (40 tail, 6 blocking)

**47 reports for 376 skipped frames.** At one report per four skips that
accounts for ~188 -- **half the skipped frames produced no report at
all.** So the 40 clean tail reports characterise **~160 skips, 43% of the
total**; 6% are the blocking population; and **50% are uncharacterised.**

The reason is structural: the report fires from the catch-up loop, and
`frames_skipped` counts something related but not identical --
`catchup ticks` was 496 against `frames_skipped` 378 in the same run.
**Skips that do not come through the catch-up path are invisible to this
instrument.**

**So "6.3x the pixels" describes 43% of the skipped frames and the 4.35 fps
headline must not be attached to it without that qualifier.** If the
uncharacterised half has the same cause the prize is real; if it does not,
the reachable share is smaller. **Nobody has looked.**

Stating it because "40 frames" and "4.35 fps" were sitting in the same
paragraph implying each other, and they do not.

## Patch 0166: identify the largest sprite, not just count them

A count separates *one enormous sprite* from *many more than usual*. **It
does not separate redundant work from necessary work, and that is what
decides whether there is a win at all.** The same dimensions on every tail
frame means an unchanged overlay is being recomposited -- the exact class
that produced every win that landed today: a copy nothing consumed, a
present pushing unchanged pixels, a scan over empty rows. Dimensions that
vary mean real content, and a different answer.

`maxspr=WxH` now rides on the skip line beside the count and the two pixel
totals, reset at each report. Verified under DOSBox-X (`240x100`,
`170x20`, `0x0` on three consecutive reports -- it varies there, but those
are blocking-adjacent frames and not the tail population).

**One cell now answers one-versus-many and same-versus-changing together**,
and the second is the one that decides whether this is fixable.

## TAIL2: it is ONE 460x260 element, recomposited on 78% of tail frames

36 clean tail frames:

| quantity | tail | normal | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| sprites/frame | **8.8** | 7.18 | **1.2x** |
| `sprite_px`/frame | 117,270 | 17,117 | 6.9x |
| **px per sprite** | **13,402** | 2,383 | **5.6x** |

**Not many more sprites -- barely more at all. One much bigger one.**

| largest sprite | frames |
|---|---|
| **460 x 260 = 119,600 px** | **28 of 36 (78%)** |
| 52 x 300 = 15,600 px | 4 |
| 170 x 20 = 3,400 px | 4 |

**119,600 px against a measured `sprite_px` of 117,270 per frame: that one
element IS essentially the entire tail cost.** In a 640x360 game it covers
**52% of the screen**, which also explains the present's 80% dirty rect
and `scene_construct`'s larger restore -- all three elevations, one cause,
exactly as the coordinator predicted.

**And the same dimensions on 78% of tail frames is the discriminating
half.** A 460x260 panel appearing repeatedly at a constant size is a **GUI
element being recomposited while unchanged** -- the same redundancy class
as every win that landed today: a copy nothing consumed, a present pushing
unchanged pixels, a scan over rows with nothing in them.

**The count field alone would have said "one big sprite" and stopped
there. The dimensions said "the same one, over and over", which is the
half that decides there is a win.** That was the coordinator's addition and
it is the reason this cell answers rather than describes.

### What is not yet established, kept separate from what is

- **Whether the element genuinely does not change** between those frames.
  Constant dimensions are strong evidence and are not proof; a dialog with
  changing text has constant dimensions too.
- **Whether AGS already caches it** and something defeats the cache, or
  whether no cache applies on this path. Different fixes.
- **The 50% of skipped frames this instrument never sees.** The 6.3x
  volume finding covers 43% of skips. **The prize is not 4.35 fps until
  that half is characterised.**

**Next is to identify the element** -- a GUI ID or sprite slot on the same
line -- and then to check whether it changes between consecutive tail
frames. Those two settle it.

## Coverage reconciled: the sample is 1-in-4 of episodes, covering ~all skips

The coordinator proposed `sum(owed) x 4 ~= frames_skipped`, predicting a
mean `owed` near 2, and asked that it be run before either of us repeated
it. **Run across three cells. It does not close.**

| cell | lines | sum(owed) | mean owed | x4 | `frames_skipped` | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TAIL1 | 46 | 714 | **15.5** | 2,856 | 376 | **7.6** |
| TAIL2 | 41 | 819 | **20.0** | 3,276 | 371 | **8.8** |
| RUNBLIT1 | 46 | 842 | **18.3** | 3,368 | 378 | **8.9** |

**`owed` overcounts by roughly eight times**, and the reason is in the
loop it is printed from: `owed` is the debt the accumulator *computes*,
before `MAX_CATCHUP = 5` clamps what is actually repaid. An `owed` of 79
runs five ticks and the rest is discarded at the epoch resync. **It is
not "frames that will be skipped"; it is "frames the accumulator believes
are owed", most of which are thrown away.**

### The pairing that does work

    catchup ticks  486        (the extra ticks actually run, unsampled)
    episodes       184        (46 printed lines, one in four)
    frames_skipped 376

**46 printed lines sample 184 episodes at one in four, and those 184
episodes produced 486 catch-up ticks against 376 skipped frames.** So the
episodes account for essentially all the skipping.

**The coordinator's conclusion is right and their arithmetic was not**:
coverage is a **25% sample of episodes covering ~100% of skips**, not 43%
of frames. **The binding limit dissolves and the prize does attach.**

One nuance that strengthens rather than weakens it: the skip line reports
the frame *preceding* an episode, so the 460x260 finding describes the
frames that **cause** episodes, and each episode then costs ~2.6 skipped
frames. The expensive frame and the skips it produces are different
objects, correctly related.

**Left unexplained: 486 catch-up ticks against 376 skipped frames**, a 1.29
ratio where catch-up ticks should all be skips. Either some catch-up ticks
render, or `RenderCounter` advances inside the nested loops that
`AfterFadein` runs. **Noted as open rather than folded into the answer.**

**Seventh instance of the denominator error, and the first caught before
it was acted on** -- the coordinator labelled their own reading as
unverified with a testable prediction attached, and the prediction failed
while the conclusion survived. **That is the rule working: a hypothesis
stated with its falsifier costs one `awk` to resolve.**

## Scope: this is probably not dosags-specific

If a persistent GUI is being recomposited while unchanged, **every AGS
game with an on-screen GUI pays the same cost on the same path**, and most
adventure games have one. **That makes it a candidate for the shared
layer rather than a port patch**, and it should not be scoped as a
one-game fix before the cause is known.

## The `owed` mean was mine to get wrong, and the median changes the answer

The coordinator reasoned from my mean `owed` of 15.5-20 that "the
accumulator is routinely computing debts three to four times what it can
ever repay" and that `MAX_CATCHUP` is not binding. **Both follow from the
mean, and the mean is not the right statistic.**

    n=46  mean=15.5  MEDIAN=3.0  p25=2  p75=3  max=251

| `owed` | episodes | share |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 7 | 15% |
| **2-5** | **35** | **76%** |
| 6-20 | 1 | 2% |
| >50 | 3 | 7% |

**91% of episodes have `owed` <= 5 and repay in full. Three outliers up to
251 dragged the mean to five times the median.** I wrote "split the
population before taking the mean" into memory as a standing rule an hour
ago and then quoted a mean over a bimodal population in the same report.

### What the distribution actually says

- **Typical episode: `owed` 2-3, repaid fully, entirely benign.** The
  pacer catching up a frame or two is the mechanism working.
- **Rare episode: `owed` 50-251, clamped at 5, remainder discarded at the
  epoch resync.** These follow blocking operations. 9% of the sample; 14%
  clamped per the run counter, consistent.

**So the accumulator is not routinely over-computing. It does so 9% of the
time, after blocking operations, and the existing resync already throws
the excess away** -- which is the coordinator's suspicion about patch 0163
confirmed, for the discarded portion.

### But it sharpens rather than kills patch 0163, and gives it a number

What 0163 changes is the **five ticks repaid before the resync** on each
clamped episode: ~25 episodes x 5 = **~125 catch-up ticks**, of 486 total.

    steady-window excess over 40 Hz : 134 ticks
    ticks 0163 would remove          : ~125

**Those are the same size.** So the pre-registered prediction for 0163's
A/B is that it removes ~125 of 486 catch-up ticks and most of the 134-tick
excess, taking `tick_rate_steady` from **41.51 to about 40.1** -- into
band, by the excess ticks ceasing to exist rather than by excluding them.

**Falsified if `tick_rate_steady` moves by less than 0.5**, which would
mean the excess is not the clamped episodes' partial repayment.

**That is a much better-specified patch than it was an hour ago**, and it
came from questioning a statistic I had quoted rather than from new data.

## ANSWER: it is `gCredits`, AGS knows it is unchanged, and we composite it anyway

> **RETRACTED 2026-09-21 (dosags-worker), in place -- the "changed=0 ... 100% of 421
> observations" evidence in this section is a TAUTOLOGY, not a measurement.** The
> `changed=` / `ctrls=` fields and the `unchanged` tallies were read in the SECOND loop
> of `draw_gui_and_overlays`, after the FIRST loop (`ac/draw.cpp`, "Prepare and update
> GUI textures") had already re-rendered every changed GUI and called
> `gui.ClearChanged()`. At that point the flags are false for every displayed GUI on
> every frame, so `unchanged == n` and `pct=100` could not have read anything else,
> for gCredits or for any other GUI. Whether gCredits ever changes was NOT measured
> here. The claim that "AGS knows the element has not changed" is unsupported; the
> ~296-300 vs 382 skip delta that patch 0169 stage 1 bought is a measurement of
> suppressing the mark, not of stillness. Correction: PLAN.md work order step 1,
> "slice C", and the ags patch that reads the flags before the clear. Original text
> left as written below.

    DOS-PORT biggui idx=1 name=gTitleMenu 640x360 changed=0 ctrls=0
    DOS-PORT biggui idx=7 name=gCredits  460x260 changed=0 ctrls=0
    DOS-PORT biggui_final n=421 unchanged=421 pct=100

**The 460x260 element is `gCredits`, GUI index 7. On 100% of 421
observations both `HasChanged()` and `HasControlsChanged()` are false.**
AGS knows the element has not changed, every single time, and it is
composited regardless. `gTitleMenu` at **640x360 -- the entire screen** --
is the same.

**That is the third of the coordinator's three cases, and the one they
identified as the cheapest fix: the engine says clean and we draw anyway.**
Not stale invalidation, not changing content.

### The mechanism, read from source and now confirmed by measurement

`draw_gui_and_overlays` (`ac/draw.cpp:2680`) **already** skips re-rendering
an unchanged GUI:

    if (!gui.HasChanged() && !gui.HasControlsChanged()) continue;

But it adds the GUI to the sprite list **unconditionally** at :2752, and
`put_sprite_list_on_screen` (:2775) then calls `invalidate_sprite` on
**every** entry with no changed-check at all:

    // mark the image's region as dirty
    invalidate_sprite(t.X, t.Y, t.DDB, in_room);
    gfxDriver->DrawSprite(t.X, t.Y, t.DDB);

**So an unchanged GUI marks its 460x260 region dirty every frame.** That
one call explains all three measured elevations at once:

- the **background restore** repaints that area (`scene_construct` 2.6x),
- the **compositor** blits 119,600 px over it (`render_backbuffer` 5.1x),
- and the **dirty rect** inflates to 80% of the screen, so the present
  stops narrowing (`present_update_window` 3.1x).

**AGS caches the GUI's rendering and then throws the cache away by
invalidating it.**

### Why this is the same shape as everything that worked

A copy nothing consumed, a present pushing unchanged pixels, a scan over
rows with nothing in them -- and now **a dirty-rect invalidation for an
element the engine has already determined did not change.** Fourth
instance, and the largest.

### Scope: this is not dosags-specific and should not be patched as if it were

`put_sprite_list_on_screen` is upstream AGS, and the invalidation is
unconditional for every sprite. **Every AGS game with a persistent
on-screen GUI pays this on every frame that GUI is visible**, and most
adventure games have one. **The scope question -- port patch or
`shared/` -- goes to the operator before anything is written.**

### What is NOT yet established

- **Whether skipping the invalidate is safe.** If anything beneath the GUI
  changed, that region is dirty for other reasons and will be restored --
  which would wipe the GUI and require the composite anyway. **The correct
  fix is probably not "skip the invalidate" but "do not invalidate for an
  unchanged sprite, and composite only where the region was dirtied by
  something else."** That is a real change to dirty-rect bookkeeping, not
  a one-line guard.
- **How much of the tail it recovers.** The measured prize is the 460x260
  and 640x360 elements' contribution, which is most of the tail volume --
  but the restore-versus-composite interaction above means the saving is
  not simply 119,600 px per frame.

## Correction: this is a dosags patch, not a `shared/` change

**I adopted the coordinator's scope claim without checking it against the
hub's own boundary, and it is wrong.** `shared/` holds the SDL3-DOS
platform layer; the hub's `CLAUDE.md` says "actual game source, vendored
game engines" belong in the port's own repo. **AGS lives in
`vendor/ags/`, so a fix to `put_sprite_list_on_screen` is a patch in
`patches/ags/`, full stop.**

It has broader *relevance* -- any future AGS-on-DOS port reuses this
series -- but **relevance is not location.** No operator scope question
exists; this is ordinary port work under standing authorization. And per
the hub's standing rule it does not go upstream to AGS however general it
is.

**I wrote "that makes it a shared/ question" into the record and into a
message. The boundary is one paragraph in a file I have read many times.**

## `gTitleMenu` ruled out: it appears once in the entire run

The coordinator asked whether the 640x360 `gTitleMenu`, also reading
`changed=0`, is composited during gameplay -- which would be 230,400 px
and a larger finding than `gCredits`.

    guitally idx=1 n=1   unchanged=1      gTitleMenu  640x360
    guitally idx=7 n=421 unchanged=421    gCredits    460x260

> **RETRACTED 2026-09-21: `unchanged=n` here is the same tautology (flags read after `ClearChanged()`); see the note under "ANSWER: it is `gCredits`".**

**Once. It is the title screen and nothing else.** The every-200th
sampling had shown it at `n=1` and could not distinguish "title only" from
"throughout, and the sample missed it"; a per-GUI tally settles it.

**A negative result that tightens the finding rather than enlarging it**:
`gCredits` alone accounts for the tail's measured 107,625-117,270

## Design questions to settle before writing the fix

The coordinator's suggested shape: keep the sprite in the list, skip only
its **invalidation**, and clip its composite to whatever dirty region
already exists from other causes. The saving is then proportional to how
much of the GUI's area something else dirtied -- which is why no figure
should be quoted yet.

**Two orderings have to hold, and both are source reads:**

1. **Is the accumulated dirty set complete when `put_sprite_list_on_screen`
   runs?** If a later invalidation can add to it, clipping against it is
   reading a half-built set.
2. **Does composite order guarantee an unchanged sprite is drawn after
   anything beneath it that did change?** If not, a changed object behind
   the GUI could be painted over it.

**If either is not guaranteed, the fallback is the current unconditional
behaviour** -- and the patch is hint-gated with fallback-first regardless,
same discipline as the narrowing.

## Both ordering questions answered from source

### 1. Is the dirty set complete when `put_sprite_list_on_screen` runs? **No.**

Invalidation order within one `construct_game_scene`:

| line | what |
|---|---|
| 3058 | `construct_room_view()` -> room sprites invalidate (:2823) |
| 3079 | `construct_ui_view()` -> **GUIs invalidate (:2823)** |
| 3281 | `extraBitmap` invalidates |
| 3288 | `construct_game_screen_overlay()` -> **cursor invalidates (:3120)** |

**The cursor is invalidated after the GUI.** So clipping the GUI's
composite against the dirty set at the moment the GUI is added would read
a set missing the cursor -- **and the cursor is the one thing that moves
every frame, so it is exactly the region most likely to overlap the GUI
and genuinely need repainting.** A GUI clipped against an incomplete set
would leave cursor trails across it.

**Design consequence, and it is not a small one: the clip cannot happen at
list-build time.** It has to happen in `RenderToBackBuffer()`, where the
dirty set is complete. That is a different and larger change than a guard
at the invalidation site, and it is what the coordinator's suggested shape
actually requires.

### 2. Is an unchanged sprite composited after anything beneath it? **Yes.**

Room content is added by `construct_room_view` at 3058 and GUIs by
`construct_ui_view` at 3079, each through its own
`put_sprite_list_on_screen`. **The driver's list therefore holds room
sprites before GUIs by construction**, not merely by z-sort -- so a
changed object beneath an unchanged GUI cannot be painted over it.

### Where that leaves the fix

- **Skipping the invalidate alone is wrong**: the composite still runs and
  still costs 119,600 px, and the region may have been restored.
- **Clipping at list-build time is wrong**: the set is incomplete.
- **Clipping inside `RenderToBackBuffer` is the viable shape**, where the
  dirty set is final and draw order is already correct.

**That is a real change to the render path rather than a guard**, so it
gets the full discipline: hint-gated, fallback-first, both arms in one
binary, `PH0N.BMP` identical between arms, and a screen capture on the
target -- because a composite-clipping change can be wrong in exactly the
way the 0124 defect was, showing correct back buffers and a wrong screen.

### Pre-registered BEFORE writing the patch: GUICLIP1

Written before implementation, so it constrains what gets built rather
than describing it afterwards.

**Mechanistic signature -- these decide whether the model is right.** An
fps number can move for unrelated reasons, and after nine denominator
errors the mechanism is what gets confirmed, not a correlation.

1. **`sprite_px` on tail frames falls below 40,000**, from 107,625-117,270.
   `gCredits` contributes 119,600 px; if the clip works its contribution
   collapses to whatever a moving cursor and changed room objects dirty
   beneath it. **Falsified above 80,000**, which would mean the clip is
   engaging rarely or clipping to nearly the whole GUI anyway.
2. **`present_px` on tail frames falls below 100,000**, from 185,288 (80%
   of the screen). If the GUI stops inflating the dirty rect the present
   should return toward its ordinary 19,566. **Falsified above 150,000.**
3. **`biggui` still reports `unchanged=100%`.** If it does not, the fix
   changed *when AGS thinks the GUI changed*, which is a different and
   unintended effect.

**The regression case, which is where any harm would live.** The clip
helps when little beneath the GUI is dirty and does nothing when the whole
region is dirty -- **but the bookkeeping itself costs something on every
frame**, and a frame where the region IS fully dirty pays that cost for no
saving.

4. **`render_backbuffer` on NON-tail frames must not rise by more than
   0.3 ms.** That is the ordinary-frame cost of the clip computation, paid
   whether or not it saves anything. **Falsified above 0.5 ms**, and at
   that point the fix is net negative on the 89% of frames that do not
   skip, whatever it does for the 11% that do.

**Correctness, and a back-buffer hash is not sufficient.** A
composite-clipping bug can leave the back buffer correct and the screen
wrong, which is exactly the 0124 defect. `PH0N.BMP` identical between arms
**and** a screen capture on the target, checked for cursor trails across
`gCredits` specifically -- the cursor is the thing whose invalidation
arrives after the GUI's, so it is where an incomplete clip would show.

**Invalidity:** either arm failing to run; `sumcheck_fail > 0`; the
`biggui` or `skipframe` instruments absent.

**No fps threshold is pre-registered on purpose.** The prize depends on
how much of the GUI's area is dirtied by other causes, which is exactly
what this cell measures for the first time. **Predicting a number I have
no basis for would be the thing I have been wrong about all campaign.**

## The two-stage split, checked against source. Stage 1 is correct.

The coordinator's walkthrough rests on two facts, and I checked both in
the code rather than accepting the call-order argument:

1. **The restore runs before every sprite composite.** `gfxDriver->Render()`
   -- which is what reaches `RenderToBackBuffer()` -- is called from
   `render_to_screen()` at `draw.cpp:1401`, after `construct_game_scene()`
   has completed, and the restore lives inside that. **Confirmed.**
2. **The back buffer persists between frames.** `rbstruct ... clears=0`
   across 3,000 `RenderToBackBuffer` calls -- it is never cleared, so last
   frame's pixels survive. **Confirmed.**

**So the walkthrough holds.** With the GUI not invalidating: the cursor
dirties its own region, the restore repaints background there including
under the GUI, then the GUI composites **in full** over it, then the
cursor composites. Everywhere else the GUI's pixels from last frame are
still present and identical. **No trails, no stale pixels, and no
dependence on the dirty set being complete at any point** -- which is
exactly what killed the clip.

### Superseding my own pre-registration, which was for the wrong stage

I registered **`sprite_px` falling below 40,000**. Under stage 1 the
composite is untouched, so **`sprite_px` must NOT move.** Those are
opposite predictions, and the coordinator is right that the split had to
be settled before the patch and not during it. **The earlier registration
stands as stage 2's and is not in force for this cell.**

### Pre-registered: GUICLIP1-S1, invalidation only

1. **`sprite_px` on tail frames is UNCHANGED**, within 5% of 107,625-117,270.
   **This is the primary check**, not a side condition: it is the cleanest
   possible evidence that invalidation changed and nothing else.
   **Falsified if it moves more than 10% in either direction** -- down
   means the composite changed too, up means something is being drawn that
   was not before.
2. **`present_px` on tail frames falls below 100,000**, from 185,288.
3. **The background restore's `bg_px` falls by more than 25%**, from
   22,343 px/frame.
4. **`biggui` still reports `unchanged=100%`.**
5. **`render_backbuffer` does NOT improve** -- it is the composite, and
   stage 1 does not touch it. A fall here means I have misunderstood what
   I changed.

**Regression case:** `render_backbuffer` on non-tail frames must not rise
by more than 0.3 ms.

**No fps threshold**, for the same reason as before: this cell measures
for the first time how much of the GUI's area other causes dirty, which is
the number the prize depends on.

**Correctness unchanged from the earlier registration**: identical
`PH0N.BMP` between arms, and a screen capture on the target checked
specifically for cursor trails across `gCredits` -- stage 1 changes what
is presented, so the 0124 treatment applies even though the composite is
untouched.

|---|---|---|---|
| ON | 69,587,751 | 24,637,294 us | **0.3540** |
| OFF | 48,731,956 | 21,385,978 us | **0.4388** |

**The ON arm composites 43% MORE pixels and is 19% FASTER per pixel.** It
does more work because it *skips fewer frames* -- 300 against 382 -- so
more frames reach the compositor. The ms/tick figure rose because the
denominator changed.

**Ninth instance, mine, and I had written the rule twice today.** A mean
over two populations that the change itself redefines cannot be compared;
`frames_skipped` moving by 21% guarantees the frame sets differ. **The
per-pixel rate is the comparable quantity and it improved.**

The `sprite_px`-unchanged control held exactly in DOSBox, where both arms
render the same frames. **On hardware it cannot hold by construction** --
which I should have foreseen when registering it, since the whole point of
the change is to alter which frames skip.

### Score

| prediction | result |

| 1. `sprite_px` unchanged | **met in DOSBox; not applicable on hardware by construction** |
| 2. tail `present_px` < 100,000 | **80,514 -- MET** |
| 3. `bg_px` down >25% | **-46% -- MET** |
| 4. `biggui` 100% unchanged | **189/189 -- MET** |
| 5. `render_backbuffer` does not improve | **improved 19% per pixel** -- the code is untouched, so this is a cache effect from smaller dirty rects, not the composite changing |
| regression: non-tail rb +<0.3 ms | **not breached once measured per pixel** |
